keyConcepts.title: How the shaft is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
Wherever a rotating shaft passes through a stationary casing there must be a running clearance, and that clearance is a leakage path for the pumped liquid. Shaft sealing controls this path. On this pump the shaft runs inside replaceable sleeves where it passes through the casing, so wear and corrosion affect the sleeves rather than the shaft.

Two arrangements are used, one or the other at both ends. Compression packing fills the stuffing box with rings squeezed by a gland follower; it throttles leakage but must leak slightly to lubricate and cool itself. A mechanical seal uses two flat faces, one rotating and one stationary, held together by springs and liquid pressure; the leakage is very small and often leaves as vapour. Mechanical seals may be single or dual, component or cartridge, and in some cases split for easy replacement.

The stuffing box or seal chamber at each end is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. Supporting systems include the seal flush or packing seal water, venting of the chamber, and, outside the seal, shaft deflectors (flingers) that throw any leakage clear of the bearing housings.

Shaft sealing is different from bearing housing sealing. The shaft seal keeps the pumped liquid in the casing; the bearing housing seals (lip seals or isolators) keep lubricant in the bearing housings and contaminants out. Both matter, because shaft seal leakage that reaches the bearing housing contaminates the lubricant.

keyConcepts.title: Why two sealing locations are required
keyConcepts.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.

Caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

keyConcepts.title: Mechanical seal versus gland packing
keyConcepts.body:
Both arrangements are legitimate and widely used on split case pumps; each has trade-offs.

Leakage: packing must leak continuously to stay cool and lubricated. A mechanical seal's leakage is very small and often not visible. Where the pumped liquid is hazardous, valuable or environmentally harmful, a mechanical seal, often a dual seal, is normally required.

Power and wear: packing rubs on the sleeve and absorbs more power, and over time it grooves the sleeve. A mechanical seal absorbs less power and the sleeve wears little, although pusher seals can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.

Maintenance: packing needs periodic gland adjustment and repacking, but in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. A mechanical seal needs little routine attention, but replacing it usually means removing the coupling spacer and the bearing housing, or lifting the rotor, unless a split or cartridge design simplifies the job.

Tolerance: packing tolerates shaft movement, brief dry periods and poor conditions better, and fails gradually by leaking more. Mechanical seals are sensitive to dry running, vibration, misalignment and poor flush, and can fail suddenly.

Cost and skills: packing is cheaper to buy; mechanical seals often cost less over their life once leakage, water use, power and sleeve wear are counted, but they need careful installation.

The choice depends on the liquid, environmental and safety requirements, site practice and life-cycle cost.

keyConcepts.title: Seal face contact and the fluid film
keyConcepts.body:
The primary seal of a mechanical seal is the interface between two flat, smooth faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary. The faces are lapped to extreme flatness, checked optically in light bands with an optical flat, because any waviness opens a leakage path or causes local contact.

Between the faces a very thin film of the sealed liquid lubricates and partly separates them. In many liquid applications the faces run in a mixed regime, partly supported by the film and partly in light contact. The film is what keeps friction, heat and wear acceptable; without it the faces run dry.

The faces are pushed together by the closing force, which is the spring force plus the liquid pressure acting on the closing area behind the flexible face. The film pressure between the faces pushes them apart. The net load divided by the face area is the face pressure, which governs film thickness, heat generation, leakage and wear. The balance ratio compares the hydraulic closing area with the face area. In an unbalanced seal, face pressure rises steeply with sealed pressure; a balanced seal uses a stepped sleeve or seal geometry to reduce the closing area so that face pressure rises more slowly, suiting higher pressures. Actual balance ratios and face pressures are design values of the seal manufacturer.

Anything that disturbs the faces, such as distortion from uneven gland tightening, thermal gradients, vibration, shaft runout or dry running, upsets the film and shortens seal life.

Caution: Dry running destroys the fluid film and can damage seal faces very quickly. Never run a mechanically sealed pump without liquid, even to check rotation.

mech-seal-de.summary: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
mech-seal-de.function: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
mech-seal-de.operatingPrinciple: Two very flat faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary in the gland plate, are pressed together by spring force and by the liquid pressure in the seal chamber. A thin fluid film between the faces lubricates and cools them while restricting leakage. Elastomer secondary seals seal each face to its mounting, and the springs keep the faces closed as they wear and as the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
mech-seal-de.construction: Baseline: a single, spring-loaded component seal. The rotating unit (rotating face, springs, shaft-side secondary seal and retainer or drive collar) is mounted on the shaft sleeve. The stationary face (seat) is held in a gland plate bolted to the face of the seal chamber, which is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. A flush connection supplies liquid to the chamber. Many pumps instead use cartridge seals, which arrive pre-assembled on their own sleeve and gland with the setting fixed by the seal manufacturer.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Shaft seals are one of the most frequent reasons for unplanned pump maintenance. Most seal failures are caused by operating and installation conditions, such as dry running, loss of flush, operation far from the best efficiency point, vibration, misalignment and incorrect fitting, rather than by a defect in the seal itself.

keyConcepts.title: How the shaft is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
Wherever a rotating shaft passes through a stationary casing there must be a running clearance, and that clearance is a leakage path for the pumped liquid. Shaft sealing controls this path. On this pump the shaft runs inside replaceable sleeves where it passes through the casing, so wear and corrosion affect the sleeves rather than the shaft.

Two arrangements are used, one or the other at both ends. Compression packing fills the stuffing box with rings squeezed by a gland follower; it throttles leakage but must leak slightly to lubricate and cool itself. A mechanical seal uses two flat faces, one rotating and one stationary, held together by springs and liquid pressure; the leakage is very small and often leaves as vapour. Mechanical seals may be single or dual, component or cartridge, and in some cases split for easy replacement.

The stuffing box or seal chamber at each end is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. Supporting systems include the seal flush or packing seal water, venting of the chamber, and, outside the seal, shaft deflectors (flingers) that throw any leakage clear of the bearing housings.

Shaft sealing is different from bearing housing sealing. The shaft seal keeps the pumped liquid in the casing; the bearing housing seals (lip seals or isolators) keep lubricant in the bearing housings and contaminants out. Both matter, because shaft seal leakage that reaches the bearing housing contaminates the lubricant.

keyConcepts.title: Why two sealing locations are required
keyConcepts.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.

Caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

keyConcepts.title: Mechanical seal versus gland packing
keyConcepts.body:
Both arrangements are legitimate and widely used on split case pumps; each has trade-offs.

Leakage: packing must leak continuously to stay cool and lubricated. A mechanical seal's leakage is very small and often not visible. Where the pumped liquid is hazardous, valuable or environmentally harmful, a mechanical seal, often a dual seal, is normally required.

Power and wear: packing rubs on the sleeve and absorbs more power, and over time it grooves the sleeve. A mechanical seal absorbs less power and the sleeve wears little, although pusher seals can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.

Maintenance: packing needs periodic gland adjustment and repacking, but in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. A mechanical seal needs little routine attention, but replacing it usually means removing the coupling spacer and the bearing housing, or lifting the rotor, unless a split or cartridge design simplifies the job.

Tolerance: packing tolerates shaft movement, brief dry periods and poor conditions better, and fails gradually by leaking more. Mechanical seals are sensitive to dry running, vibration, misalignment and poor flush, and can fail suddenly.

Cost and skills: packing is cheaper to buy; mechanical seals often cost less over their life once leakage, water use, power and sleeve wear are counted, but they need careful installation.

The choice depends on the liquid, environmental and safety requirements, site practice and life-cycle cost.

keyConcepts.title: Leakage control
keyConcepts.body:
Packing and mechanical seals control leakage in fundamentally different ways.

Packing works by throttling, and it needs a controlled leakage: the liquid passing along the sleeve lubricates the packing and carries away frictional heat. The gland follower is adjusted to give the leakage rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends. Tightening to stop the leak completely makes the packing overheat, harden and burn, scores the sleeve, raises power absorption and eventually leads to more leakage, not less. New packing is started with generous leakage and taken up gradually as it beds in. Adjust the nuts evenly in small steps and allow time between adjustments.

A mechanical seal has very small leakage across its faces, much of which evaporates and is not visible. A steady visible drip generally indicates a problem, although some seals show slight leakage while bedding in; the seal manufacturer states what is acceptable. Rising leakage over time shows face wear, damage or a secondary seal problem.

In both cases, leakage must be collected and drained safely, for example to a gland drain or the baseplate drain rim, especially where the liquid is hot, hazardous or slippery, and it must be kept away from the bearing housings, where shaft deflectors and housing seals provide protection. Under suction lift, a sealing point can leak air in rather than liquid out; reduced performance or noise may be the only sign.

Caution: Gland adjustment on a running pump puts hands close to the rotating shaft and coupling. Do it only where the site procedure permits, with all guards fitted and loose clothing and tools kept clear.

mech-seal-nde.summary: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
mech-seal-nde.function: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
mech-seal-nde.operatingPrinciple: Two very flat faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary in the gland plate, are pressed together by spring force and by the liquid pressure in the seal chamber. A thin fluid film between the faces lubricates and cools them while restricting leakage. Elastomer secondary seals seal each face to its mounting, and the springs keep the faces closed as they wear and as the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
mech-seal-nde.construction: Baseline: a single, spring-loaded component seal. The rotating unit (rotating face, springs, shaft-side secondary seal and retainer or drive collar) is mounted on the shaft sleeve. The stationary face (seat) is held in a gland plate bolted to the face of the seal chamber, which is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. A flush connection supplies liquid to the chamber. Many pumps instead use cartridge seals, which arrive pre-assembled on their own sleeve and gland with the setting fixed by the seal manufacturer.

The shaft seal keeps the pumped liquid in the casing; the bearing housing seals (lip seals or isolators) keep lubricant in the bearing housings and contaminants out. Both matter, because shaft seal leakage that reaches the bearing housing contaminates the lubricant.

keyConcepts.title: Why two sealing locations are required
keyConcepts.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.

Caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission
keyConcepts.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

The torque path runs from the motor rotor through the motor shaft, the motor key and hub, the first flexible element, the spacer, the second flexible element, the pump hub and key, and into the pump shaft, which carries it to the impeller. Keys transmit torque through shear and bearing pressure on their sides; in some designs hubs are mounted by an interference fit that carries torque by friction, with or without a key.

The coupling must carry the steady operating torque and also transient torques. A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

Coupling size, type, bore fits and fastener tightening values come from the coupling manufacturer and the OEM. A coupling that has been under-selected, or assembled with the wrong bolts, can fail suddenly, which is one reason the guard must always be in place.

keyConcepts.title: What a flexible coupling does
keyConcepts.body:
A flexible coupling transmits torque while accommodating small amounts of angular, parallel and axial misalignment between two shafts. Some types also damp torsional vibration and shock. It cannot make poor alignment harmless: misalignment still produces reaction forces and moments on the bearings, wears or fatigues the flexible element, and causes vibration and heat. The coupling's misalignment capacity is for small changes in service, such as thermal growth and settling, not for installation errors.

A spacer coupling has two flexible planes separated by a spacer. This lets it take parallel offset as a small angle at each plane, and removing the spacer gives access to the drive-end seal and bearing housing, or allows the rotor to be lifted out, without moving the motor.

Common element types differ in important ways. Elastomeric couplings (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) are tolerant and damp vibration, but the elements age and wear, and some are not fail-safe if the element fails. Disc couplings use flexing stainless steel laminations; they need no lubrication and have low maintenance, but have limited misalignment capacity and definite axial stiffness, so their axial setting matters. Gear couplings carry high torque for their size, but need lubrication and can lock up and transmit axial force if the teeth wear or the lubricant fails. Grid couplings use a spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, offer some damping and need lubrication.

Allowable misalignment and service requirements are given in the coupling manufacturer's data.

keyConcepts.title: Angular misalignment
keyConcepts.body:
Angular misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines meet at an angle instead of lying on one straight line. It is usually described separately in the vertical and horizontal planes, and is commonly expressed as the difference in gap measured across the coupling face divided by the diameter at which it was measured, or as a slope.

As the shafts rotate, angular misalignment makes the flexible element bend back and forth once per revolution. In a spacer coupling the angle is taken at the two flexible planes. The effects include cyclic stress and wear in the element, extra reaction moments at the coupling-end bearings, heat in elastomeric elements, and vibration, typically with significant axial components at once and twice running speed.

Angularity in the vertical plane is corrected by changing the shims under the front and rear feet of the movable machine (normally the motor) by different amounts. Horizontal angularity is corrected by moving the front and rear of the movable machine sideways by different amounts, using the jacking screws. Because angular and parallel corrections interact, alignment calculations or alignment tools work out the moves needed at each foot.

Acceptable angular misalignment depends on speed and coupling type and must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Parallel (offset) misalignment
keyConcepts.body:
Parallel, or offset, misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines are parallel but displaced from each other. Like angularity, it is described in the vertical and horizontal planes and is measured at a stated position, usually at the coupling or at the flexible planes.

In a spacer coupling, offset is taken up as an angle at each flexible plane. For small angles that angle is approximately the offset divided by the distance between the flexible planes, so for the same offset a longer spacer gives a smaller angle at each element. Real installations normally have a combination of offset and angularity in both planes.

Offset causes radial forces on the coupling-end bearings and cyclic loading of the element, and typically shows as radial vibration at once and twice running speed. It also adds to seal and bearing problems through shaft deflection.

Vertical offset is corrected by adding or removing equal shim thickness under all feet of the movable machine. Horizontal offset is corrected by moving the whole movable machine sideways with the jacking screws.

Pump and motor shafts often grow by different amounts as they reach operating temperature, so the cold alignment target may deliberately include an offset that disappears when the machines are hot. Any such allowance must come from the OEM, and acceptable offset from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Coupling guard safety
keyConcepts.body:
Rotating couplings and shaft ends are among the most dangerous parts of a pump set. They can catch clothing, hair, gloves, rags or tools in a fraction of a second, causing entanglement, amputation or death. At operating speed a coupling can look blurred or almost stationary, which misleads people about the danger.

The coupling guard is a fixed guard: it is fastened so that it can only be removed with a tool, it covers the coupling and all exposed shaft between the bearing housing and the motor, and any openings are sized and placed so that fingers and hands cannot reach rotating parts. Machinery safety regulations and standards require such guarding; safety-distance standards such as ISO 13857 relate opening sizes to reach distances. In potentially explosive atmospheres, guard materials and clearances may also need to meet hazardous-area requirements so that contact cannot cause sparks.

Rules that apply on every site:

Never run the pump with the guard removed, open or damaged.

Remove the guard only after the driver has been electrically isolated and locked out under the permit system, and zero energy has been verified. Consider also that liquid flowing back through the pump can turn the rotor.

Refit and secure the guard before the isolation is removed and before any test run.

For an uncoupled motor rotation check, remove or secure the motor key and keep clear of the shaft end.

Check the guard on rounds for security, damage and rubbing marks.

Caution: The 3D viewer can hide or make the guard transparent for learning purposes. A real pump must never be operated without its guard fitted and secure.

keyConcepts.title: Importance of foundation stiffness
keyConcepts.body:
The foundation's job is to hold the pump and motor so steadily that alignment does not change and vibration is not amplified. It must carry the static weight of the machines, baseplate and liquid; react the torque between pump and motor; resist the dynamic forces from residual unbalance and hydraulic pulsation; and take any loads that the piping applies.

Stiffness and mass work together. A stiff, massive foundation deflects little under load, so the shafts stay aligned, and it raises the natural frequencies of the installed system. Ideally those natural frequencies are well separated from running speed and its main multiples, because operating near a resonance can turn a small force into large vibration. A flexible or lightweight foundation, or one standing on soft or settling ground, lets the baseplate move and the alignment drift.

The baseplate alone is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to the foundation so that both act as one body. Many installations isolate the foundation block from the surrounding floor slab with a joint, so that vibration is not passed to the building and other machines do not shake the pump.

Rules of thumb relating foundation mass to machine mass are often quoted, but foundation design should follow the OEM's loading data, the applicable guidance and the work of a civil or structural engineer.

keyConcepts.title: Grouting
keyConcepts.body:
Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation. When it is placed correctly it makes full contact with both surfaces, spreads the load, bonds the baseplate to the foundation so they behave as one stiff structure, adds damping and protects the underside of the baseplate.

The usual sequence is: prepare the foundation surface by removing the weak top layer to sound concrete and cleaning it; set the baseplate on its levelling screws or packers and level it as the OEM specifies; build formwork; prepare anchor bolt sleeves and protect the levelling screw threads; then place the grout through the grout holes, working from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, until the space is completely filled. The grout is then cured as its manufacturer specifies.

Epoxy grouts generally offer higher strength, better bond and better resistance to oil and chemicals, and cure quickly, but they are sensitive to temperature during placement and cure and are more expensive. Non-shrink cementitious grouts are cheaper and simpler to use but need careful curing, and they are attacked by oil over time.

After curing, the baseplate is tapped to find hollow-sounding voids, which are filled by injection as the grout manufacturer recommends. Only then are the anchor bolts tightened and, in many procedures, the levelling screws backed off so the grout carries the load. Alignment is then checked again.

Factory pre-grouted baseplates reduce the risk of voids under the deck but still need field grouting.

Caution: Grout materials, thicknesses, temperatures and curing times must come from the grout manufacturer, the OEM and the project specification.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment and the baseplate
keyConcepts.body:
Good shaft alignment depends on a good baseplate installation; the baseplate is the reference to which both machines are bolted.

Before grouting, the baseplate is levelled and its machined pads checked for flatness and co-planarity, against values from the OEM, using levelling screws or packers. If the pads are twisted or uneven, the machines will distort when they are bolted down, producing soft foot that no amount of alignment can correct. After grouting and anchor bolt tightening the pads are checked again, because grouting and bolting can shift the baseplate.

The pump is normally fixed first as the stationary machine, because the piping will be attached to it; its feet should sit on the pads with little or no shimming. The motor is the movable machine. Its pads are often slightly low so that it sits on a shim pack, allowing adjustment both up and down, and the jacking screws on the baseplate allow controlled sideways moves.

A typical sequence is: rough alignment before piping is connected; connection of piping without strain; checks for soft foot and pipe strain; precise alignment; and recording of the results. Some sites dowel the machines after final alignment. Alignment is re-checked after commissioning runs and whenever the baseplate, piping or foundation has been disturbed.

keyConcepts.title: Pipe strain
keyConcepts.body:
Pipe strain is the force and moment that the connected piping applies to the pump nozzles. It arises when flanges are pulled together that did not line up, when pipes and valves are not properly supported, when thermal expansion is not accommodated, and when expansion joints are left unrestrained.

In a split case pump, nozzle loads act on the lower casing half. Excessive loads can distort the casing, upsetting internal clearances and the split joint; shift the pump on its pads; and move the shaft out of alignment with the motor. The results are bearing overloading, seal failures, coupling wear, vibration and casing joint leaks. An unrestrained expansion joint is especially damaging, because the pressure inside it pushes on the pump with a force equal to the pressure times the joint's effective area.

Good practice is to support the pipes independently near the pump, so that the pump does not carry their weight; to make flanges meet squarely and concentrically, with the right gap, before any bolt is tightened; to restrain expansion joints with tie rods or anchors; and to make the final connection at the pump after the pipework is fixed. A practical check is to mount dial indicators on the coupling, or use the alignment system, and watch for movement while the flange bolts are tightened or loosened; significant movement shows strain that must be corrected in the piping, not by forcing the pump.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM.

Caution: Never use the pump as an anchor for the piping, and never pull misaligned flanges together with the bolts.

casing-upper.summary: The upper casing half is the top part of the pressure-containing volute casing.
casing-upper.function: The upper casing half is the top part of the pressure-containing volute casing. It closes the impeller chamber, the upper parts of the volute and suction chambers and the upper halves of both seal chambers, and it can be lifted off in one piece to give access to the complete rotor.
casing-upper.operatingPrinciple:
In operation it is a stationary pressure boundary. Internal pressure acting over its projected area tries to lift it off the lower half; this separating force is resisted by the preloaded joint studs and nuts, while the gasket (or sealing compound, depending on design) seals the joint.

Its internal surfaces form part of the hydraulic passages, so their shape and surface condition influence the velocity and pressure distribution around the impeller in the same way as the lower half.
casing-upper.construction: Typically a single casting with a machined flat split flange, clearance holes for the joint studs, dowel holes, the upper halves of the casing wear-ring bores and seal chamber bores, lifting lugs and vent connections. Bores that are split across the joint are usually finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together, so they are round and concentric only when the halves are correctly reassembled. In this baseline arrangement no suction or discharge piping is attached to the upper half.

inspection: With the half removed, inspect the joint face for nicks, erosion channels across the sealing land (wire drawing), corrosion and gasket residue, and clean it without scoring.

maintenance: Lift only with the designated lugs and rated lifting gear, keeping the half level and guided off the dowels so it cannot swing into the impeller or seals.
Repairs to a pressure-retaining casting must follow the OEM and site repair procedures.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Because both nozzles are on the lower half in this arrangement, the upper half can be removed for internal inspection without disconnecting the main piping or disturbing the motor. Its stiffness and the accuracy of its joint face govern how well the joint seals and how round the split bores remain, and therefore how well the wear rings and shaft seals perform. A crack or casting defect in it is a pressure-boundary defect.

keyConcepts.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
keyConcepts.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.

keyConcepts.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
keyConcepts.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.

Caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.

Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing geometry affects hydraulic performance
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller adds the energy, but the casing largely decides how much of it reaches the discharge flange and how smoothly the pump runs.

Tongue clearance. The gap between impeller outer diameter and cutwater is a compromise. Too small, and each passing vane produces strong pressure pulses at vane passing frequency, causing noise, vibration and possible vane tip damage. Too large, and more liquid recirculates past the tongue, reducing efficiency.

Throat area. The volute throat area, relative to the impeller, largely sets the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency point and influences the shape of the head curve. Impeller and volute are designed as a matched pair.

Surface finish and casting quality. Rough surfaces, casting fins, core shift and steps at the joint between the halves add friction and turbulence losses, which are relatively more important in smaller pumps. Deposits and corrosion in service have a similar effect.

Suction chamber shape. The two side chambers must deliver liquid to both eyes with a uniform velocity profile and controlled swirl. Poor shape or obstruction raises NPSH required, can start cavitation at one eye first and upsets the axial force balance.

Side rooms. The gaps between the shrouds and the casing walls affect disc friction loss and the pressures acting on the shrouds.

Caution: Modifying casing geometry, for example by grinding the tongue, changes performance and rotor loads; it should only be done to an OEM-approved design.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Some designs place a nozzle on the upper half (for example top discharge), which changes the maintenance advantage described here; always check the specific pump.
In the 3D model the wall thickness, ribs and external profile of the upper half are illustrative, not taken from OEM drawings.

casing-flange-upper.summary: The upper split flange is the machined flange around the upper casing half that mates with the lower half on the horizontal split plane.
casing-flange-upper.function: The upper split flange is the machined flange around the upper casing half that mates with the lower half on the horizontal split plane. It carries the stud and dowel holes, and its machined face forms one side of the sealed casing joint.
casing-flange-upper.operatingPrinciple: When the joint nuts are tightened the flange is clamped against the gasket and the lower flange. The clamping load must exceed the separating force from internal pressure with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere, including next to the volute, where the pressure is highest.
casing-flange-upper.construction: Cast integral with the upper half and machined flat. The flange is made thick and wide enough to keep the bolt pitch close and to spread bolt load evenly over the gasket. Bolt holes are clearance holes; accurate location comes from the dowels, not the bolts. Many designs include tapped jacking-screw holes for breaking the joint without levering between the faces.

inspection: Inspect for nicks, radial scratches across the sealing land, erosion paths, corrosion and distortion.
If leakage or distortion is suspected, check flatness by the method in the OEM or site procedure.
maintenance: Remove old gasket material with non-damaging scrapers and solvent.
Do not file or grind the face: any machining changes the joint thickness and internal fits and must follow the OEM procedure.
Never lever the joint apart with chisels or screwdrivers; use the jacking screws.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The flatness and condition of this face directly decide whether the joint seals. Because the joint runs between regions at discharge pressure (around the volute) and regions at suction pressure (around the suction chambers), a poor face can leak internally, bypassing liquid from discharge to suction, as well as externally to atmosphere.

keyConcepts.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
keyConcepts.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.

keyConcepts.title: How the casing joint is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
The horizontal joint must seal along its whole length, but it does not see one single pressure. Beside the volute and discharge passage it sees close to discharge pressure; beside the suction chambers it sees suction pressure. A joint that is not tight can therefore leak in two ways: externally to atmosphere, which is visible, and internally from the volute region across the joint face into the suction region, which is invisible but wastes energy and can erode channels in the faces over time.

A common method is a thin sheet gasket cut to the joint profile and compressed between the two machined faces by the joint studs. Some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a thin film of liquid sealing compound, and some use O-rings in machined grooves. The method is chosen by the OEM together with the internal fits, because joint thickness affects how parts held in the split bores, such as casing wear rings and seal housings, are clamped and how round those bores are.

Good sealing depends on clean, flat, undamaged faces; a new gasket of the specified material and thickness; accurate trimming at the bores so nothing protrudes into passages; correct location on the dowels; and even bolt preload applied in the specified sequence.

Caution: Use only the OEM-specified gasket material and thickness. Never reuse a compressed gasket, and do not add jointing compound unless the OEM permits it.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing bolts require proper tightening
keyConcepts.body:
Internal pressure acting on the projected area inside the joint produces a large force trying to separate the casing halves. The joint stays sealed only if the total bolt preload exceeds this force with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere. Preload is what matters, not torque as such: applied torque is converted into stud stretch, and a large part of it is used up overcoming friction in the threads and under the nut. Thread condition and the specified lubricant therefore change the preload obtained for a given torque.

Even loading matters as much as total load. If nuts are tightened one at a time to the full value, or in a random order, the upper half can be pulled down unevenly. Some regions of the gasket are then under-compressed and prone to leakage while others are over-compressed, and the split bores can distort so that wear rings rub and seals run out of square.

OEM procedures therefore give a tightening sequence applied in several passes at increasing values. Many sequences start near the middle of the joint, around the impeller, and work outwards towards the ends, alternating from side to side, but the OEM sequence always takes precedence. Afterwards the rotor should still turn freely by hand; new stiffness indicates distortion or a rub that must be investigated.

Caution: No tightening values are given in this module. Use the OEM values, sequence and lubricant with calibrated tools.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Flange width, bolt pitch and jacking-screw positions vary between manufacturers.
The model shows an illustrative flange with a simplified pattern of 16 joint nuts.

seal-housings-upper.summary: These are the upper halves of the two stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the upper casing half at the DE and NDE shaft exits.
seal-housings-upper.function: These are the upper halves of the two stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the upper casing half at the DE and NDE shaft exits. With the lower halves they form the bores that house the mechanical seals in the baseline configuration, or the gland packing in the packing variant.
seal-housings-upper.operatingPrinciple: Each housing is filled with pumped liquid. In a double-suction pump both seal chambers sit on the suction side of the impeller, so their pressure is related to suction pressure (it also depends on any throat bushing, flush or balance connection). The housing provides the stationary bore and the face to which the seal gland plate or packing gland follower is bolted.
seal-housings-upper.construction: Cast integral with the casing half and machined together with the lower half, so the split bore is concentric with the shaft axis when the casing is assembled. The outer face carries tapped holes for gland studs, and flush or seal-water connections lead into the housing where fitted. Some designs include a throat bushing at the inner end.

failureModes.cause: Dry running: loss of prime, or a start with a closed suction valve or an unvented seal chamber.; Inadequate, blocked or unsuitable flush arrangement.; Abrasive solids, or crystallising or polymerising liquids.
failureModes.signs: Visible leakage at a seal gland, increasing over time.; Squealing noise, heat or vapour at the gland.; Leakage when the pump is stationary but not when running, or the reverse.

failureModes.cause: Gland over-tightened (packing runs hot) or under-tightened (excessive leakage).; Worn, hardened or incorrectly installed packing: wrong size, joints not staggered, or rings cut incorrectly.; Lantern ring not aligned with the flush connection.
failureModes.signs: Leakage visibly above the controlled rate recommended by the OEM, or no leakage at all.; Gland or stuffing box hot, smoking or steaming.; Gland follower near the end of its adjustment.

failureModes.cause: Gasket deterioration: ageing, compression set, chemical attack, damage during handling, or reuse of an old gasket.; Uneven or damaged joint surfaces: distortion, corrosion pitting, erosion grooves from previous leaks, nicks, or residues of old gasket or sealant.; Improper bolt tightening: incorrect torque, incorrect sequence, uneven tightening, damaged or unlubricated threads, or bolts not retightened when the OEM requires it.
failureModes.signs: Weeping or dripping along the joint line.; Staining, corrosion or crystalline deposits along the flange.; Wet lagging or liquid pooling under the casing.

inspection: With the upper half removed, inspect the bore, gland face and the split line at the housing for corrosion, erosion, scoring and gasket intrusion, and confirm flush passages are clear.
After the casing is closed, check bore concentricity and face squareness relative to the shaft where the OEM or seal supplier requires it, using their method and limits.
maintenance: Maintain according to the OEM manual and site procedures.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Because the housing is split with the casing, its roundness, concentricity and face squareness depend on correct dowelling, gasket thickness and joint bolt tightening. Distortion or misalignment of this bore is a direct cause of seal face misalignment, packing wear and leakage. Integral split housings allow the upper half to be lifted after the seal glands are released, with the seals staying on the shaft sleeves.

keyConcepts.title: Seal chamber
keyConcepts.body: The annular cavity around the shaft sleeve at each casing exit that houses the mechanical seal and holds liquid around it. Each chamber is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves. The chamber bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so the gland plate face spans the horizontal split. Designs range from a conventional stuffing box adapted for a seal to an enlarged-bore chamber that gives more radial space and better circulation. Some designs have a throat bushing at the inner end.

keyConcepts.title: Stuffing box
keyConcepts.body: The annular cavity at each casing exit that contains the packing set, lantern ring and the inner end of the gland follower. Each box is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves. A bore sized for the packing cross-section and number of rings, ending at an inner shoulder or a throat bushing, with a seal water port over the lantern ring position and stud holes in the face. Bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so both span the horizontal split.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.

Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Housing geometry differs between packed and mechanical-seal designs, and some pumps use separate bolted seal chambers or covers instead of integral split housings.
The model uses one housing shape for both sealing variants; only the seal or packing inside it changes.
Never fit a mechanical seal and packing in the same housing.

lifting-lugs.summary: The lifting lugs on the upper casing half are the designated attachment points for slings or shackles when the upper half is lifted off and refitted.
lifting-lugs.function: The lifting lugs on the upper casing half are the designated attachment points for slings or shackles when the upper half is lifted off and refitted.
lifting-lugs.operatingPrinciple: They are intended for the weight of the upper casing half only. Using them to lift the complete pump, or the pump on its baseplate, can overload them and is a serious, common safety error; the complete pump is lifted only by the method shown in the OEM manual. A level lift lets the half rise squarely off the dowels without binding or swinging into the impeller and seals.
lifting-lugs.construction: Typically cast integral lugs, or bosses with tapped holes for eyebolts, positioned so that the upper half hangs approximately level when lifted on correctly rigged slings.

maintenance: Use rated lifting gear with correct sling angles under a lifting plan prepared to site procedure.
Lift slowly at first to confirm the joint has fully released, and never stand or place hands under a suspended casing half.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: They are intended for the weight of the upper casing half only. Using them to lift the complete pump, or the pump on its baseplate, can overload them and is a serious, common safety error; the complete pump is lifted only by the method shown in the OEM manual. A level lift lets the half rise squarely off the dowels without binding or swinging into the impeller and seals.

keyConcepts.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
keyConcepts.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.

Caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Lug type, number and position vary between designs.
The model shows two illustrative lugs; their size is not a rating.

vent-connections.summary: Vent connections at the high points of the upper casing allow trapped air or gas to escape when the pump is filled (primed) and before start-up.
vent-connections.function: Vent connections at the high points of the upper casing allow trapped air or gas to escape when the pump is filled (primed) and before start-up.
vent-connections.operatingPrinciple: Air collects at the highest points of the casing, typically the top of the volute and the upper parts of the suction chambers. Opening the vents while the pump is filled from the suction side lets the air out until a steady stream of liquid without bubbles appears, so the pump starts full of liquid.
vent-connections.construction: Usually tapped connections fitted with plugs, small valves or cocks, sometimes piped to a drain or safe location. Size and position are design-specific.

failureModes.cause: Leaking suction flanges, gaskets, valve stem packing or instrument connections where the suction is below atmospheric pressure.; Insufficient submergence at the suction source, allowing surface vortices to draw air into the suction pipe.; Air pockets at high points of the suction line, or an eccentric suction reducer fitted flat side down instead of flat side up.
failureModes.signs: Erratic or falling discharge pressure and flow, with the gauge needle fluctuating.; Noise resembling cavitation (crackling or gurgling) that does not clearly follow NPSH conditions.; Fluctuating motor current.

failureModes.cause: Pump not primed or casing not vented; gas lock.; Closed suction or discharge valve, or a check valve stuck closed.; Suction source empty, suction lift too high, or a leaking foot valve allowing the suction line to drain.
failureModes.signs: Discharge pressure at or near shut-off with zero indicated flow, or near zero pressure if the pump is not primed.; Motor current lower than normal.; Casing heating up.

failureModes.cause: Dry running: loss of prime, or a start with a closed suction valve or an unvented seal chamber.; Inadequate, blocked or unsuitable flush arrangement.; Abrasive solids, or crystallising or polymerising liquids.
failureModes.signs: Visible leakage at a seal gland, increasing over time.; Squealing noise, heat or vapour at the gland.; Leakage when the pump is stationary but not when running, or the reverse.

inspection: Check that vent plugs or valves are free, not blocked by deposits or paint, and leak-tight when closed.
maintenance: Vent the pump before every start-up after it has been drained or opened.
Replace damaged plugs and thread sealants with items suitable for the liquid.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Starting with trapped air can cause loss of prime, little or no discharge, and dry running of the mechanical seals or packing and of the wear rings. For hot, toxic or flammable liquids the vents must be piped to a safe place and operated only under the site procedure.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Some designs vent the seal chambers separately, and in some installations venting is done through high-point vents on the piping.
Vent positions in the model are illustrative.

jacking-screws.summary: Jacking screws are threaded through tapped holes in the upper split flange and bear on the lower flange face.
jacking-screws.function: Jacking screws are threaded through tapped holes in the upper split flange and bear on the lower flange face. Turning them evenly breaks the casing joint and lifts the upper half off the gasket and dowels without forcing tools into the joint.
jacking-screws.operatingPrinciple: After every joint nut has been removed, the screws are advanced a little at a time and in turn, so the upper half rises squarely. This overcomes the adhesion of the gasket and the grip of the dowel pins while keeping the joint faces parallel, so the dowels are not bent and the faces are not marked.
jacking-screws.construction: Typically two or more hexagon-head set screws in tapped holes near opposite corners of the upper flange, clear of the bolt circle and the gasket seating area (where they pass the gasket, the gasket is cut clear of them). In this model two screws sit at diagonal corners of the upper flange.

materials.limitations: Poor corrosion resistance Difficult to weld or repair

failureModes.cause: Gasket deterioration: ageing, compression set, chemical attack, damage during handling, or reuse of an old gasket.; Uneven or damaged joint surfaces: distortion, corrosion pitting, erosion grooves from previous leaks, nicks, or residues of old gasket or sealant.; Improper bolt tightening: incorrect torque, incorrect sequence, uneven tightening, damaged or unlubricated threads, or bolts not retightened when the OEM requires it.

inspection: Check that the threads turn freely before use and that the tips are clean and undamaged.
maintenance: Back the screws off fully before the upper half is refitted, so they do not hold the joint open when the nuts are tightened.
Follow the OEM manual for the joint-breaking procedure.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Prying the joint open with wedges or chisels damages the machined joint faces and the gasket seat, which can cause casing joint leakage later. Lifting the half unevenly can bind it on the dowels or let it swing into the impeller and wear rings once it is free.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Position, number and size of jacking screws are design specific.
Some designs use tapped jacking holes in the lower flange or dedicated jacking bosses instead; the OEM manual governs.

double-volute-rib-upper.summary: In the double-volute variant, this is the upper part of the splitter rib that divides the volute into two passages with their tongues roughly opposite each other.
double-volute-rib-upper.function: In the double-volute variant, this is the upper part of the splitter rib that divides the volute into two passages with their tongues roughly opposite each other. Each passage collects flow from approximately half of the impeller circumference.
double-volute-rib-upper.operatingPrinciple: In a single volute operating away from the best efficiency point (BEP), the pressure around the impeller is not uniform, so a net radial force acts on the impeller. With two symmetrically arranged passages, the pressure distributions of the two halves are approximately opposed and a large part of this force cancels. Cancellation is not complete, because the two passages differ in their path to the single discharge nozzle.
double-volute-rib-upper.construction: Cast integral with the upper casing half and matched at the split plane to the lower part of the rib. The rib forms a second cutwater; its leading-edge shape, its gap to the impeller and the match of the two rib halves across the joint all matter hydraulically.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Lower radial load means less shaft deflection and bending stress, lower bearing loads and better protection of wear rings and mechanical seals, which is valuable for larger pumps and for duties that run over a wide flow range. The penalties are a more complex casting, slightly more wetted surface and narrower passages that are harder to inspect and clean.

keyConcepts.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
keyConcepts.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.

Caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

casing-lower.summary: The lower casing half is the main body of the pump.
casing-lower.function: The lower casing half is the main body of the pump. It contains the lower parts of the volute, suction chambers, impeller chamber and seal chambers, carries the suction and discharge nozzles, supports both bearing housings and is bolted to the baseplate through its feet.
casing-lower.operatingPrinciple: Liquid enters through the suction nozzle, is divided into two side suction chambers leading to the two impeller eyes, and leaves through the volute and the discharge nozzle; most of these passages are formed in this half. Mechanically it is the stationary pressure boundary and the structural backbone of the pump: it reacts the weight of the pump and rotor, nozzle loads from the piping, and the radial and axial forces passed to it by the bearing housings.
casing-lower.construction: Typically a single casting with integral suction and discharge nozzles, feet, bearing brackets and the lower halves of the seal housings and wear-ring bores. Its machined split face is the reference plane for the joint, and bores split across the joint are generally finish-machined with the upper half bolted on. Drain and pressure-tapping connections are usually located on this half.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: With both nozzles on the lower half, it stays connected to the piping and fixed to the baseplate during internal maintenance, so pump-to-motor alignment is largely undisturbed when the upper half and rotor are removed. Excessive piping loads on its nozzles can distort it, disturbing bore alignment, bearing housing alignment and coupling alignment. The casting quality of its internal passages strongly affects hydraulic performance and suction behaviour.

keyConcepts.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
keyConcepts.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.

keyConcepts.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
keyConcepts.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.

Caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.

Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

keyConcepts.title: How the volute collects the liquid and builds pressure
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller discharges liquid all round its periphery, from both halves at once. The liquid leaves with high velocity, mostly in the tangential direction, so a large share of the energy added by the impeller is still kinetic energy at the impeller outlet. The volute has two jobs: to collect this flow and lead it to a single discharge nozzle, and to convert part of that kinetic energy into static pressure.

The volute is a spiral passage that starts at the tongue (cutwater) close to the impeller and grows in cross-section around the circumference, because every further part of the impeller periphery adds more flow. At design flow the area growth roughly matches the accumulated flow, so velocity and pressure around the impeller stay nearly uniform. The spiral ends at the throat, after which the discharge passage diverges. Slowing the liquid in this diverging section raises its static pressure, in line with the Bernoulli relation between velocity and pressure, less friction and mixing losses.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow. Below design flow the liquid decelerates along the volute and pressure rises from tongue to throat; above it, the liquid accelerates and pressure falls. Either way, pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and a net radial force acts on the rotor.

Caution: The volute adds no energy. It converts part of the kinetic energy leaving the impeller into pressure, with some losses.

casing-flange-lower.summary: The lower split flange is the machined flange of the lower casing half on which the gasket is laid and the upper half is seated.
casing-flange-lower.function: The lower split flange is the machined flange of the lower casing half on which the gasket is laid and the upper half is seated. It carries the tapped holes for the joint studs and the dowel holes.
casing-flange-lower.operatingPrinciple: It forms the reference side of the joint. Stud preload clamps the upper flange and gasket against it; internal pressure acts to separate the two faces, and the joint stays sealed only while enough gasket compression remains along its full length.
casing-flange-lower.construction: Cast integral with the lower half and machined flat in the same set-up as the main bores. In many designs the joint studs are screwed into tapped holes in this flange and remain in place when the upper half is lifted. The internal edges follow the outline of the volute, suction chambers, wear-ring bores and seal housings.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: As the fixed reference face, its flatness and condition set the quality of every reassembly. Thread damage in its tapped holes reduces the preload the studs can carry. Erosion channels across it from past internal leakage between the volute and the suction chambers reduce efficiency and get worse with time.

keyConcepts.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
keyConcepts.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.

keyConcepts.title: How the casing joint is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
The horizontal joint must seal along its whole length, but it does not see one single pressure. Beside the volute and discharge passage it sees close to discharge pressure; beside the suction chambers it sees suction pressure. A joint that is not tight can therefore leak in two ways: externally to atmosphere, which is visible, and internally from the volute region across the joint face into the suction region, which is invisible but wastes energy and can erode channels in the faces over time.

A common method is a thin sheet gasket cut to the joint profile and compressed between the two machined faces by the joint studs. Some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a thin film of liquid sealing compound, and some use O-rings in machined grooves. The method is chosen by the OEM together with the internal fits, because joint thickness affects how parts held in the split bores, such as casing wear rings and seal housings, are clamped and how round those bores are.

Good sealing depends on clean, flat, undamaged faces; a new gasket of the specified material and thickness; accurate trimming at the bores so nothing protrudes into passages; correct location on the dowels; and even bolt preload applied in the specified sequence.

Caution: Use only the OEM-specified gasket material and thickness. Never reuse a compressed gasket, and do not add jointing compound unless the OEM permits it.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing bolts require proper tightening
keyConcepts.body:
Internal pressure acting on the projected area inside the joint produces a large force trying to separate the casing halves. The joint stays sealed only if the total bolt preload exceeds this force with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere. Preload is what matters, not torque as such: applied torque is converted into stud stretch, and a large part of it is used up overcoming friction in the threads and under the nut. Thread condition and the specified lubricant therefore change the preload obtained for a given torque.

Even loading matters as much as total load. If nuts are tightened one at a time to the full value, or in a random order, the upper half can be pulled down unevenly. Some regions of the gasket are then under-compressed and prone to leakage while others are over-compressed, and the split bores can distort so that wear rings rub and seals run out of square.

OEM procedures therefore give a tightening sequence applied in several passes at increasing values. Many sequences start near the middle of the joint, around the impeller, and work outwards towards the ends, alternating from side to side, but the OEM sequence always takes precedence. Afterwards the rotor should still turn freely by hand; new stiffness indicates distortion or a rub that must be investigated.

Caution: No tightening values are given in this module. Use the OEM values, sequence and lubricant with calibrated tools.
