suction-nozzle.summary: The suction nozzle is the flanged inlet cast on the lower casing half.
suction-nozzle.function: The suction nozzle is the flanged inlet cast on the lower casing half. It receives liquid from the suction pipe and delivers it to the internal suction passages, where the flow divides towards the two impeller eyes.
suction-nozzle.operatingPrinciple: Liquid arrives here at the lowest pressure in the system on the pump side. The nozzle and the passages just downstream accelerate the flow gently towards the splitter. Whatever velocity profile and swirl the upstream piping produces is carried into the casing, so the piping arrangement affects how evenly the flow divides between the two eyes.
suction-nozzle.construction: Horizontal and on the opposite side of the casing from the discharge nozzle (side suction, side discharge), cast integral with the lower half. It is usually larger than the discharge nozzle to keep inlet velocity low. The flange is drilled to the specified flange standard and rating, and a pressure tapping is normally provided close to it.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: It is the reference point for suction pressure and NPSH available, and the place where suction pipe loads enter the casing. Fittings close to it, especially an elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft, can send more liquid to one eye than the other, which raises the local NPSH required on that side and causes uneven loading, noise and vibration. Leaks at the suction flange gasket are a common route for air ingress when suction pressure is below atmospheric.

keyConcepts.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
keyConcepts.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.

Caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

keyConcepts.title: Why liquid enters from both sides
keyConcepts.body:
Feeding the impeller from both sides divides the total flow between two eyes. Several tendencies follow, although the size of each benefit depends on the individual design.

Suction performance. For a given total flow and speed, each eye handles only part of the flow, so inlet velocities can be lower for a given eye size. Lower inlet velocity tends to reduce NPSH required, which helps where available suction head is limited, or allows a higher speed for the same NPSH margin. For this reason suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.

Flow capacity. For a given impeller diameter and speed, a double-suction impeller can usually pass more flow than a comparable single-suction impeller because it has roughly twice the inlet area. This makes the type common for large flows at moderate head, for example in water supply, cooling water, irrigation and fire service.

Axial thrust. With the inlets facing in opposite directions, the axial hydraulic forces on the two halves largely oppose each other in a symmetrical arrangement, so thrust bearing duty is much lower than for a single-suction impeller of similar size, though not zero.

The trade-offs are a more complex casting, two shaft seals, a rotor supported at both ends, and sensitivity to uneven inflow from the suction piping.

Caution: These are tendencies, not guarantees. Actual NPSH required and flow capacity come from the OEM performance curves, and conventions for calculating specific speed (total flow or flow per eye) should always be stated when comparing values.

keyConcepts.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
keyConcepts.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.

Caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.

Upstream straight lengths, reducer type and elbow orientation should follow the OEM and recognised intake and piping guidance; a common practice on horizontal suction lines is an eccentric reducer installed flat side up to avoid an air pocket.
Some designs use top suction.
Nozzle proportions in the model are illustrative.

discharge-nozzle.summary: The discharge nozzle is the flanged outlet on the lower casing half that leads liquid from the volute throat to the discharge pipe.
discharge-nozzle.function: The discharge nozzle is the flanged outlet on the lower casing half that leads liquid from the volute throat to the discharge pipe.
discharge-nozzle.operatingPrinciple: Downstream of the volute throat the passage normally diverges like a diffuser, slowing the liquid and converting part of its remaining kinetic energy into static pressure before the flange. The whole nozzle is at discharge pressure.
discharge-nozzle.construction: Horizontal, cast integral with the lower half on the side opposite the suction nozzle. It is usually smaller than the suction nozzle. The flange is made to the specified standard and pressure rating, with a pressure tapping normally provided near it.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Pressure measured here, corrected for gauge elevation and velocity head, is used with suction pressure to determine the head the pump is producing. Discharge pipe weight, thermal expansion and reaction forces must be carried by supports and anchors, not by the nozzle; excessive nozzle loads can distort the casing and disturb internal and coupling alignment. Isolation and non-return valves are installed in the discharge pipework, not on the nozzle itself.

keyConcepts.title: How the volute collects the liquid and builds pressure
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller discharges liquid all round its periphery, from both halves at once. The liquid leaves with high velocity, mostly in the tangential direction, so a large share of the energy added by the impeller is still kinetic energy at the impeller outlet. The volute has two jobs: to collect this flow and lead it to a single discharge nozzle, and to convert part of that kinetic energy into static pressure.

The volute is a spiral passage that starts at the tongue (cutwater) close to the impeller and grows in cross-section around the circumference, because every further part of the impeller periphery adds more flow. At design flow the area growth roughly matches the accumulated flow, so velocity and pressure around the impeller stay nearly uniform. The spiral ends at the throat, after which the discharge passage diverges. Slowing the liquid in this diverging section raises its static pressure, in line with the Bernoulli relation between velocity and pressure, less friction and mixing losses.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow. Below design flow the liquid decelerates along the volute and pressure rises from tongue to throat; above it, the liquid accelerates and pressure falls. Either way, pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and a net radial force acts on the rotor.

Caution: The volute adds no energy. It converts part of the kinetic energy leaving the impeller into pressure, with some losses.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM, and by the applicable pump standard where the pump is built to one.
Some designs use top or angled discharge.
The diffuser shape of the model nozzle is illustrative.

seal-housings-lower.summary: These are the lower halves of the DE and NDE stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the lower casing half.
seal-housings-lower.function: These are the lower halves of the DE and NDE stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the lower casing half. With the upper halves they complete the bores for the mechanical seals (baseline) or gland packing (variant).
seal-housings-lower.operatingPrinciple: Together with the upper halves they contain liquid at a pressure related to suction pressure and provide the stationary bore and gland face for the sealing arrangement. Because they stay with the lower half, they also support the seal or packing while the upper half is removed.
seal-housings-lower.construction: Cast integral with the lower half and machined with the upper half in place. In many designs a drain or leakage-collection arrangement is provided below the gland area to lead away packing leakage or any seal leakage. Flush, seal-water or quench connections may enter through either half depending on design.

failureModes.cause: Dry running: loss of prime, or a start with a closed suction valve or an unvented seal chamber.; Inadequate, blocked or unsuitable flush arrangement.; Abrasive solids, or crystallising or polymerising liquids.
failureModes.signs: Visible leakage at a seal gland, increasing over time.; Squealing noise, heat or vapour at the gland.; Leakage when the pump is stationary but not when running, or the reverse.

failureModes.cause: Gland over-tightened (packing runs hot) or under-tightened (excessive leakage).; Worn, hardened or incorrectly installed packing: wrong size, joints not staggered, or rings cut incorrectly.; Lantern ring not aligned with the flush connection.
failureModes.signs: Leakage visibly above the controlled rate recommended by the OEM, or no leakage at all.; Gland or stuffing box hot, smoking or steaming.; Gland follower near the end of its adjustment.

failureModes.cause: Gasket deterioration: ageing, compression set, chemical attack, damage during handling, or reuse of an old gasket.; Uneven or damaged joint surfaces: distortion, corrosion pitting, erosion grooves from previous leaks, nicks, or residues of old gasket or sealant.; Improper bolt tightening: incorrect torque, incorrect sequence, uneven tightening, damaged or unlubricated threads, or bolts not retightened when the OEM requires it.
failureModes.signs: Weeping or dripping along the joint line.; Staining, corrosion or crystalline deposits along the flange.; Wet lagging or liquid pooling under the casing.

inspection: Inspect the bore and gland face for corrosion, erosion and scoring; clear leakage drains and flush passages; check gland stud threads.
Check the split line at the housing for a step or gasket intrusion after reassembly.
maintenance: Maintain according to the OEM manual and site procedures.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Their alignment with the upper halves depends on the dowels, gasket and joint bolting, so a poorly assembled casing can produce an oval or stepped seal bore. Blocked leakage drains let liquid accumulate and reach the deflectors and bearing housings.

keyConcepts.title: Seal chamber
keyConcepts.body: The annular cavity around the shaft sleeve at each casing exit that houses the mechanical seal and holds liquid around it. Each chamber is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves. The chamber bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so the gland plate face spans the horizontal split. Designs range from a conventional stuffing box adapted for a seal to an enlarged-bore chamber that gives more radial space and better circulation. Some designs have a throat bushing at the inner end.

keyConcepts.title: Stuffing box
keyConcepts.body: The annular cavity at each casing exit that contains the packing set, lantern ring and the inner end of the gland follower. Each box is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves. A bore sized for the packing cross-section and number of rings, ending at an inner shoulder or a throat bushing, with a seal water port over the lantern ring position and stud holes in the face. Bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so both span the horizontal split.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.

Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Some designs use separate bolted seal chamber covers.
The model uses one illustrative housing shape for both sealing variants.

bearing-brackets.summary: The bearing brackets are cast extensions of the lower casing half at each end that support the DE and NDE bearing housings and hold them, and therefore the shaft, concentric with the casing bores.
bearing-brackets.function: The bearing brackets are cast extensions of the lower casing half at each end that support the DE and NDE bearing housings and hold them, and therefore the shaft, concentric with the casing bores.
bearing-brackets.operatingPrinciple: They transfer rotor weight and radial loads from both bearings, and residual axial thrust from the NDE locating bearing, into the casing and from there to the baseplate. Because the bearing housings bolt onto them, they define where the shaft axis sits relative to the wear-ring and seal bores.
bearing-brackets.construction: Integral with the lower half, with machined seating faces and holes for the bearing housing hold-down bolts. Many designs use dowels, spigots or locating faces so the bearing housings return to the same position after removal; some include adjusting or jacking screws for setting rotor height and centring.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Bracket stiffness and machining accuracy affect rotor centring in the casing, the uniformity of wear-ring clearances, seal alignment and vibration behaviour. Because the bearing housings remain on the lower half brackets, the upper casing half can be removed without disturbing the bearings.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Some pumps use separate bolted brackets or pedestals rather than integral brackets.
The bracket shape in the model is simplified.

casing-feet.summary: The casing feet are the mounting pads by which the pump casing is bolted to the pump mounting pads on the baseplate.
casing-feet.function: The casing feet are the mounting pads by which the pump casing is bolted to the pump mounting pads on the baseplate.
casing-feet.operatingPrinciple: They carry the pump weight, nozzle loads and dynamic forces into the baseplate and foundation. When the pump runs hot, the casing grows thermally from its supports, so the height of the feet relative to the shaft centreline influences how much the shaft rises.
casing-feet.construction: Cast integral with the lower half (in this model) and machined on their underside, with holes for hold-down bolts and, in many installations, provision for dowelling to the baseplate after final alignment. Some designs place the supports near the shaft centreline height (centreline mounting) to limit vertical shaft movement from thermal expansion.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Uneven support (soft foot) distorts the casing when the hold-down bolts are tightened, changing alignment and internal clearances. Loose or cracked feet can lead to vibration and misalignment.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

pressure-tappings.summary: Pressure tapping connections close to the suction and discharge flanges allow gauges or transmitters to measure the pressures used to determine pump head and NPSH available.
pressure-tappings.function: Pressure tapping connections close to the suction and discharge flanges allow gauges or transmitters to measure the pressures used to determine pump head and NPSH available.
pressure-tappings.operatingPrinciple: Pump total head is the difference in total head between the discharge and suction measuring points: H = (p2 - p1) / (rho g) + (z2 - z1) + (v2^2 - v1^2) / (2g), where p is static gauge pressure, z the elevation of each gauge reference point, v the mean velocity in the pipe at that point, rho the liquid density and g gravitational acceleration. Taking readings close to the flanges keeps pipe friction out of the result.
pressure-tappings.construction: Small tapped connections in the nozzles, usually fitted with plugs, isolation valves or gauge assemblies, with pulsation dampers (snubbers) where needed.

double-volute-rib-lower.summary: In the double-volute variant, this is the lower part of the splitter rib.
double-volute-rib-lower.function: In the double-volute variant, this is the lower part of the splitter rib. It continues the dividing wall between the two volute passages and guides one of the passages around to join the other before the common discharge nozzle.
double-volute-rib-lower.operatingPrinciple: With the upper part of the rib, it creates a second volute passage whose tongue is roughly opposite the main tongue. Some residual radial force remains.
double-volute-rib-lower.construction: Cast integral with the lower casing half and matched at the split plane to the upper rib. Its surfaces form walls of two passages, so casting accuracy on both faces matters.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: By reducing radial load, the rib helps limit shaft deflection at the wear rings and seals and reduces bearing loads. Because the lower rib is a long, thin wall inside the casing, it must be robust enough for pressure differences across it and for any solids carried by the liquid.

keyConcepts.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
keyConcepts.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.

Caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction influences hydraulic loading
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller experiences three broad kinds of hydraulic load: axial, radial and fluctuating.

Axial forces come mainly from pressure on the outer faces of the shrouds. Liquid in each side room rotates at a fraction of impeller speed, so its pressure falls from the periphery towards the wear ring. In a single-suction impeller the eye side is at suction pressure inside the wear ring while the back shroud sees higher pressure over a larger area, giving a net thrust towards the suction. In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

Radial forces come from the pressure distribution around the impeller periphery. Double suction does not reduce them in itself: they depend on head, impeller diameter, total outlet width and operating point relative to BEP, and they are addressed by volute design, for example a double volute.

Fluctuating forces arise as each vane passes the tongue, giving pulses at vane passing frequency, and from recirculation at part load. Staggering the DE and NDE vane sets, as many designs do, spreads these pulses in time and reduces their amplitude.

The torque reaction on the impeller passes to the shaft through the key.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft deflection
keyConcepts.body:
Under radial load the shaft bends, and the deflection at the impeller, wear rings and seal faces often matters more for reliability than the stress. For a simply supported uniform shaft with a central point load F over span L, the mid-span deflection is delta = F L^3 / (48 E I), with I = pi d^4 / 64 for a solid round section and E the elastic modulus. The slope at each support is theta = F L^2 / (16 E I).

These relations show the sensitivity: deflection rises with the cube of span and falls with the fourth power of diameter, so designs are often compared using a shaft flexibility index proportional to L^3 / d^4.

The main deflecting loads are the radial hydraulic force, which in a single volute grows as operation moves away from BEP, impeller and shaft weight, coupling forces and unbalance. Excessive deflection can close the wear-ring clearance on one side and cause rubbing, tilt the mechanical seal faces and increase leakage or face wear, wear packing and sleeves unevenly, and misalign the bearings, raising their temperature. Typical evidence is one-sided rub marks on wear rings and sleeves.

Remedies are mainly operational and design-related: running close to BEP, a double volute for wide operating ranges, a stiffer shaft, and correct coupling alignment.

Caution: Allowable deflection at the seals and wear rings is set by the OEM and seal supplier. Simple beam formulas ignore stepped diameters, bearing flexibility and fluid-film stiffness.

volute-tongue.summary: The volute tongue (cutwater) is the point where the volute wall comes closest to the impeller and separates the start of the volute spiral from the discharge throat.
volute-tongue.function: The volute tongue (cutwater) is the point where the volute wall comes closest to the impeller and separates the start of the volute spiral from the discharge throat. This marker identifies its location on the lower casing half.
volute-tongue.operatingPrinciple: At design flow the tongue divides the stream cleanly: liquid leaving the impeller either passes into the throat towards discharge or continues around the spiral. Away from design flow the liquid meets the tongue at an angle, causing incidence losses, local high velocity, pressure fluctuations and, at low flow, recirculation around the tongue. Each vane passing the tongue produces a pressure pulse at vane passing frequency, equal to the number of vanes multiplied by the rotational speed.
volute-tongue.construction: Cast as part of the volute in the lower casing half in this model. Its leading-edge radius, angle and radial gap from the impeller outer diameter are hydraulic design choices.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The tongue gap is a compromise: a very small gap increases pressure pulsations, noise and vibration and can damage vane tips; a large gap tends to increase recirculation and reduce efficiency. Trimming the impeller diameter increases this gap. Erosion or cavitation damage at the tongue changes performance and pulsation levels.

keyConcepts.title: How the volute collects the liquid and builds pressure
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller discharges liquid all round its periphery, from both halves at once. The liquid leaves with high velocity, mostly in the tangential direction, so a large share of the energy added by the impeller is still kinetic energy at the impeller outlet. The volute has two jobs: to collect this flow and lead it to a single discharge nozzle, and to convert part of that kinetic energy into static pressure.

The volute is a spiral passage that starts at the tongue (cutwater) close to the impeller and grows in cross-section around the circumference, because every further part of the impeller periphery adds more flow. At design flow the area growth roughly matches the accumulated flow, so velocity and pressure around the impeller stay nearly uniform. The spiral ends at the throat, after which the discharge passage diverges. Slowing the liquid in this diverging section raises its static pressure, in line with the Bernoulli relation between velocity and pressure, less friction and mixing losses.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow. Below design flow the liquid decelerates along the volute and pressure rises from tongue to throat; above it, the liquid accelerates and pressure falls. Either way, pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and a net radial force acts on the rotor.

Caution: The volute adds no energy. It converts part of the kinetic energy leaving the impeller into pressure, with some losses.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing geometry affects hydraulic performance
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller adds the energy, but the casing largely decides how much of it reaches the discharge flange and how smoothly the pump runs.

Tongue clearance. The gap between impeller outer diameter and cutwater is a compromise. Too small, and each passing vane produces strong pressure pulses at vane passing frequency, causing noise, vibration and possible vane tip damage. Too large, and more liquid recirculates past the tongue, reducing efficiency.

Throat area. The volute throat area, relative to the impeller, largely sets the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency point and influences the shape of the head curve. Impeller and volute are designed as a matched pair.

Surface finish and casting quality. Rough surfaces, casting fins, core shift and steps at the joint between the halves add friction and turbulence losses, which are relatively more important in smaller pumps. Deposits and corrosion in service have a similar effect.

Suction chamber shape. The two side chambers must deliver liquid to both eyes with a uniform velocity profile and controlled swirl. Poor shape or obstruction raises NPSH required, can start cavitation at one eye first and upsets the axial force balance.

Side rooms. The gaps between the shrouds and the casing walls affect disc friction loss and the pressures acting on the shrouds.

Caution: Modifying casing geometry, for example by grinding the tongue, changes performance and rotor loads; it should only be done to an OEM-approved design.

In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

casing-gasket.summary: The casing joint gasket seals the horizontal split joint between the upper and lower casing halves, preventing leakage to atmosphere and internal leakage between high-pressure and low-pressure regions along the joint.
casing-gasket.function: The casing joint gasket seals the horizontal split joint between the upper and lower casing halves, preventing leakage to atmosphere and internal leakage between high-pressure and low-pressure regions along the joint.
casing-gasket.operatingPrinciple: Bolt preload compresses the gasket so that it fills the small irregularities of the two flange faces. Internal pressure then acts to separate the faces; the joint stays sealed as long as enough residual compression remains on the gasket everywhere along its length.
casing-gasket.construction: Commonly a thin sheet gasket cut to the profile of the joint face, with holes for studs and dowels and cut-outs around the internal passages. It must be trimmed accurately at the wear-ring and seal-housing bores. Some designs instead use a metal-to-metal joint with a liquid sealing compound, or O-ring seals in grooves.

inspection: Clean and inspect both faces, lay the gasket without wrinkles or overlaps, and trim it at the bores only as the OEM instructs.
Check for external leaks after start-up.
maintenance: Replace the gasket every time the joint is opened, using the OEM-specified material and thickness.
Use jointing compounds or adhesives only if the OEM permits them.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Gasket material and thickness are part of the pump design: thickness affects how components held in the split bores (such as casing wear rings and seal housings) are clamped, and the roundness of those bores. A wrong, reused or poorly trimmed gasket can leak, protrude into the hydraulic passages or seal bores, or distort internal fits.

keyConcepts.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
keyConcepts.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.

keyConcepts.title: How the casing joint is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
The horizontal joint must seal along its whole length, but it does not see one single pressure. Beside the volute and discharge passage it sees close to discharge pressure; beside the suction chambers it sees suction pressure. A joint that is not tight can therefore leak in two ways: externally to atmosphere, which is visible, and internally from the volute region across the joint face into the suction region, which is invisible but wastes energy and can erode channels in the faces over time.

A common method is a thin sheet gasket cut to the joint profile and compressed between the two machined faces by the joint studs. Some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a thin film of liquid sealing compound, and some use O-rings in machined grooves. The method is chosen by the OEM together with the internal fits, because joint thickness affects how parts held in the split bores, such as casing wear rings and seal housings, are clamped and how round those bores are.

Good sealing depends on clean, flat, undamaged faces; a new gasket of the specified material and thickness; accurate trimming at the bores so nothing protrudes into passages; correct location on the dowels; and even bolt preload applied in the specified sequence.

Caution: Use only the OEM-specified gasket material and thickness. Never reuse a compressed gasket, and do not add jointing compound unless the OEM permits it.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing bolts require proper tightening
keyConcepts.body:
Internal pressure acting on the projected area inside the joint produces a large force trying to separate the casing halves. The joint stays sealed only if the total bolt preload exceeds this force with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere. Preload is what matters, not torque as such: applied torque is converted into stud stretch, and a large part of it is used up overcoming friction in the threads and under the nut. Thread condition and the specified lubricant therefore change the preload obtained for a given torque.

Even loading matters as much as total load. If nuts are tightened one at a time to the full value, or in a random order, the upper half can be pulled down unevenly. Some regions of the gasket are then under-compressed and prone to leakage while others are over-compressed, and the split bores can distort so that wear rings rub and seals run out of square.

OEM procedures therefore give a tightening sequence applied in several passes at increasing values. Many sequences start near the middle of the joint, around the impeller, and work outwards towards the ends, alternating from side to side, but the OEM sequence always takes precedence. Afterwards the rotor should still turn freely by hand; new stiffness indicates distortion or a rub that must be investigated.

Caution: No tightening values are given in this module. Use the OEM values, sequence and lubricant with calibrated tools.

keyConcepts.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
keyConcepts.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.

Caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Correct location keeps the casing wear-ring bores and seal housings round and concentric with the rotor, keeps the two halves of the volute and suction chambers aligned without steps, and stops the joint shifting under load. Missing or damaged dowels can lead to wear-ring rubs, seal failures and joint leakage.

keyConcepts.title: How the casing joint is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
The horizontal joint must seal along its whole length, but it does not see one single pressure. Beside the volute and discharge passage it sees close to discharge pressure; beside the suction chambers it sees suction pressure. A joint that is not tight can therefore leak in two ways: externally to atmosphere, which is visible, and internally from the volute region across the joint face into the suction region, which is invisible but wastes energy and can erode channels in the faces over time.

A common method is a thin sheet gasket cut to the joint profile and compressed between the two machined faces by the joint studs. Some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a thin film of liquid sealing compound, and some use O-rings in machined grooves. The method is chosen by the OEM together with the internal fits, because joint thickness affects how parts held in the split bores, such as casing wear rings and seal housings, are clamped and how round those bores are.

Good sealing depends on clean, flat, undamaged faces; a new gasket of the specified material and thickness; accurate trimming at the bores so nothing protrudes into passages; correct location on the dowels; and even bolt preload applied in the specified sequence.

Caution: Use only the OEM-specified gasket material and thickness. Never reuse a compressed gasket, and do not add jointing compound unless the OEM permits it.

keyConcepts.title: Why dowel pins are used
keyConcepts.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.

Caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

casing-wear-ring-de.summary: The drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the DE impeller eye.
casing-wear-ring-de.function: The drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the DE impeller eye. It forms the DE running clearance with the DE impeller wear ring.
casing-wear-ring-de.operatingPrinciple: It restricts leakage from the DE side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure, back into the DE eye at suction pressure. Its clearance also influences the pressure distribution on the outer face of the DE shroud and so the axial force acting on that side of the impeller.
casing-wear-ring-de.construction: Seated in the DE wear-ring bore, which is split across the casing joint, and prevented from turning by an anti-rotation feature. Its bore is the stationary half of the DE running clearance.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Its clearance should stay similar to that of the NDE ring. Unequal clearances at the two eyes change the side-room pressures differently and are one source of residual axial thrust, which the NDE locating bearing must carry.

keyConcepts.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.

Caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

keyConcepts.title: Why residual axial thrust still exists
keyConcepts.body:
Real pumps depart from the ideal symmetrical arrangement in several ways. Each departure leaves a net axial force, the residual thrust, which can act towards either end and can change with operating conditions.

Asymmetric inflow: elbows, valves or strainers near the suction, or vortices in the intake, give the two eyes different flow and velocity profiles. Wear-ring clearances: new rings have tolerances, and in service the rings at the two eyes rarely wear at the same rate; a larger clearance on one side increases leakage through that side room and changes its swirl and pressure. Casting variations: shroud profiles, vane positions and side-room widths are never perfectly identical. Rotor axial position: if the impeller is not centred on the volute, the side rooms differ; centring is set during assembly by the OEM procedure. Off-design operation: at low flow, recirculation at the eyes and outlet need not be symmetrical, and the force can fluctuate. Unequal seal chamber pressures act on the shaft cross-section. Transients such as starting, stopping and one-sided cavitation add temporary thrust.

In this design the residual thrust is carried by the NDE locating bearing. Because its direction can reverse, the baseline uses paired angular-contact bearings mounted back to back, which carry axial load in both directions; the deep-groove ball bearing variant also carries moderate axial load in both directions.

Caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A rise in NDE bearing temperature or a change in axial vibration after wear-ring renewal, rotor reassembly or piping changes can indicate increased residual thrust and should be investigated.

keyConcepts.title: Why wear rings and clearances affect performance
keyConcepts.body:
Each eye has a pair of wear rings, one on the impeller and one in the casing, separated by a small radial running clearance. Outside the gap is the side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure; inside is the eye, at suction pressure, so liquid leaks back continuously. As a simple approximation the leakage behaves like flow through an annular orifice, QL = Cd A sqrt(2 dp / rho), where A is the clearance area and dp the pressure difference, so leakage rises roughly in proportion to the clearance.

Efficiency. The leakage has received energy from the impeller but is not delivered, so the impeller must pass more flow than the pump delivers. As rings wear, delivered flow at a given head falls, head at a given flow falls, and power per unit of delivered flow rises.

Suction behaviour. The leakage jet re-enters the eye and disturbs the inlet flow; heavy leakage can raise NPSH required and promote eye recirculation.

Pressure distribution and thrust. Leakage through each side room modifies its swirl and pressure, so unequal DE and NDE clearances unbalance the shroud forces and increase residual thrust.

Rotordynamics. The liquid film in a tight annular gap acts like a weak bearing, adding stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). Worn rings lose this support, which tends to lower the wet critical speed and increase vibration.

Caution: A clearance that is too tight risks rubbing, galling and seizure. Use the OEM clearances and renewal limits, and measure both eyes.

casing-wear-ring-nde.summary: The non-drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the NDE impeller eye.
casing-wear-ring-nde.function: The non-drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the NDE impeller eye. It forms the NDE running clearance with the NDE impeller wear ring.

casing-wear-ring-nde.construction: Seated in the NDE wear-ring bore, split across the casing joint, with an anti-rotation feature. It mirrors the DE ring.

suction-passages.summary: The suction passages carry liquid from the suction nozzle into the casing and divide it into two side suction chambers, one leading to each impeller eye.
suction-passages.function: The suction passages carry liquid from the suction nozzle into the casing and divide it into two side suction chambers, one leading to each impeller eye. This translucent volume shows the splitter region and both chambers.
suction-passages.operatingPrinciple:
Liquid enters the lower half horizontally, flows beneath the shaft region and is split into two streams that turn and travel axially in opposite directions to the DE and NDE eyes. In many designs the chambers are shaped (for example semi-spiral) to accelerate the flow slightly and give each eye a reasonably uniform inflow with controlled swirl.

The two streams are intended to be similar, but in practice they are not exactly equal: the share reaching each eye depends on casing geometry, casting accuracy, upstream piping and operating point.
suction-passages.construction: Formed by cored passages mainly in the lower casing half and closed by the upper half. A dividing rib or splitter directs the flow into the two chambers, which surround the shaft between the seal housings and the impeller eyes.

failureModes.mode: Unequal flow distribution between the two eyes
failureModes.cause: Suction elbow lying in the plane of the shaft, installed close to the suction nozzle.; Insufficient straight pipe upstream of the suction nozzle compared with the OEM recommendation or pump piping guidance.; Partly open valve, strainer or other fitting close to the suction nozzle.
failureModes.signs: Cavitation-type noise, sometimes louder towards one end of the casing.; Non-drive-end (locating) bearing running warmer than its own baseline, or its temperature fluctuating.; Increased vibration, possibly with a larger axial component.

failureModes.cause: Insufficient NPSH available: low suction source level, excessive suction lift, or high suction-side friction losses from a long, undersized or fouled suction line.; Partly closed suction valve, or blocked suction strainer or intake screen, adding loss immediately upstream of the pump.; Liquid temperature higher than the design basis, which raises the vapour pressure and reduces NPSH available.
failureModes.signs: Crackling, rattling or gravel-like noise from the casing near the suction side, often changing with flow.; Fluctuating discharge pressure, flow and motor current.; Increased broadband vibration at the bearing housings compared with the baseline.

failureModes.cause: Leaking suction flanges, gaskets, valve stem packing or instrument connections where the suction is below atmospheric pressure.; Insufficient submergence at the suction source, allowing surface vortices to draw air into the suction pipe.; Air pockets at high points of the suction line, or an eccentric suction reducer fitted flat side down instead of flat side up.
failureModes.signs: Erratic or falling discharge pressure and flow, with the gauge needle fluctuating.; Noise resembling cavitation (crackling or gurgling) that does not clearly follow NPSH conditions.; Fluctuating motor current.

failureModes.cause: Falling level in the suction tank or sump, or reduced pressure in the suction vessel.; Blocked suction strainer, foot valve or intake screen.; Partly closed or failed suction isolation valve, for example a gate detached from its stem.
failureModes.signs: Suction gauge reading lower than normal for the same flow.; Cavitation noise and fluctuating discharge pressure.; Falling flow and head.

failureModes.cause: Missing, damaged or unsuitable suction strainer or intake screen.; Construction or maintenance debris left in the pipework, such as rags, gasket offcuts, welding debris or tools.; Fibrous or solids-laden liquid beyond the solids-handling capability of the pump.
failureModes.signs: Gradual or sudden drop in flow and head at the same valve setting and speed.; Increased vibration, often with a once-per-revolution (unbalance-type) component.; Change in motor current, commonly a reduction as flow falls, although the direction depends on the pump curve and the nature of the blockage.

inspection: With the casing open, inspect suction chamber surfaces for deposits, debris, erosion and casting flash, and remove obstructions.
maintenance: Compare cavitation or erosion damage at the DE and NDE eyes; a clear difference may indicate uneven inflow and should prompt a review of the suction piping.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Suction passage shape governs flow uniformity at the eyes and the pressure loss before the impeller, both of which affect NPSH required, cavitation inception, noise and the balance of axial forces. Distorted or swirling inflow, whether from casting defects, deposits or poor upstream piping, can make one eye work harder than the other.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing geometry affects hydraulic performance
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller adds the energy, but the casing largely decides how much of it reaches the discharge flange and how smoothly the pump runs.

Tongue clearance. The gap between impeller outer diameter and cutwater is a compromise. Too small, and each passing vane produces strong pressure pulses at vane passing frequency, causing noise, vibration and possible vane tip damage. Too large, and more liquid recirculates past the tongue, reducing efficiency.

Throat area. The volute throat area, relative to the impeller, largely sets the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency point and influences the shape of the head curve. Impeller and volute are designed as a matched pair.

Surface finish and casting quality. Rough surfaces, casting fins, core shift and steps at the joint between the halves add friction and turbulence losses, which are relatively more important in smaller pumps. Deposits and corrosion in service have a similar effect.

Suction chamber shape. The two side chambers must deliver liquid to both eyes with a uniform velocity profile and controlled swirl. Poor shape or obstruction raises NPSH required, can start cavitation at one eye first and upsets the axial force balance.

Side rooms. The gaps between the shrouds and the casing walls affect disc friction loss and the pressures acting on the shrouds.

Caution: Modifying casing geometry, for example by grinding the tongue, changes performance and rotor loads; it should only be done to an OEM-approved design.

keyConcepts.title: What double suction means
keyConcepts.body:
A double-suction (double-entry) impeller has two inlets, called eyes, one on each side, instead of the single eye of an end-suction impeller. It can be pictured as two single-suction impellers placed back to back and cast as one piece: a central hub and web separate two sets of vanes, each enclosed by its own outer shroud, and both halves discharge from a common outer periphery into one volute.

In this pump, liquid enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half and is divided into two side suction chambers. One feeds the drive-end eye and the other the non-drive-end eye, so the two streams approach the impeller axially from opposite directions. Inside the impeller each stream turns outwards through its own vane passages, and the two streams merge at the impeller outlet and leave through the single discharge nozzle.

The pump is still single-stage: the liquid passes through one impeller once. Double suction describes the number of inlets, not the number of stages. Because the shaft passes right through the impeller and needs support on both sides, double-suction impellers pair naturally with between-bearings rotors and axially split casings, although they are also used elsewhere, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.

keyConcepts.title: Why liquid enters from both sides
keyConcepts.body:
Feeding the impeller from both sides divides the total flow between two eyes. Several tendencies follow, although the size of each benefit depends on the individual design.

Suction performance. For a given total flow and speed, each eye handles only part of the flow, so inlet velocities can be lower for a given eye size. Lower inlet velocity tends to reduce NPSH required, which helps where available suction head is limited, or allows a higher speed for the same NPSH margin. For this reason suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.

Flow capacity. For a given impeller diameter and speed, a double-suction impeller can usually pass more flow than a comparable single-suction impeller because it has roughly twice the inlet area. This makes the type common for large flows at moderate head, for example in water supply, cooling water, irrigation and fire service.

Axial thrust. With the inlets facing in opposite directions, the axial hydraulic forces on the two halves largely oppose each other in a symmetrical arrangement, so thrust bearing duty is much lower than for a single-suction impeller of similar size, though not zero.

The trade-offs are a more complex casting, two shaft seals, a rotor supported at both ends, and sensitivity to uneven inflow from the suction piping.

Caution: These are tendencies, not guarantees. Actual NPSH required and flow capacity come from the OEM performance curves, and conventions for calculating specific speed (total flow or flow per eye) should always be stated when comparing values.

keyConcepts.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
keyConcepts.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.

Caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

impeller-chamber.summary: The impeller chamber is the liquid-filled space in which the impeller rotates, including the side rooms between the outer faces of the impeller shrouds and the casing walls.
impeller-chamber.function: The impeller chamber is the liquid-filled space in which the impeller rotates, including the side rooms between the outer faces of the impeller shrouds and the casing walls.
impeller-chamber.operatingPrinciple: Liquid in each side room is dragged into rotation by the shroud and turns at a fraction of impeller speed. This rotating liquid creates a pressure that falls from the impeller outer diameter towards the wear rings, acting on the outer face of each shroud. In a double-suction impeller these shroud forces act in opposite directions on the two sides, which is the basis of axial thrust balance. Leakage through the wear-ring clearances flows inwards through the side rooms and modifies their swirl and pressure.
impeller-chamber.construction: Bounded by the casing walls of both halves, the wear rings and the impeller. Side-room widths and wall shapes are design-specific.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction influences hydraulic loading
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller experiences three broad kinds of hydraulic load: axial, radial and fluctuating.

Axial forces come mainly from pressure on the outer faces of the shrouds. Liquid in each side room rotates at a fraction of impeller speed, so its pressure falls from the periphery towards the wear ring. In a single-suction impeller the eye side is at suction pressure inside the wear ring while the back shroud sees higher pressure over a larger area, giving a net thrust towards the suction. In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

Radial forces come from the pressure distribution around the impeller periphery. Double suction does not reduce them in itself: they depend on head, impeller diameter, total outlet width and operating point relative to BEP, and they are addressed by volute design, for example a double volute.

Fluctuating forces arise as each vane passes the tongue, giving pulses at vane passing frequency, and from recirculation at part load. Staggering the DE and NDE vane sets, as many designs do, spreads these pulses in time and reduces their amplitude.

The torque reaction on the impeller passes to the shaft through the key.

keyConcepts.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.

Caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

keyConcepts.title: Why wear rings and clearances affect performance
keyConcepts.body:
Each eye has a pair of wear rings, one on the impeller and one in the casing, separated by a small radial running clearance. Outside the gap is the side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure; inside is the eye, at suction pressure, so liquid leaks back continuously. As a simple approximation the leakage behaves like flow through an annular orifice, QL = Cd A sqrt(2 dp / rho), where A is the clearance area and dp the pressure difference, so leakage rises roughly in proportion to the clearance.

Efficiency. The leakage has received energy from the impeller but is not delivered, so the impeller must pass more flow than the pump delivers. As rings wear, delivered flow at a given head falls, head at a given flow falls, and power per unit of delivered flow rises.

Suction behaviour. The leakage jet re-enters the eye and disturbs the inlet flow; heavy leakage can raise NPSH required and promote eye recirculation.

Pressure distribution and thrust. Leakage through each side room modifies its swirl and pressure, so unequal DE and NDE clearances unbalance the shroud forces and increase residual thrust.

Rotordynamics. The liquid film in a tight annular gap acts like a weak bearing, adding stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). Worn rings lose this support, which tends to lower the wet critical speed and increase vibration.

Caution: A clearance that is too tight risks rubbing, galling and seizure. Use the OEM clearances and renewal limits, and measure both eyes.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Simplified volume in the model; side-room gaps are exaggerated for visibility.

volute-passage.summary: The volute passage is the spiral channel around the impeller that collects liquid leaving the full impeller periphery, from both halves of the impeller, and leads it through the throat to the single discharge nozzle.
volute-passage.function: The volute passage is the spiral channel around the impeller that collects liquid leaving the full impeller periphery, from both halves of the impeller, and leads it through the throat to the single discharge nozzle.
volute-passage.operatingPrinciple:
Starting at the tongue, the volute cross-section increases progressively around the circumference because each further part of the impeller adds more flow. At design flow this keeps velocity and pressure around the impeller roughly uniform. Liquid leaves the impeller with high, largely tangential velocity; the volute and the diverging passage after the throat convert part of this kinetic energy into static pressure.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow, the pressure around the impeller becomes non-uniform, and a net radial force acts on the rotor.
volute-passage.construction: Mostly formed in the lower casing half and closed by the upper half. The throat is the minimum section where the spiral ends and the discharge passage begins. In the double-volute variant a splitter rib divides the volute into two passages.

failureModes.signs: Fluctuating discharge pressure and flow, or surging.; Rumbling, crackling or random noise at low flow.; Vibration with broadband, sub-synchronous or vane-pass components.

failureModes.signs: Rising trend in measured vibration.; Change in noise, or visible movement of piping and baseplate.; Loosening fasteners and fretting marks.

inspection: Inspect volute surfaces, throat and tongue for erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage, deposits and blockage.
maintenance: Heavy deposits reduce passage area and roughen surfaces, which can reduce head and efficiency.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Throat area and area distribution largely determine the flow at which the pump reaches best efficiency and strongly influence the shape of the head curve near BEP and the radial load on the rotor. Surface roughness and casting accuracy affect friction losses, which matter more in smaller pumps.

keyConcepts.title: How the volute collects the liquid and builds pressure
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller discharges liquid all round its periphery, from both halves at once. The liquid leaves with high velocity, mostly in the tangential direction, so a large share of the energy added by the impeller is still kinetic energy at the impeller outlet. The volute has two jobs: to collect this flow and lead it to a single discharge nozzle, and to convert part of that kinetic energy into static pressure.

The volute is a spiral passage that starts at the tongue (cutwater) close to the impeller and grows in cross-section around the circumference, because every further part of the impeller periphery adds more flow. At design flow the area growth roughly matches the accumulated flow, so velocity and pressure around the impeller stay nearly uniform. The spiral ends at the throat, after which the discharge passage diverges. Slowing the liquid in this diverging section raises its static pressure, in line with the Bernoulli relation between velocity and pressure, less friction and mixing losses.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow. Below design flow the liquid decelerates along the volute and pressure rises from tongue to throat; above it, the liquid accelerates and pressure falls. Either way, pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and a net radial force acts on the rotor.

Caution: The volute adds no energy. It converts part of the kinetic energy leaving the impeller into pressure, with some losses.

keyConcepts.title: Why casing geometry affects hydraulic performance
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller adds the energy, but the casing largely decides how much of it reaches the discharge flange and how smoothly the pump runs.

Tongue clearance. The gap between impeller outer diameter and cutwater is a compromise. Too small, and each passing vane produces strong pressure pulses at vane passing frequency, causing noise, vibration and possible vane tip damage. Too large, and more liquid recirculates past the tongue, reducing efficiency.

Throat area. The volute throat area, relative to the impeller, largely sets the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency point and influences the shape of the head curve. Impeller and volute are designed as a matched pair.

Surface finish and casting quality. Rough surfaces, casting fins, core shift and steps at the joint between the halves add friction and turbulence losses, which are relatively more important in smaller pumps. Deposits and corrosion in service have a similar effect.

Suction chamber shape. The two side chambers must deliver liquid to both eyes with a uniform velocity profile and controlled swirl. Poor shape or obstruction raises NPSH required, can start cavitation at one eye first and upsets the axial force balance.

Side rooms. The gaps between the shrouds and the casing walls affect disc friction loss and the pressures acting on the shrouds.

Caution: Modifying casing geometry, for example by grinding the tongue, changes performance and rotor loads; it should only be done to an OEM-approved design.

keyConcepts.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
keyConcepts.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.

Caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: What double suction means
keyConcepts.body:
A double-suction (double-entry) impeller has two inlets, called eyes, one on each side, instead of the single eye of an end-suction impeller. It can be pictured as two single-suction impellers placed back to back and cast as one piece: a central hub and web separate two sets of vanes, each enclosed by its own outer shroud, and both halves discharge from a common outer periphery into one volute.

In this pump, liquid enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half and is divided into two side suction chambers. One feeds the drive-end eye and the other the non-drive-end eye, so the two streams approach the impeller axially from opposite directions. Inside the impeller each stream turns outwards through its own vane passages, and the two streams merge at the impeller outlet and leave through the single discharge nozzle.

The pump is still single-stage: the liquid passes through one impeller once. Double suction describes the number of inlets, not the number of stages. Because the shaft passes right through the impeller and needs support on both sides, double-suction impellers pair naturally with between-bearings rotors and axially split casings, although they are also used elsewhere, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
The volute shape and area progression in the model are illustrative; real profiles are designed by the OEM for each hydraulic size.

impeller-hub.summary: The hub is the central part of the impeller that fits on the shaft, and the central web is the disc that separates the two halves of the impeller.
impeller-hub.function: The hub is the central part of the impeller that fits on the shaft, and the central web is the disc that separates the two halves of the impeller. Together they carry torque from the shaft to the vanes and separate the two incoming streams.
impeller-hub.operatingPrinciple: Torque passes from the shaft through the key into the hub, then through the web to the vanes and shrouds. The web acts as a common back plate for both halves, turning each incoming axial stream outwards into the vane passages.
impeller-hub.construction: Cast with the rest of the impeller. The hub is bored and keyed, and its end faces are machined square to the bore because the shaft sleeves bear against them to locate the impeller axially. In many designs O-rings or gaskets between the hub faces and the sleeves keep pumped liquid off the shaft.
