keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The bore fit, keyway and end-face squareness determine how accurately the impeller runs concentric and true on the shaft, which affects balance, wear-ring clearance uniformity and runout. Damaged hub faces can allow liquid under the sleeves and onto the shaft.

keyConcepts.title: Impeller balance
keyConcepts.body: The impeller balance arrangement refers to how the impeller's mass distribution is corrected so it rotates without significant unbalance. Corrections are commonly made by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds. Material is removed by machining or grinding on the shroud outer faces at the positions found on the balancing machine, within the depth and location limits set by the OEM, without thinning shrouds excessively or cutting into vanes.

keyConcepts.title: What double suction means
keyConcepts.body:
A double-suction (double-entry) impeller has two inlets, called eyes, one on each side, instead of the single eye of an end-suction impeller. It can be pictured as two single-suction impellers placed back to back and cast as one piece: a central hub and web separate two sets of vanes, each enclosed by its own outer shroud, and both halves discharge from a common outer periphery into one volute.

In this pump, liquid enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half and is divided into two side suction chambers. One feeds the drive-end eye and the other the non-drive-end eye, so the two streams approach the impeller axially from opposite directions. Inside the impeller each stream turns outwards through its own vane passages, and the two streams merge at the impeller outlet and leave through the single discharge nozzle.

The pump is still single-stage: the liquid passes through one impeller once. Double suction describes the number of inlets, not the number of stages. Because the shaft passes right through the impeller and needs support on both sides, double-suction impellers pair naturally with between-bearings rotors and axially split casings, although they are also used elsewhere, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.

keyConcepts.title: How liquid moves through the impeller passages
keyConcepts.body:
Each half of the impeller works in the same way. Liquid leaves its side suction chamber and enters the eye moving mainly axially, sometimes with a little pre-swirl set by the chamber shape. In the eye it turns from axial towards radial, guided by the shroud on the outside and the hub and central web on the inside, and meets the vane leading edges.

Velocity triangles describe the flow. Relative to the rotating vanes the liquid has a relative velocity w; the vanes move at peripheral speed u = omega r; the absolute velocity c seen by a stationary observer is the vector sum of w and u. Near design flow the relative flow meets the vanes with small incidence. Away from design flow incidence increases, raising losses and possibly triggering cavitation or recirculation at the eye.

As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller and its angular momentum increases. The Euler equation gives the ideal head: H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g, where cu is the tangential component of absolute velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). Static pressure rises through the passages because of the centrifugal effect and because the relative velocity is slowed in the widening, backward-curved passages. At the outlet the liquid has higher pressure and high absolute velocity, and the two streams merge into the volute.

Caution: The Euler head is an ideal value. Real head is lower because the flow does not follow the vanes perfectly (slip) and because of hydraulic losses.

keyConcepts.title: Protecting the shaft from corrosion
keyConcepts.body:
A pump shaft is highly stressed and subject to fatigue, and corrosion greatly reduces fatigue strength: pits act as stress raisers, and corrosion fatigue can crack a shaft at stresses a clean shaft would tolerate. Protecting the shaft is therefore a reliability issue, not a cosmetic one.

Isolation. In many split case designs the wetted length of the shaft is covered by the sleeves and impeller hub, with O-rings or gaskets at each joint, so the pumped liquid never reaches the shaft. Damaged or omitted O-rings let liquid creep under the sleeves, where crevice corrosion can develop out of sight.

Material selection. Where the shaft may be wetted, its material must suit the liquid; stainless or duplex grades are used in corrosive services. Shaft, sleeve and impeller materials should be compatible, because dissimilar metals in contact in a conductive liquid such as seawater can promote galvanic corrosion of the less noble metal.

Keeping water out of bearings. Deflectors (flingers) and bearing housing seals stop leakage running along the shaft into the bearing housings, protecting journals and bearings.

Idle periods. Stand-by pumps and spare rotors should be protected according to OEM and site preservation procedures, since standing liquid and condensation can pit journals and other surfaces.

impeller-shroud-nde.summary: The NDE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the non-drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the NDE eye, where the NDE impeller wear ring is fitted.
impeller-shroud-nde.function: The NDE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the non-drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the NDE eye, where the NDE impeller wear ring is fitted.
impeller-shroud-nde.operatingPrinciple: It contains the liquid between the vanes so it cannot short-circuit across the vane edges. Its outer face is exposed to the rotating liquid in the NDE side room; the pressure on this face, opposing the pressure on the DE shroud, is one half of the axial force balance.
impeller-shroud-nde.construction: Cast integral with the vanes and hub. At the eye it carries the impeller wear ring or a machined wear surface. Its outer face is also where balance corrections are commonly made, within OEM limits.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Its profile and the side-room gap affect disc friction loss and the axial force on the NDE side. Wear or damage at the eye affects wear-ring clearance and leakage.

keyConcepts.title: Impeller balance
keyConcepts.body: The impeller balance arrangement refers to how the impeller's mass distribution is corrected so it rotates without significant unbalance. Corrections are commonly made by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds. Material is removed by machining or grinding on the shroud outer faces at the positions found on the balancing machine, within the depth and location limits set by the OEM, without thinning shrouds excessively or cutting into vanes.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction influences hydraulic loading
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller experiences three broad kinds of hydraulic load: axial, radial and fluctuating.

Axial forces come mainly from pressure on the outer faces of the shrouds. Liquid in each side room rotates at a fraction of impeller speed, so its pressure falls from the periphery towards the wear ring. In a single-suction impeller the eye side is at suction pressure inside the wear ring while the back shroud sees higher pressure over a larger area, giving a net thrust towards the suction. In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

Radial forces come from the pressure distribution around the impeller periphery. Double suction does not reduce them in itself: they depend on head, impeller diameter, total outlet width and operating point relative to BEP, and they are addressed by volute design, for example a double volute.

Fluctuating forces arise as each vane passes the tongue, giving pulses at vane passing frequency, and from recirculation at part load. Staggering the DE and NDE vane sets, as many designs do, spreads these pulses in time and reduces their amplitude.

The torque reaction on the impeller passes to the shaft through the key.

keyConcepts.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.

Caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

keyConcepts.title: Why impeller balance is important
keyConcepts.body:
No impeller is perfectly uniform. Variations in shroud and vane thickness, machining offsets and the keyway mean that the mass centre does not lie exactly on the rotation axis. This residual unbalance U (mass multiplied by its radius) produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, which rises with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the force for the same unbalance.

The force rotates with the shaft and is reacted by both bearings, so it appears as vibration at running speed (1x). It adds cyclic load to the bearings and shaft, makes seal faces and packing work with more movement, and can make the wear rings rub, which opens clearances and reduces efficiency. Near a critical speed the response is amplified.

A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (static plus couple unbalance). Two-plane dynamic balancing is therefore commonly used, with correction by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds within OEM limits. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11; the grade, and whether the impeller alone or the complete rotor is balanced, come from the OEM or purchaser specification. The key convention used during balancing must match the assembled rotor.

Balance can change in service through erosion, corrosion, deposits, repairs and trimming. Mechanical balancing cannot correct hydraulic unbalance from vane-to-vane differences.

The labels 'front' (NDE) and 'rear' (DE) used in this module only identify the sides; they do not mean the front and back shrouds of a single-suction impeller.
Shape is illustrative.

impeller-shroud-de.summary: The DE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the DE eye, where the DE impeller wear ring is fitted.
impeller-shroud-de.function: The DE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the DE eye, where the DE impeller wear ring is fitted.
impeller-shroud-de.operatingPrinciple: It mirrors the NDE shroud. The pressure of the rotating liquid in the DE side room acts on its outer face in the opposite direction to the corresponding force on the NDE shroud, so the two largely balance when the arrangement is symmetrical.
impeller-shroud-de.construction: Cast integral with the vanes and hub, carrying the DE impeller wear ring or wear surface at the eye. Its outer face is a common location for balance corrections, within OEM limits.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Any difference between DE and NDE shroud geometry, side-room gaps or wear-ring clearances upsets the axial force balance. Damage at the eye increases DE leakage.

keyConcepts.title: Impeller balance
keyConcepts.body: The impeller balance arrangement refers to how the impeller's mass distribution is corrected so it rotates without significant unbalance. Corrections are commonly made by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds. Material is removed by machining or grinding on the shroud outer faces at the positions found on the balancing machine, within the depth and location limits set by the OEM, without thinning shrouds excessively or cutting into vanes.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction influences hydraulic loading
keyConcepts.body:
The impeller experiences three broad kinds of hydraulic load: axial, radial and fluctuating.

Axial forces come mainly from pressure on the outer faces of the shrouds. Liquid in each side room rotates at a fraction of impeller speed, so its pressure falls from the periphery towards the wear ring. In a single-suction impeller the eye side is at suction pressure inside the wear ring while the back shroud sees higher pressure over a larger area, giving a net thrust towards the suction. In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

Radial forces come from the pressure distribution around the impeller periphery. Double suction does not reduce them in itself: they depend on head, impeller diameter, total outlet width and operating point relative to BEP, and they are addressed by volute design, for example a double volute.

Fluctuating forces arise as each vane passes the tongue, giving pulses at vane passing frequency, and from recirculation at part load. Staggering the DE and NDE vane sets, as many designs do, spreads these pulses in time and reduces their amplitude.

The torque reaction on the impeller passes to the shaft through the key.

keyConcepts.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.

Caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

keyConcepts.title: Why impeller balance is important
keyConcepts.body:
No impeller is perfectly uniform. Variations in shroud and vane thickness, machining offsets and the keyway mean that the mass centre does not lie exactly on the rotation axis. This residual unbalance U (mass multiplied by its radius) produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, which rises with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the force for the same unbalance.

The force rotates with the shaft and is reacted by both bearings, so it appears as vibration at running speed (1x). It adds cyclic load to the bearings and shaft, makes seal faces and packing work with more movement, and can make the wear rings rub, which opens clearances and reduces efficiency. Near a critical speed the response is amplified.

A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (static plus couple unbalance). Two-plane dynamic balancing is therefore commonly used, with correction by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds within OEM limits. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11; the grade, and whether the impeller alone or the complete rotor is balanced, come from the OEM or purchaser specification. The key convention used during balancing must match the assembled rotor.

Balance can change in service through erosion, corrosion, deposits, repairs and trimming. Mechanical balancing cannot correct hydraulic unbalance from vane-to-vane differences.

impeller-vanes-nde.summary: The NDE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the NDE eye.
impeller-vanes-nde.function: The NDE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the NDE eye. They transfer energy from the rotating impeller to the liquid entering from the non-drive-end side.
impeller-vanes-nde.operatingPrinciple: Liquid entering the eye meets the vane leading edges; near design flow the relative flow approaches roughly in line with the vane inlet angle (low incidence). As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller, increasing its angular momentum, so its pressure and absolute velocity rise. Backward-curved vanes, usual in centrifugal pumps, tend to give a head that falls steadily as flow increases.
impeller-vanes-nde.construction: Cast between the NDE shroud and the central web. Vane number, inlet and outlet angles, thickness and wrap are hydraulic design choices. In many designs the NDE vanes are angularly offset (staggered) from the DE vanes.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The vane inlet region largely determines NPSH required and cavitation behaviour on this side; the outlet region influences head and pressure pulsations. Damage or blockage on one side makes the two halves unequal, affecting hydraulic balance and vibration.

keyConcepts.title: How liquid moves through the impeller passages
keyConcepts.body:
Each half of the impeller works in the same way. Liquid leaves its side suction chamber and enters the eye moving mainly axially, sometimes with a little pre-swirl set by the chamber shape. In the eye it turns from axial towards radial, guided by the shroud on the outside and the hub and central web on the inside, and meets the vane leading edges.

Velocity triangles describe the flow. Relative to the rotating vanes the liquid has a relative velocity w; the vanes move at peripheral speed u = omega r; the absolute velocity c seen by a stationary observer is the vector sum of w and u. Near design flow the relative flow meets the vanes with small incidence. Away from design flow incidence increases, raising losses and possibly triggering cavitation or recirculation at the eye.

As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller and its angular momentum increases. The Euler equation gives the ideal head: H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g, where cu is the tangential component of absolute velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). Static pressure rises through the passages because of the centrifugal effect and because the relative velocity is slowed in the widening, backward-curved passages. At the outlet the liquid has higher pressure and high absolute velocity, and the two streams merge into the volute.

Caution: The Euler head is an ideal value. Real head is lower because the flow does not follow the vanes perfectly (slip) and because of hydraulic losses.

keyConcepts.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
keyConcepts.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.

Caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

impeller-vanes-de.summary: The DE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the DE eye.
impeller-vanes-de.function: The DE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the DE eye. They transfer energy to the liquid entering from the drive-end side.
impeller-vanes-de.operatingPrinciple: They work in the same way as the NDE vanes. Both vane sets discharge into the same volute, so the two streams merge at the impeller outlet. impeller-eye-nde.summary: The NDE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the non-drive-end side, between the hub and the shroud lip, through which liquid from the NDE suction chamber enters the impeller.
impeller-eye-nde.function: The NDE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the non-drive-end side, between the hub and the shroud lip, through which liquid from the NDE suction chamber enters the impeller. This marker identifies it in the model.
impeller-eye-nde.operatingPrinciple: The lowest pressure in the pump occurs around the eye and the vane leading edges. If local pressure falls to the vapour pressure of the liquid, vapour bubbles form and then collapse as pressure rises inside the passages: this is cavitation. Eye area and inlet velocity are therefore central to NPSH required. Suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.
impeller-eye-nde.construction: Defined by the shroud inner lip (with its wear ring), the hub surface and the vane leading edges.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Dividing the flow between two eyes reduces the flow each eye must handle. For a given total flow and speed this tends to allow lower eye velocities and lower NPSH required than a comparable single-suction impeller, although the real benefit depends on the design. In practice each eye receives a share set by the inflow conditions, not exactly half.

keyConcepts.title: What double suction means
keyConcepts.body:
A double-suction (double-entry) impeller has two inlets, called eyes, one on each side, instead of the single eye of an end-suction impeller. It can be pictured as two single-suction impellers placed back to back and cast as one piece: a central hub and web separate two sets of vanes, each enclosed by its own outer shroud, and both halves discharge from a common outer periphery into one volute.

In this pump, liquid enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half and is divided into two side suction chambers. One feeds the drive-end eye and the other the non-drive-end eye, so the two streams approach the impeller axially from opposite directions. Inside the impeller each stream turns outwards through its own vane passages, and the two streams merge at the impeller outlet and leave through the single discharge nozzle.

The pump is still single-stage: the liquid passes through one impeller once. Double suction describes the number of inlets, not the number of stages. Because the shaft passes right through the impeller and needs support on both sides, double-suction impellers pair naturally with between-bearings rotors and axially split casings, although they are also used elsewhere, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.

keyConcepts.title: Why liquid enters from both sides
keyConcepts.body:
Feeding the impeller from both sides divides the total flow between two eyes. Several tendencies follow, although the size of each benefit depends on the individual design.

Suction performance. For a given total flow and speed, each eye handles only part of the flow, so inlet velocities can be lower for a given eye size. Lower inlet velocity tends to reduce NPSH required, which helps where available suction head is limited, or allows a higher speed for the same NPSH margin. For this reason suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.

Flow capacity. For a given impeller diameter and speed, a double-suction impeller can usually pass more flow than a comparable single-suction impeller because it has roughly twice the inlet area. This makes the type common for large flows at moderate head, for example in water supply, cooling water, irrigation and fire service.

Axial thrust. With the inlets facing in opposite directions, the axial hydraulic forces on the two halves largely oppose each other in a symmetrical arrangement, so thrust bearing duty is much lower than for a single-suction impeller of similar size, though not zero.

The trade-offs are a more complex casting, two shaft seals, a rotor supported at both ends, and sensitivity to uneven inflow from the suction piping.

Caution: These are tendencies, not guarantees. Actual NPSH required and flow capacity come from the OEM performance curves, and conventions for calculating specific speed (total flow or flow per eye) should always be stated when comparing values.

keyConcepts.title: How liquid moves through the impeller passages
keyConcepts.body:
Each half of the impeller works in the same way. Liquid leaves its side suction chamber and enters the eye moving mainly axially, sometimes with a little pre-swirl set by the chamber shape. In the eye it turns from axial towards radial, guided by the shroud on the outside and the hub and central web on the inside, and meets the vane leading edges.

Velocity triangles describe the flow. Relative to the rotating vanes the liquid has a relative velocity w; the vanes move at peripheral speed u = omega r; the absolute velocity c seen by a stationary observer is the vector sum of w and u. Near design flow the relative flow meets the vanes with small incidence. Away from design flow incidence increases, raising losses and possibly triggering cavitation or recirculation at the eye.

As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller and its angular momentum increases. The Euler equation gives the ideal head: H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g, where cu is the tangential component of absolute velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). Static pressure rises through the passages because of the centrifugal effect and because the relative velocity is slowed in the widening, backward-curved passages. At the outlet the liquid has higher pressure and high absolute velocity, and the two streams merge into the volute.

Caution: The Euler head is an ideal value. Real head is lower because the flow does not follow the vanes perfectly (slip) and because of hydraulic losses.

keyConcepts.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
keyConcepts.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.

Caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

impeller-eye-de.summary: The DE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the drive-end side, through which liquid from the DE suction chamber enters the impeller.
impeller-eye-de.function: The DE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the drive-end side, through which liquid from the DE suction chamber enters the impeller. This marker identifies it in the model.
impeller-eye-de.operatingPrinciple: It works in the same way as the NDE eye, with flow approaching from the opposite axial direction. The DE suction chamber surrounds the shaft on the coupling side, so its flow path differs slightly from the NDE chamber in many designs.
impeller-eye-de.construction: Defined by the DE shroud lip and wear ring, the hub surface and the DE vane leading edges.

failureModes.cause: Insufficient NPSH available: low suction source level, excessive suction lift, or high suction-side friction losses from a long, undersized or fouled suction line.; Partly closed suction valve, or blocked suction strainer or intake screen, adding loss immediately upstream of the pump.; Liquid temperature higher than the design basis, which raises the vapour pressure and reduces NPSH available.
failureModes.signs: Crackling, rattling or gravel-like noise from the casing near the suction side, often changing with flow.; Fluctuating discharge pressure, flow and motor current.; Increased broadband vibration at the bearing housings compared with the baseline.

failureModes.mode: Unequal flow distribution between the two eyes
failureModes.cause: Suction elbow lying in the plane of the shaft, installed close to the suction nozzle.; Insufficient straight pipe upstream of the suction nozzle compared with the OEM recommendation or pump piping guidance.; Partly open valve, strainer or other fitting close to the suction nozzle.
failureModes.signs: Cavitation-type noise, sometimes louder towards one end of the casing.; Non-drive-end (locating) bearing running warmer than its own baseline, or its temperature fluctuating.; Increased vibration, possibly with a larger axial component.

failureModes.cause: Falling level in the suction tank or sump, or reduced pressure in the suction vessel.; Blocked suction strainer, foot valve or intake screen.; Partly closed or failed suction isolation valve, for example a gate detached from its stem.
failureModes.signs: Suction gauge reading lower than normal for the same flow.; Cavitation noise and fluctuating discharge pressure.; Falling flow and head.

failureModes.cause: Missing, damaged or unsuitable suction strainer or intake screen.; Construction or maintenance debris left in the pipework, such as rags, gasket offcuts, welding debris or tools.; Fibrous or solids-laden liquid beyond the solids-handling capability of the pump.
failureModes.signs: Gradual or sudden drop in flow and head at the same valve setting and speed.; Increased vibration, often with a once-per-revolution (unbalance-type) component.; Change in motor current, commonly a reduction as flow falls, although the direction depends on the pump curve and the nature of the blockage.

failureModes.cause: Leaking suction flanges, gaskets, valve stem packing or instrument connections where the suction is below atmospheric pressure.; Insufficient submergence at the suction source, allowing surface vortices to draw air into the suction pipe.; Air pockets at high points of the suction line, or an eccentric suction reducer fitted flat side down instead of flat side up.
failureModes.signs: Erratic or falling discharge pressure and flow, with the gauge needle fluctuating.; Noise resembling cavitation (crackling or gurgling) that does not clearly follow NPSH conditions.; Fluctuating motor current.

inspection: Inspect as for the NDE eye and record differences between the two sides.
maintenance: Maintain according to the OEM manual and site procedures.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: If the DE eye receives more or less flow than the NDE eye, or a distorted velocity profile, its local NPSH required and its share of axial force change; cavitation may start on one side before the other.

impeller-bore.summary: The impeller bore is the machined central hole through the hub that fits on the shaft impeller seat and centres the impeller on the shaft axis.
impeller-bore.function: The impeller bore is the machined central hole through the hub that fits on the shaft impeller seat and centres the impeller on the shaft axis.
impeller-bore.operatingPrinciple: The fit between bore and seat keeps the impeller concentric while it rotates. In this keyed design torque is transmitted mainly through the key; the fit provides centring and resists fretting.
impeller-bore.construction: Precision machined and normally held concentric with the wear-ring diameters and square to the hub faces. The fit class (clearance, transition or light interference) is OEM-specific.

keyConcepts.body: An oversize or worn bore lets the impeller sit off-centre, causing unbalance, wear-ring rubs and fretting; an excessively tight fit makes removal difficult and can damage parts.

impeller-keyway.summary: The impeller keyway is the axial slot in the impeller bore that receives the impeller key, which locks the impeller to the shaft in rotation.
impeller-keyway.function: The impeller keyway is the axial slot in the impeller bore that receives the impeller key, which locks the impeller to the shaft in rotation.
impeller-keyway.operatingPrinciple: The key sits partly in the shaft keyway and partly in the impeller keyway. Torque passes from the shaft keyway wall into the key and from the key into the side wall of the impeller keyway.
impeller-keyway.construction: Machined (typically broached or slotted) along the bore. Width tolerance and angular position relative to the vanes are controlled.

impeller-key.summary: The impeller key is a rectangular key that transmits torque from the shaft to the impeller.
impeller-key.function: The impeller key is a rectangular key that transmits torque from the shaft to the impeller.
impeller-key.operatingPrinciple: In operation the key is loaded in shear across its section at the shaft-to-hub interface and in compression on its sides. For a key of width w and engaged length L on a shaft of diameter d carrying torque T, the average shear stress is approximately tau = 2T / (d w L), assuming the force acts at the shaft surface and is evenly spread along the key. Real stress is not uniform, so design uses margins and the OEM's sizing.
impeller-key.construction: Usually a parallel key fitted in the shaft keyway and engaging the impeller keyway; length, section and material are set by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: A correctly fitted key prevents relative rotation and fretting. A key that is too high can lift the impeller off-centre; one that is too loose allows movement. Key length and fit also matter for rotor balance.

keyConcepts.title: Why impeller balance is important
keyConcepts.body:
No impeller is perfectly uniform. Variations in shroud and vane thickness, machining offsets and the keyway mean that the mass centre does not lie exactly on the rotation axis. This residual unbalance U (mass multiplied by its radius) produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, which rises with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the force for the same unbalance.

The force rotates with the shaft and is reacted by both bearings, so it appears as vibration at running speed (1x). It adds cyclic load to the bearings and shaft, makes seal faces and packing work with more movement, and can make the wear rings rub, which opens clearances and reduces efficiency. Near a critical speed the response is amplified.

A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (static plus couple unbalance). Two-plane dynamic balancing is therefore commonly used, with correction by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds within OEM limits. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11; the grade, and whether the impeller alone or the complete rotor is balanced, come from the OEM or purchaser specification. The key convention used during balancing must match the assembled rotor.

Balance can change in service through erosion, corrosion, deposits, repairs and trimming. Mechanical balancing cannot correct hydraulic unbalance from vane-to-vane differences.

keyConcepts.title: How the shaft transmits torque
keyConcepts.body:
Power flows from the motor shaft through the motor coupling hub, the flexible elements and spacer, and the pump coupling hub into the pump shaft at its drive-end extension. The shaft then carries the torque past the DE bearing and DE seal to the impeller seat, where the impeller key transfers it into the hub. The NDE section beyond the impeller carries only small torques from bearing and seal friction.

Torque, power and speed are related by P = T omega, with omega = 2 pi N / 60 for N in rev/min. In practical units, T (N m) = 9549 x P (kW) / N (rev/min). For example, a pump absorbing 200 kW at 1480 rev/min transmits about 9549 x 200 / 1480, roughly 1290 N m, through its DE shaft section. This is an illustrative calculation only.

At each keyed joint the torque is passed as a tangential force at the shaft surface, approximately F = 2T / d, carried by contact pressure on the key sides and by shear across the key section. Keyed joints are therefore checked for key shear, key-side bearing pressure and keyway stress. Starting transients, for example direct-on-line starting, can produce torques above the steady running value, so the OEM sizes the shaft and keys with margin for such conditions.

Caution: The worked figure is illustrative. Shaft and key sizing for a real pump is done by the OEM, including starting and transient torques.

keyConcepts.title: Torsional stress in the shaft
keyConcepts.body:
When a solid round shaft of diameter d carries a torque T, the shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface: tau = T r / J, where J = pi d^4 / 32 is the polar second moment of area. At the surface (r = d / 2) this gives tau = 16 T / (pi d^3). For a hollow shaft of outer diameter D and bore di, tau = 16 T D / (pi (D^4 - di^4)). These formulas assume a straight, homogeneous, linear-elastic shaft of uniform circular section in pure torsion, away from changes of section.

The angle of twist over a length L is theta = T L / (G J), where G is the shear modulus. Twist is rarely limiting in a short pump shaft, but the torsional natural frequencies of the complete pump, coupling and motor train may need checking, for example with variable-speed drives.

In a pump shaft torsion never acts alone: the DE section between coupling and impeller carries full torque together with bending. For a solid shaft the maximum shear stress theory gives tau_max = (16 / (pi d^3)) sqrt(M^2 + T^2), and the distortion-energy (von Mises) approach gives sigma_e = sqrt(sigma^2 + 3 tau^2). Keyways, shoulders and threads raise local stresses above these nominal values, so stress concentration factors and fatigue criteria are applied in real design.

Caution: Nominal formulas ignore stress concentration and fatigue. They are for understanding, not for sizing a shaft.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Its wear, together with that of the DE casing ring, sets the DE clearance. If DE and NDE clearances become unequal, side-room pressures differ and residual axial thrust changes.

keyConcepts.title: Why wear rings and clearances affect performance
keyConcepts.body:
Each eye has a pair of wear rings, one on the impeller and one in the casing, separated by a small radial running clearance. Outside the gap is the side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure; inside is the eye, at suction pressure, so liquid leaks back continuously. As a simple approximation the leakage behaves like flow through an annular orifice, QL = Cd A sqrt(2 dp / rho), where A is the clearance area and dp the pressure difference, so leakage rises roughly in proportion to the clearance.

Efficiency. The leakage has received energy from the impeller but is not delivered, so the impeller must pass more flow than the pump delivers. As rings wear, delivered flow at a given head falls, head at a given flow falls, and power per unit of delivered flow rises.

Suction behaviour. The leakage jet re-enters the eye and disturbs the inlet flow; heavy leakage can raise NPSH required and promote eye recirculation.

Pressure distribution and thrust. Leakage through each side room modifies its swirl and pressure, so unequal DE and NDE clearances unbalance the shroud forces and increase residual thrust.

Rotordynamics. The liquid film in a tight annular gap acts like a weak bearing, adding stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). Worn rings lose this support, which tends to lower the wet critical speed and increase vibration.

Caution: A clearance that is too tight risks rubbing, galling and seizure. Use the OEM clearances and renewal limits, and measure both eyes.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
Geometry is illustrative.

shaft.summary: The pump shaft carries the impeller between the two bearings and transmits torque from the motor, via the coupling, to the impeller.
shaft.function: The pump shaft carries the impeller between the two bearings and transmits torque from the motor, via the coupling, to the impeller. It also carries the sleeves, seals, deflectors, bearings and the pump coupling hub.
shaft.operatingPrinciple:
Torque enters at the coupling end (DE) and leaves through the impeller key, so the section between coupling and impeller carries essentially full torque, while the NDE end carries only small torques such as bearing and seal friction. The shaft is also loaded in bending by impeller weight, radial hydraulic force and coupling forces, and is supported by the DE floating bearing and the NDE locating bearing, which also carries residual axial thrust.

Because the shaft rotates under largely stationary loads, every point on its surface goes through a complete reversal of bending stress each revolution, so fatigue strength is a key design criterion.
shaft.construction: A stepped, machined round bar with an impeller seat and keyway, threads for sleeve nuts and bearing locknuts, bearing journals, shoulders and a keyed coupling end. Critical diameters are ground or finish turned to close tolerances and concentricity. In many designs the shaft is isolated from the pumped liquid by sleeves, the impeller hub and O-rings, often described as a dry shaft.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Shaft stiffness governs deflection at the wear rings and seals and the critical speeds; strength governs fatigue margin at stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders and threads; straightness and concentricity affect runout and balance.

keyConcepts.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
keyConcepts.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.

Caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

keyConcepts.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
keyConcepts.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.

Caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: Why impeller balance is important
keyConcepts.body:
No impeller is perfectly uniform. Variations in shroud and vane thickness, machining offsets and the keyway mean that the mass centre does not lie exactly on the rotation axis. This residual unbalance U (mass multiplied by its radius) produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, which rises with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the force for the same unbalance.

The force rotates with the shaft and is reacted by both bearings, so it appears as vibration at running speed (1x). It adds cyclic load to the bearings and shaft, makes seal faces and packing work with more movement, and can make the wear rings rub, which opens clearances and reduces efficiency. Near a critical speed the response is amplified.

A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (static plus couple unbalance). Two-plane dynamic balancing is therefore commonly used, with correction by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds within OEM limits. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11; the grade, and whether the impeller alone or the complete rotor is balanced, come from the OEM or purchaser specification. The key convention used during balancing must match the assembled rotor.

Balance can change in service through erosion, corrosion, deposits, repairs and trimming. Mechanical balancing cannot correct hydraulic unbalance from vane-to-vane differences.

keyConcepts.title: How the shaft transmits torque
keyConcepts.body:
Power flows from the motor shaft through the motor coupling hub, the flexible elements and spacer, and the pump coupling hub into the pump shaft at its drive-end extension. The shaft then carries the torque past the DE bearing and DE seal to the impeller seat, where the impeller key transfers it into the hub. The NDE section beyond the impeller carries only small torques from bearing and seal friction.

Torque, power and speed are related by P = T omega, with omega = 2 pi N / 60 for N in rev/min. In practical units, T (N m) = 9549 x P (kW) / N (rev/min). For example, a pump absorbing 200 kW at 1480 rev/min transmits about 9549 x 200 / 1480, roughly 1290 N m, through its DE shaft section. This is an illustrative calculation only.

At each keyed joint the torque is passed as a tangential force at the shaft surface, approximately F = 2T / d, carried by contact pressure on the key sides and by shear across the key section. Keyed joints are therefore checked for key shear, key-side bearing pressure and keyway stress. Starting transients, for example direct-on-line starting, can produce torques above the steady running value, so the OEM sizes the shaft and keys with margin for such conditions.

Caution: The worked figure is illustrative. Shaft and key sizing for a real pump is done by the OEM, including starting and transient torques.

shaft-keyways.summary: The shaft keyways are axial slots machined in the shaft that receive the impeller key and the coupling key, locking these parts to the shaft in rotation.
shaft-keyways.function: The shaft keyways are axial slots machined in the shaft that receive the impeller key and the coupling key, locking these parts to the shaft in rotation.
shaft-keyways.operatingPrinciple: Torque is transferred by contact pressure between the key sides and the keyway walls. The coupling keyway carries the full driving torque into the shaft; the impeller keyway carries it out to the impeller.
shaft-keyways.construction: Milled into the shaft at the impeller seat and at the coupling end. Keyway ends are either rounded (end-milled, profile type) or run out gradually (sled-runner type) depending on design; the end form and root radii influence stress concentration.

keyConcepts.body: Keyways are among the most highly stressed locations on the shaft, combining torsional stress with reversing bending stress and a geometric stress raiser. Fatigue cracks in shafts commonly start at keyway ends or root corners, so keyway geometry and finish matter for shaft life.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft bending
keyConcepts.body:
Between its two bearings the shaft behaves like a beam. The main transverse loads are the weight of impeller and shaft, the radial hydraulic force from the volute, the rotating force from residual unbalance, and forces from the coupling, which increase with misalignment. Because the impeller sits roughly at mid-span in this design, a simple model is a simply supported beam with a central point load F over span L. The maximum bending moment is then M = F L / 4 at the load, and the bending stress at the surface of a solid round section of diameter d is sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3).

The key feature of a pump shaft is that it rotates while most of these loads, such as gravity and the volute radial force, stay fixed in direction. A point on the surface passes from tension to compression and back every revolution, so the bending stress is fully reversed. Over millions of cycles this is a fatigue problem: stresses must stay below the material's fatigue strength, with allowance for stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders, threads and press fits, and for surface condition and corrosion.

In a single volute the radial hydraulic load grows as operation moves away from BEP, so prolonged running at very low or very high flow raises bending stress and fatigue risk.

Caution: The beam formulas assume a uniform solid shaft, rigid simple supports and a single central load. Real shafts are stepped and run in flexible bearings; design checks are the OEM responsibility.

keyConcepts.title: Torsional stress in the shaft
keyConcepts.body:
When a solid round shaft of diameter d carries a torque T, the shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface: tau = T r / J, where J = pi d^4 / 32 is the polar second moment of area. At the surface (r = d / 2) this gives tau = 16 T / (pi d^3). For a hollow shaft of outer diameter D and bore di, tau = 16 T D / (pi (D^4 - di^4)). These formulas assume a straight, homogeneous, linear-elastic shaft of uniform circular section in pure torsion, away from changes of section.

The angle of twist over a length L is theta = T L / (G J), where G is the shear modulus. Twist is rarely limiting in a short pump shaft, but the torsional natural frequencies of the complete pump, coupling and motor train may need checking, for example with variable-speed drives.

In a pump shaft torsion never acts alone: the DE section between coupling and impeller carries full torque together with bending. For a solid shaft the maximum shear stress theory gives tau_max = (16 / (pi d^3)) sqrt(M^2 + T^2), and the distortion-energy (von Mises) approach gives sigma_e = sqrt(sigma^2 + 3 tau^2). Keyways, shoulders and threads raise local stresses above these nominal values, so stress concentration factors and fatigue criteria are applied in real design.

Caution: Nominal formulas ignore stress concentration and fatigue. They are for understanding, not for sizing a shaft.

shaft-shoulders.summary: Shaft shoulders are the steps between diameters that give positive axial location to the bearings and, depending on design, to other parts such as spacers or the coupling hub.
shaft-shoulders.function: Shaft shoulders are the steps between diameters that give positive axial location to the bearings and, depending on design, to other parts such as spacers or the coupling hub.
shaft-shoulders.operatingPrinciple: At the NDE the locating bearing inner ring is clamped against a shoulder by the locknut, so residual axial thrust passes from the shaft through the shoulder into the bearing. Every change of diameter also concentrates stress under bending and torsion.
shaft-shoulders.construction: Machined square to the axis with a fillet radius at the root. At bearing seats the fillet must be smaller than the bearing ring's corner chamfer so the ring seats fully, as given in bearing manufacturer data; elsewhere larger radii reduce stress concentration.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Shoulder squareness affects bearing alignment and running accuracy. Sharp or damaged fillets are fatigue crack initiation sites.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft impeller seat
keyConcepts.body: The impeller seat is the machined shaft diameter on which the impeller hub bore fits; its locating diameter centres the impeller on the shaft axis. Usually one of the largest shaft diameters, ground or finish turned concentric with the bearing journals and carrying the impeller keyway. The sleeves and the threads for the sleeve nuts lie outboard of it on each side.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft bending
keyConcepts.body:
Between its two bearings the shaft behaves like a beam. The main transverse loads are the weight of impeller and shaft, the radial hydraulic force from the volute, the rotating force from residual unbalance, and forces from the coupling, which increase with misalignment. Because the impeller sits roughly at mid-span in this design, a simple model is a simply supported beam with a central point load F over span L. The maximum bending moment is then M = F L / 4 at the load, and the bending stress at the surface of a solid round section of diameter d is sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3).

The key feature of a pump shaft is that it rotates while most of these loads, such as gravity and the volute radial force, stay fixed in direction. A point on the surface passes from tension to compression and back every revolution, so the bending stress is fully reversed. Over millions of cycles this is a fatigue problem: stresses must stay below the material's fatigue strength, with allowance for stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders, threads and press fits, and for surface condition and corrosion.

In a single volute the radial hydraulic load grows as operation moves away from BEP, so prolonged running at very low or very high flow raises bending stress and fatigue risk.

Caution: The beam formulas assume a uniform solid shaft, rigid simple supports and a single central load. Real shafts are stepped and run in flexible bearings; design checks are the OEM responsibility.

keyConcepts.title: Torsional stress in the shaft
keyConcepts.body:
When a solid round shaft of diameter d carries a torque T, the shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface: tau = T r / J, where J = pi d^4 / 32 is the polar second moment of area. At the surface (r = d / 2) this gives tau = 16 T / (pi d^3). For a hollow shaft of outer diameter D and bore di, tau = 16 T D / (pi (D^4 - di^4)). These formulas assume a straight, homogeneous, linear-elastic shaft of uniform circular section in pure torsion, away from changes of section.

The angle of twist over a length L is theta = T L / (G J), where G is the shear modulus. Twist is rarely limiting in a short pump shaft, but the torsional natural frequencies of the complete pump, coupling and motor train may need checking, for example with variable-speed drives.

In a pump shaft torsion never acts alone: the DE section between coupling and impeller carries full torque together with bending. For a solid shaft the maximum shear stress theory gives tau_max = (16 / (pi d^3)) sqrt(M^2 + T^2), and the distortion-energy (von Mises) approach gives sigma_e = sqrt(sigma^2 + 3 tau^2). Keyways, shoulders and threads raise local stresses above these nominal values, so stress concentration factors and fatigue criteria are applied in real design.

Caution: Nominal formulas ignore stress concentration and fatigue. They are for understanding, not for sizing a shaft.

shaft-bearing-journals.summary: The bearing journals are the precision shaft diameters on which the inner rings of the DE and NDE rolling bearings are mounted.
shaft-bearing-journals.function: The bearing journals are the precision shaft diameters on which the inner rings of the DE and NDE rolling bearings are mounted.
shaft-bearing-journals.operatingPrinciple: The inner rings rotate with the shaft relative to a largely stationary load direction, so they are commonly given an interference fit to stop them creeping on the shaft; the fit is chosen to the bearing manufacturer's and OEM's recommendations. The two journals do different jobs: at the NDE the locating bearing is clamped axially between a shaft shoulder and the locknut and carries residual axial thrust; at the DE the floating bearing allows axial movement, commonly by letting its outer ring slide in the housing, so the shaft can expand thermally without loading the bearings axially.
shaft-bearing-journals.construction: Ground diameters with controlled roundness, cylindricity and surface finish, concentric with the impeller seat, with adjacent shoulders and threaded sections for locknuts.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Journal size, form and finish influence bearing internal clearance after mounting, ring seating and bearing life. A damaged or undersize journal lets the inner ring creep, generating wear, heat and eventually bearing failure.

keyConcepts.title: Critical speed
keyConcepts.body:
A rotor on its bearings has natural frequencies of lateral (bending) vibration. When running speed coincides with one of them, even a small unbalance force excites a large response; that speed is a critical speed.

A simple estimate treats the rotor as a single mass m on a massless shaft of lateral stiffness k: omega_c = sqrt(k / m). Since the static deflection under the rotor's own weight is delta = m g / k, this can also be written omega_c = sqrt(g / delta), or approximately N_c = 946 / sqrt(delta) rev/min with delta in millimetres. A stiffer or lighter rotor therefore has a higher critical speed. Real rotors are analysed with methods that include distributed mass, stepped diameters and bearing and support flexibility.

Pump rotors behave differently dry and wet. Running in liquid adds mass, while the close clearances at the wear rings add stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). As the rings wear this support decreases and the wet critical speed tends to fall, possibly towards running speed.

Many single-stage between-bearings pumps are designed with the first critical speed sufficiently above the operating speed range (a stiff-shaft design), but this is design-specific, and separation margins are set by the OEM and applicable specification. With variable-speed drives the whole speed range must be considered, including resonances of bearing housings, baseplate and foundation.

Caution: The single-mass formula is a rough first estimate that ignores bearing flexibility, gyroscopic effects and fluid forces. Rotordynamic assessment of a real pump is the OEM responsibility.

keyConcepts.title: Protecting the shaft from corrosion
keyConcepts.body:
A pump shaft is highly stressed and subject to fatigue, and corrosion greatly reduces fatigue strength: pits act as stress raisers, and corrosion fatigue can crack a shaft at stresses a clean shaft would tolerate. Protecting the shaft is therefore a reliability issue, not a cosmetic one.

Isolation. In many split case designs the wetted length of the shaft is covered by the sleeves and impeller hub, with O-rings or gaskets at each joint, so the pumped liquid never reaches the shaft. Damaged or omitted O-rings let liquid creep under the sleeves, where crevice corrosion can develop out of sight.

Material selection. Where the shaft may be wetted, its material must suit the liquid; stainless or duplex grades are used in corrosive services. Shaft, sleeve and impeller materials should be compatible, because dissimilar metals in contact in a conductive liquid such as seawater can promote galvanic corrosion of the less noble metal.

Keeping water out of bearings. Deflectors (flingers) and bearing housing seals stop leakage running along the shaft into the bearing housings, protecting journals and bearings.

Idle periods. Stand-by pumps and spare rotors should be protected according to OEM and site preservation procedures, since standing liquid and condensation can pit journals and other surfaces.

keyConcepts.title: Why shaft stiffness matters
keyConcepts.body:
Stiffness is the shaft's resistance to bending under load. For the simple central-load model the lateral stiffness at the impeller is k = 48 E I / L^3, with I = pi d^4 / 64, so k is proportional to E d^4 / L^3. Doubling the diameter increases stiffness sixteen-fold; doubling the bearing span reduces it to one eighth.

An important practical point is that the steels used for shafts, whether carbon, alloy or stainless, have broadly similar elastic moduli. Choosing a stronger steel raises the allowable stress but does little for stiffness, which comes mainly from geometry: diameter and span.

Stiffness controls several things at once. It limits deflection at the wear rings, keeping clearances uniform and avoiding rubs. It limits movement and tilt at the mechanical seal faces and uneven wear of packing and sleeves. It limits the slope at the bearings, keeping them aligned. And it raises the lateral critical speeds, since omega_c is proportional to sqrt(k / m), helping to keep them away from the running speed range.

The designer balances stiffness against other needs: a larger shaft needs larger seals and bearings, and in a double-suction impeller a larger shaft and hub take up eye area, which raises inlet velocity. Supporting the impeller near mid-span between two bearings is an efficient way to obtain stiffness with a moderate diameter.

Caution: These proportionalities come from simple beam theory and are for comparison only; they ignore stepped sections and bearing flexibility.

shaft-coupling-end.summary: The coupling mounting section is the drive-end shaft extension on which the pump coupling hub is fitted.
shaft-coupling-end.function: The coupling mounting section is the drive-end shaft extension on which the pump coupling hub is fitted. All the driving torque enters the pump shaft here.
shaft-coupling-end.operatingPrinciple: Motor torque passes through the coupling into the pump hub and then into the shaft through the coupling key and fit. This section carries torsion plus bending from coupling weight and from the reaction forces a flexible coupling produces when it accommodates misalignment.
shaft-coupling-end.construction: A parallel or tapered extension with a keyway, often with a tapped hole or thread in the end for the hub retainer. The fit type depends on the coupling and the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: It is often a reduced diameter carrying full torque, so it is a critical section for torsional and combined stress. Its runout is checked as part of shaft alignment because it affects the readings and the coupling's running.

keyConcepts.title: How the shaft transmits torque
keyConcepts.body:
Power flows from the motor shaft through the motor coupling hub, the flexible elements and spacer, and the pump coupling hub into the pump shaft at its drive-end extension. The shaft then carries the torque past the DE bearing and DE seal to the impeller seat, where the impeller key transfers it into the hub. The NDE section beyond the impeller carries only small torques from bearing and seal friction.

Torque, power and speed are related by P = T omega, with omega = 2 pi N / 60 for N in rev/min. In practical units, T (N m) = 9549 x P (kW) / N (rev/min). For example, a pump absorbing 200 kW at 1480 rev/min transmits about 9549 x 200 / 1480, roughly 1290 N m, through its DE shaft section. This is an illustrative calculation only.

At each keyed joint the torque is passed as a tangential force at the shaft surface, approximately F = 2T / d, carried by contact pressure on the key sides and by shear across the key section. Keyed joints are therefore checked for key shear, key-side bearing pressure and keyway stress. Starting transients, for example direct-on-line starting, can produce torques above the steady running value, so the OEM sizes the shaft and keys with margin for such conditions.

Caution: The worked figure is illustrative. Shaft and key sizing for a real pump is done by the OEM, including starting and transient torques.

keyConcepts.body:

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

shaft-sleeve-de.summary: The DE shaft sleeve covers the shaft from the DE face of the impeller hub out through the DE seal chamber, protecting the shaft and carrying the DE seal or packing running surface.
shaft-sleeve-de.function: The DE shaft sleeve covers the shaft from the DE face of the impeller hub out through the DE seal chamber, protecting the shaft and carrying the DE seal or packing running surface.
shaft-sleeve-de.operatingPrinciple: It is clamped against the impeller hub by the DE sleeve nut, so it also forms half of the impeller's axial location. It rotates with the shaft inside the stationary DE seal chamber.
shaft-sleeve-de.construction: A machined tube with square end faces, a sealing arrangement at the hub joint where fitted, and a drive key or pin. It is renewable.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Its condition directly affects DE seal or packing life, and its end faces affect impeller axial position and runout.

keyConcepts.title: Impeller locking
keyConcepts.body: The impeller locating and locking arrangement fixes the impeller's axial position on the shaft. In this design the impeller hub is clamped between the DE and NDE shaft sleeves, which are held by sleeve nuts threaded onto the shaft on each side. Sleeves slide over the shaft and abut the hub; sleeve nuts retain them and are secured by locking screws or similar devices. In many designs the nut threads are handed so that the drag of rotation tends to tighten rather than loosen them. O-rings or gaskets at the sleeve-to-hub joints keep liquid off the shaft in many designs.

keyConcepts.title: Purpose of the shaft sleeves
keyConcepts.body:
The shaft sleeves on each side of the impeller do several jobs at once.

Wear protection. With gland packing, the packing rubs continuously on the rotating surface beneath it and gradually wears a groove. With a mechanical seal, the secondary sealing elements can fret the surface they sit on. Putting a renewable sleeve under these parts means the shaft itself is not worn; replacing a sleeve is far quicker and cheaper than repairing or replacing a shaft.

Corrosion protection. In many designs the sleeves, the impeller hub and the O-rings or gaskets at their joints keep pumped liquid off the shaft, so the shaft can be made from a strong, economical material while the wetted sleeves use a corrosion-resistant one.

Running surface. The sleeve provides the finish, hardness and runout that the packing or seal needs. Under packing the surface may be hard-coated in some designs.

Impeller location. Each sleeve is clamped between the impeller hub and a sleeve nut, so the two sleeves position and hold the impeller axially on the shaft.

In the mechanical seal variant the sleeves also carry the seal rotating parts, or a cartridge seal's own sleeve fitted over them. Sleeve end faces must be square, and their O-rings renewed whenever they are disturbed.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The condition and alignment of the housing bore decide the bearing fit, its running temperature and the position of the shaft relative to the casing, wear rings and seal. A distorted, worn or misaligned housing can pinch the bearing, stop the floating bearing from moving, or let the outer ring creep (turn slowly) in the bore.

keyConcepts.title: Radial loads on the bearings
keyConcepts.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. Dynamic loads are added by residual unbalance, hydraulic pulsations and rotor-dynamic effects.

The hydraulic radial force exists because the pressure around the impeller periphery is not perfectly uniform. In a single-volute casing it is typically smallest near the best efficiency point (BEP) and grows as the flow moves away from BEP, towards both shut-off and run-out. A double-volute casing, with its splitter rib, substantially reduces this force by setting two opposed volute passages against each other, but does not remove it. The direction of the force also changes with flow rate, so the bearings see a load that varies in both size and direction.

Both bearings share the radial load; how much each carries depends on where the impeller sits along the span and on any overhung load at the coupling end (see 'Bearing reactions'). The drive-end floating bearing carries radial load only; the non-drive-end locating bearing carries its radial share plus the residual axial thrust.

Sustained operation far from BEP increases radial load, shaft deflection, the risk of wear-ring and seal contact, and bearing temperature.

Caution: A double volute or robust bearings do not make every operating point acceptable. Operate within the allowable operating region stated by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing temperature
keyConcepts.body:
Temperature is one of the simplest and most useful indicators of bearing condition. After start-up it rises and then settles at a level set by load, speed, lubricant, ambient conditions and how easily heat flows away to the casing and baseplate. The settled value, recorded at commissioning at a known operating point, becomes the baseline for that bearing.

Trend monitoring compares readings with that baseline, with the other bearing, with ambient temperature and with the operating point at the time. A gradual rise can indicate lubricant degradation, contamination or developing damage. A sudden rise can point to loss of lubricant, over-greasing, a floating bearing that has locked, increased thrust, misalignment or a rubbing housing seal. A short-lived rise after regreasing is normal while excess grease is purged.

Temperature may be measured by permanently installed resistance temperature detectors or thermocouples, where fitted, or with contact or infrared thermometers on the housing surface. Readings taken by different methods or at different points are not directly comparable; a housing surface is cooler than the bearing outer ring. For trending, use the same method at the same marked point every time.

Alarm and trip settings and acceptable temperatures must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site procedure.

Caution: Do not judge temperature by touching the housing; it can be hot enough to burn, and the coupling and shaft are close by. Use instruments and keep clear of rotating parts.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing vibration
keyConcepts.body:
Vibration is measured at the bearing housings because that is where the rotor's forces pass into the stationary structure. Readings are normally taken in three directions (horizontal, vertical and axial) at both bearings, with permanently mounted sensors or portable instruments at marked points so that results can be trended.

Overall vibration, often expressed as velocity, indicates the general condition of the machine and is compared with the OEM's limits, the applicable vibration standard or site criteria. Spectrum analysis then helps find the cause. A dominant component at running speed (1x) commonly suggests unbalance. 1x and 2x components with high axial readings often suggest misalignment. Vane-pass frequency (number of impeller vanes multiplied by running speed) relates to the interaction between impeller and volute tongue. Broad-band, random vibration may indicate cavitation or recirculation. Non-synchronous frequencies linked to bearing geometry indicate rolling-bearing defects.

Early bearing defects produce small, high-frequency impacts that are often hidden in overall readings, so techniques such as acceleration enveloping (demodulation), shock pulse or other high-frequency methods are used. The defect frequencies for outer race, inner race, rolling elements and cage are calculated from the bearing geometry and speed.

At the non-drive-end locating bearing, axial vibration deserves particular attention because it reflects thrust conditions. As with temperature, trends matter more than single readings.

Caution: Use acceptance limits from the OEM, the applicable standard or the site procedure; do not import limits from unrelated machines.

bearing-de.summary: Carries the radial load at the coupling end of the rotor (its share of the impeller's hydraulic radial force, the rotor weight and any loads from the coupling) while letting the shaft expand axially.
bearing-de.function: Carries the radial load at the coupling end of the rotor (its share of the impeller's hydraulic radial force, the rotor weight and any loads from the coupling) while letting the shaft expand axially. In the baseline arrangement it is not intended to carry axial load.
bearing-de.operatingPrinciple:
A deep-groove ball bearing: balls roll between inner- and outer-ring raceways, spaced by a cage, separated from the raceways by a very thin elastohydrodynamic lubricant film. The inner ring rotates with the shaft and is clamped against a shaft shoulder by the locknut and lockwasher. The outer ring is stationary and has a fit in the housing bore that allows it to slide, with axial clearance left at the covers. When the shaft lengthens relative to the casing as it warms, the whole bearing moves with the shaft and the outer ring slides in the bore. This is the 'floating' bearing; the axial position of the rotor is set by the locating bearing at the non-drive end.

The inner ring sees a rotating load (the load direction moves round it as it turns), which is why it needs an interference fit on the shaft; the outer ring sees a stationary load, which allows the looser fit needed for floating.
