keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Correct floating is essential. If the outer ring cannot slide, because of a wrong fit, corrosion or fretting in the bore, a cover that clamps it, or the wrong gasket thickness, the shaft's thermal growth is resisted and both bearings see an induced axial load. The result is overheating and early failure of both bearings. Deep-groove ball bearings can carry some axial load, but in this arrangement their duty is radial.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft bending
keyConcepts.body:
Between its two bearings the shaft behaves like a beam. The main transverse loads are the weight of impeller and shaft, the radial hydraulic force from the volute, the rotating force from residual unbalance, and forces from the coupling, which increase with misalignment. Because the impeller sits roughly at mid-span in this design, a simple model is a simply supported beam with a central point load F over span L. The maximum bending moment is then M = F L / 4 at the load, and the bending stress at the surface of a solid round section of diameter d is sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3).

The key feature of a pump shaft is that it rotates while most of these loads, such as gravity and the volute radial force, stay fixed in direction. A point on the surface passes from tension to compression and back every revolution, so the bending stress is fully reversed. Over millions of cycles this is a fatigue problem: stresses must stay below the material's fatigue strength, with allowance for stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders, threads and press fits, and for surface condition and corrosion.

In a single volute the radial hydraulic load grows as operation moves away from BEP, so prolonged running at very low or very high flow raises bending stress and fatigue risk.

Caution: The beam formulas assume a uniform solid shaft, rigid simple supports and a single central load. Real shafts are stepped and run in flexible bearings; design checks are the OEM responsibility.

keyConcepts.title: Radial loads on the bearings
keyConcepts.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. Dynamic loads are added by residual unbalance, hydraulic pulsations and rotor-dynamic effects.

The hydraulic radial force exists because the pressure around the impeller periphery is not perfectly uniform. In a single-volute casing it is typically smallest near the best efficiency point (BEP) and grows as the flow moves away from BEP, towards both shut-off and run-out. A double-volute casing, with its splitter rib, substantially reduces this force by setting two opposed volute passages against each other, but does not remove it. The direction of the force also changes with flow rate, so the bearings see a load that varies in both size and direction.

Both bearings share the radial load; how much each carries depends on where the impeller sits along the span and on any overhung load at the coupling end (see 'Bearing reactions'). The drive-end floating bearing carries radial load only; the non-drive-end locating bearing carries its radial share plus the residual axial thrust.

Sustained operation far from BEP increases radial load, shaft deflection, the risk of wear-ring and seal contact, and bearing temperature.

Caution: A double volute or robust bearings do not make every operating point acceptable. Operate within the allowable operating region stated by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing reactions: a simple beam model
keyConcepts.body:
For a first estimate, treat the rotor as a simply supported beam: the drive-end bearing is one support, the non-drive-end bearing the other, and L is the span between bearing centres. Let a radial load F act at the impeller, at distance a from the drive-end bearing and distance b from the non-drive-end bearing, so that a + b = L.

Taking moments about the non-drive-end bearing: R_DE × L = F × b, so R_DE = F × b / L. Taking moments about the drive-end bearing: R_NDE = F × a / L. As a check, R_DE + R_NDE = F. The bearing nearer the load carries the larger share; with the impeller at mid-span each carries half.

The rotor weight W acts vertically downwards, while the hydraulic radial force acts in a direction set by the operating point. In practice each load is resolved into vertical and horizontal components, the reactions are found for each component, and the components are combined vectorially to give the resultant reaction at each bearing.

An overhung load outside the span, such as a coupling weight W_c at distance c outboard of the drive-end bearing, increases R_DE by W_c × (L + c) / L and reduces R_NDE by W_c × c / L.

This model ignores shaft flexibility, bearing stiffness, dynamic loads and misalignment forces; OEMs use more detailed rotor analysis. It is, however, the starting point for most bearing-load calculations in machine design.

Caution: This is a teaching model for understanding load sharing, not a substitute for the OEM's bearing selection and rotor analysis.

keyConcepts.title: Locating and floating bearing arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
The two bearings in this pump do different jobs, and they are not interchangeable.

The non-drive-end bearing is the locating (fixed) bearing. Both of its rings are clamped: the inner rings against a shaft shoulder by the locknut, the outer rings between a housing shoulder and the blind end cover. It holds the rotor in a defined axial position and carries residual thrust in both directions as well as its share of radial load. In the baseline it is a back-to-back pair of angular-contact ball bearings; a single deep-groove ball bearing is the variant for lighter thrust duty.

The drive-end bearing is the floating (non-locating) bearing. Its inner ring is clamped to the shaft, but its outer ring can slide axially in the housing bore, so it carries radial load only.

Why only one locating bearing? The shaft and casing run at different temperatures and may be made of different materials, so they change length by different amounts. If both bearings were fixed axially, that difference would be forced into the bearings as an axial load, possibly a large one, causing heat, high contact stress and early failure. One locating bearing fixes the rotor; the floating bearing absorbs the change in length.

The locating bearing also fixes the impeller's axial position in the volute and wear rings, which matters for hydraulic symmetry and therefore for the level of residual thrust. Some manufacturers put the locating bearing at the drive end, or use other bearing types.

Caution: A floating bearing that has seized in its bore, or has been clamped by a wrong cover or gasket, silently turns the arrangement into two locating bearings. Check axial freedom after assembly as the OEM specifies.

assumptions: Educational geometry model with illustrative proportions - not OEM CAD, no manufacturer dimensions or ratings.
'Floating' refers to axial freedom, not radial looseness.

Other designs use a cylindrical roller bearing as the floating bearing (axial movement then takes place inside the bearing), spherical roller bearings, or hydrodynamic sleeve bearings on large machines.
Silicon nitride appears only in hybrid bearings for special duties; cages may be pressed steel, brass or polyamide.

keyConcepts.title: Common bearing failures
keyConcepts.body:
Most rolling-bearing failures in pumps start with a cause outside the bearing itself.

Lubrication problems: too little lubricant, the wrong grade, degraded oil, over-greasing that causes churning and heat, or incompatible greases mixed together. Signs include rising temperature, noise and discoloured or glazed surfaces.

Contamination: water from seal or packing leakage, or from washdown and condensation, and solid particles. Water causes corrosion and weakens the film; particles dent the raceways and start early spalling. Milky oil and dented, rusty or etched raceways are typical findings.

Misalignment and excessive load: shaft-to-motor misalignment, pipe strain, soft foot, or thrust above design from off-design operation or wear. These produce abnormal wear paths, overheating and early fatigue; at the locating bearing, excess thrust shows as high axial vibration and heat.

Mounting errors: hammering, force passed through the rolling elements, wrong fits, angular-contact pairs mounted in the wrong orientation or mixed between sets, a floating bearing that cannot move, or a loose locknut.

Standstill damage: false brinelling, which marks raceways at ball spacing when a stationary standby pump is exposed to vibration from nearby machines.

Electrical erosion: current passing through the bearing, more common in motor bearings with variable-speed drives, produces pitting and fluting.

ISO 15243 classifies the damage modes. Examining the failed bearing, its lubricant and its mounting surfaces is the key to fixing the root cause rather than just replacing the bearing.

Caution: Replacing a failed bearing without finding why it failed usually leads to a repeat failure.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Water contamination of the lubricant is a leading cause of rolling-bearing failure in pumps, and the inboard seal sits directly beside the shaft seal or packing. Lip seals can groove the shaft over time; isolators avoid contact wear but depend on correct installation.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing lubrication
keyConcepts.body:
Rolling bearings depend on a very thin lubricant film between the rolling elements and the raceways. Under the high contact pressures this film is elastohydrodynamic: the lubricant's viscosity rises sharply under pressure and the surfaces deform elastically, so a film can separate them even though the contact area is tiny. The lubricant also reduces friction at the cage, protects the surfaces from corrosion and, in the case of oil, carries heat away.

Film thickness depends on the lubricant's viscosity at operating temperature, on speed and on load. Too thin a film, from the wrong grade, overheated or degraded oil, or water contamination, allows metal-to-metal contact, surface distress and early fatigue. Too much lubricant also does harm: excess oil or grease is churned by the rolling elements and generates heat.

Contamination matters as much as quantity. Hard particles dent the raceways, and water, a real risk next to a leaking seal or packing, weakens the film, promotes corrosion and shortens fatigue life. Housing seals, shaft deflectors and clean handling of lubricants are part of the lubrication system.

In this pump each bearing housing has its own lubricant. The baseline is an oil bath with constant-level oilers, sight glasses and drain plugs; the variant is grease with grease nipples and relief plugs. Lubricant type, grade, quantity, level and change or regreasing intervals must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site lubrication schedule.

keyConcepts.title: Common bearing failures
keyConcepts.body:
Most rolling-bearing failures in pumps start with a cause outside the bearing itself.

Lubrication problems: too little lubricant, the wrong grade, degraded oil, over-greasing that causes churning and heat, or incompatible greases mixed together. Signs include rising temperature, noise and discoloured or glazed surfaces.

Contamination: water from seal or packing leakage, or from washdown and condensation, and solid particles. Water causes corrosion and weakens the film; particles dent the raceways and start early spalling. Milky oil and dented, rusty or etched raceways are typical findings.

Misalignment and excessive load: shaft-to-motor misalignment, pipe strain, soft foot, or thrust above design from off-design operation or wear. These produce abnormal wear paths, overheating and early fatigue; at the locating bearing, excess thrust shows as high axial vibration and heat.

Mounting errors: hammering, force passed through the rolling elements, wrong fits, angular-contact pairs mounted in the wrong orientation or mixed between sets, a floating bearing that cannot move, or a loose locknut.

Standstill damage: false brinelling, which marks raceways at ball spacing when a stationary standby pump is exposed to vibration from nearby machines.

Electrical erosion: current passing through the bearing, more common in motor bearings with variable-speed drives, produces pitting and fluting.

ISO 15243 classifies the damage modes. Examining the failed bearing, its lubricant and its mounting surfaces is the key to fixing the root cause rather than just replacing the bearing.

Caution: Replacing a failed bearing without finding why it failed usually leads to a repeat failure.

keyConcepts.title: How the shaft is sealed
keyConcepts.body:
Wherever a rotating shaft passes through a stationary casing there must be a running clearance, and that clearance is a leakage path for the pumped liquid. Shaft sealing controls this path. On this pump the shaft runs inside replaceable sleeves where it passes through the casing, so wear and corrosion affect the sleeves rather than the shaft.

Two arrangements are used, one or the other at both ends. Compression packing fills the stuffing box with rings squeezed by a gland follower; it throttles leakage but must leak slightly to lubricate and cool itself. A mechanical seal uses two flat faces, one rotating and one stationary, held together by springs and liquid pressure; the leakage is very small and often leaves as vapour. Mechanical seals may be single or dual, component or cartridge, and in some cases split for easy replacement.

The stuffing box or seal chamber at each end is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. Supporting systems include the seal flush or packing seal water, venting of the chamber, and, outside the seal, shaft deflectors (flingers) that throw any leakage clear of the bearing housings.

Shaft sealing is different from bearing housing sealing. The shaft seal keeps the pumped liquid in the casing; the bearing housing seals (lip seals or isolators) keep lubricant in the bearing housings and contaminants out. Both matter, because shaft seal leakage that reaches the bearing housing contaminates the lubricant.

keyConcepts.title: Leakage control
keyConcepts.body:
Packing and mechanical seals control leakage in fundamentally different ways.

Packing works by throttling, and it needs a controlled leakage: the liquid passing along the sleeve lubricates the packing and carries away frictional heat. The gland follower is adjusted to give the leakage rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends. Tightening to stop the leak completely makes the packing overheat, harden and burn, scores the sleeve, raises power absorption and eventually leads to more leakage, not less. New packing is started with generous leakage and taken up gradually as it beds in. Adjust the nuts evenly in small steps and allow time between adjustments.

A mechanical seal has very small leakage across its faces, much of which evaporates and is not visible. A steady visible drip generally indicates a problem, although some seals show slight leakage while bedding in; the seal manufacturer states what is acceptable. Rising leakage over time shows face wear, damage or a secondary seal problem.

In both cases, leakage must be collected and drained safely, for example to a gland drain or the baseplate drain rim, especially where the liquid is hot, hazardous or slippery, and it must be kept away from the bearing housings, where shaft deflectors and housing seals provide protection. Under suction lift, a sealing point can leak air in rather than liquid out; reduced performance or noise may be the only sign.

Caution: Gland adjustment on a running pump puts hands close to the rotating shaft and coupling. Do it only where the site procedure permits, with all guards fitted and loose clothing and tools kept clear.

oiler-de.summary: A constant-level oiler automatically tops up the bearing housing sump to hold a set oil level, and carries a visible reserve of oil.
oiler-de.function: A constant-level oiler automatically tops up the bearing housing sump to hold a set oil level, and carries a visible reserve of oil.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The oiler makes up small losses, but it cannot lower a level that is too high, does not show oil condition, and cannot keep up with a housing that leaks faster than it can supply. Rapid consumption points to leaking housing seals or gaskets. Pressure differences between the inside of the housing and the atmosphere, and in some designs the direction of shaft rotation relative to the oiler's position, can upset the level, so the oiler must be fitted and set as the OEM specifies.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing lubrication
keyConcepts.body:
Rolling bearings depend on a very thin lubricant film between the rolling elements and the raceways. Under the high contact pressures this film is elastohydrodynamic: the lubricant's viscosity rises sharply under pressure and the surfaces deform elastically, so a film can separate them even though the contact area is tiny. The lubricant also reduces friction at the cage, protects the surfaces from corrosion and, in the case of oil, carries heat away.

Film thickness depends on the lubricant's viscosity at operating temperature, on speed and on load. Too thin a film, from the wrong grade, overheated or degraded oil, or water contamination, allows metal-to-metal contact, surface distress and early fatigue. Too much lubricant also does harm: excess oil or grease is churned by the rolling elements and generates heat.

Contamination matters as much as quantity. Hard particles dent the raceways, and water, a real risk next to a leaking seal or packing, weakens the film, promotes corrosion and shortens fatigue life. Housing seals, shaft deflectors and clean handling of lubricants are part of the lubrication system.

In this pump each bearing housing has its own lubricant. The baseline is an oil bath with constant-level oilers, sight glasses and drain plugs; the variant is grease with grease nipples and relief plugs. Lubricant type, grade, quantity, level and change or regreasing intervals must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site lubrication schedule.

keyConcepts.title: Oil versus grease lubrication
keyConcepts.body:
Both methods are widely used on split case pumps, and the choice is made by the OEM for the bearing size, speed, load, temperature and maintenance regime.

Oil bath lubrication (the baseline): the lower part of the bearing runs in an oil sump held at a set level by a constant-level oiler and checked through a sight glass. Oil removes heat well, suits higher speeds and loads, and makes condition easy to check: level, colour and water can be seen, samples can be taken, and contaminants are removed when the oil is drained. In return it needs correct level setting, effective housing seals to keep oil in and water out, and regular attention to oilers and oil changes. Leaks and incorrect levels are common problems.

Grease lubrication (the variant): grease is a base oil held in a thickener, which stays in the bearing and helps seal it against contaminants. The arrangement is simpler, with no level to control and less risk of leakage. However, grease removes little heat, and its success depends on getting the type, quantity and regreasing interval right. Over-greasing causes churning and high temperature, under-greasing starves the bearing, and mixing incompatible greases can destroy lubrication. The relief plug must be used as the OEM instructs so that old grease can escape.

Some larger pumps use oil rings, flinger discs, oil mist or circulating oil systems instead.

Caution: Never mix lubricants or change grease type without confirming compatibility with the OEM or lubricant supplier.

bearing-housing-nde.summary: Supports and encloses the non-drive-end (outboard) locating bearing, passes both radial load and the rotor's residual axial thrust into the casing, and fixes the rotor's axial position relative to the casing.
bearing-housing-nde.function: Supports and encloses the non-drive-end (outboard) locating bearing, passes both radial load and the rotor's residual axial thrust into the casing, and fixes the rotor's axial position relative to the casing.
bearing-housing-nde.operatingPrinciple: The locating bearing's outer rings are clamped between a shoulder in the housing and the blind end cover. Thrust in one direction passes from the shaft through the inner rings and balls to the outer rings, then into the housing shoulder; thrust in the other direction passes into the end cover and its bolts. Either way it reaches the housing and, through the hold-down bolts and location features, the bracket on the lower casing half. Because the rotor is fixed axially here, the housing position also sets the impeller's axial position in the volute.
bearing-housing-nde.construction: A cast housing similar to the drive-end housing, but with a machined thrust shoulder, a blind outboard end and a seal only on the inboard side. It carries the same lubrication fittings as the drive end for the selected lubrication variant.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: This housing, its fixings and the bracket must carry axial load as well as radial load. Its position governs impeller centring, which matters for hydraulic symmetry, wear-ring clearance and the level of residual thrust. Temperature and axial vibration measured here are key indicators of thrust conditions.

keyConcepts.title: Radial loads on the bearings
keyConcepts.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. Dynamic loads are added by residual unbalance, hydraulic pulsations and rotor-dynamic effects.

The hydraulic radial force exists because the pressure around the impeller periphery is not perfectly uniform. In a single-volute casing it is typically smallest near the best efficiency point (BEP) and grows as the flow moves away from BEP, towards both shut-off and run-out. A double-volute casing, with its splitter rib, substantially reduces this force by setting two opposed volute passages against each other, but does not remove it. The direction of the force also changes with flow rate, so the bearings see a load that varies in both size and direction.

Both bearings share the radial load; how much each carries depends on where the impeller sits along the span and on any overhung load at the coupling end (see 'Bearing reactions'). The drive-end floating bearing carries radial load only; the non-drive-end locating bearing carries its radial share plus the residual axial thrust.

Sustained operation far from BEP increases radial load, shaft deflection, the risk of wear-ring and seal contact, and bearing temperature.

Caution: A double volute or robust bearings do not make every operating point acceptable. Operate within the allowable operating region stated by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Axial loads on the rotor
keyConcepts.body:
Axial (thrust) loads act along the shaft axis. A double-suction impeller is nominally symmetrical, so the hydraulic thrusts from its two sides largely cancel, but never exactly.

Residual hydraulic thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances in the impeller and casing halves, an impeller not exactly centred in the volute, unequal wear-ring clearances (especially as the rings wear unevenly), unequal flow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping layout, recirculation or cavitation starting at one eye at part load, and transient conditions such as start-up, shutdown and pressure surges. Mechanical sources add to it: axial force through the coupling (for example a gear coupling that locks under torque, or a disc coupling installed at the wrong axial spacing), and thermally induced load if the floating bearing is unable to move.

This residual thrust can act in either direction and can change direction with operating conditions or as the pump wears. It therefore has to be carried by a bearing that takes thrust both ways and holds the rotor in a defined axial position: the locating bearing at the non-drive end. The drive-end bearing is deliberately left free axially so that it carries radial load only.

Rotor weight does not create axial load on a horizontal shaft, although it does on a vertical one; load paths always depend on machine orientation.

Caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A locating (thrust) bearing is always required.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction affects thrust-bearing duty
keyConcepts.body:
In a single-suction closed impeller, the pressure behind the back shroud acts over a larger area than the pressure on the front shroud, where the eye is at low suction pressure. The result is a substantial net axial thrust towards the suction side. Single-suction pumps therefore need balancing features (balance holes, back wear rings or pump-out vanes) and a thrust bearing sized for what remains.

A double-suction impeller is, in effect, two single-suction impellers back to back on one hub. Liquid enters through two opposed eyes and the pressure distributions on the two shrouds are mirror images, so their thrusts largely cancel. The thrust bearing in a double-suction pump therefore typically carries a residual load that is small in comparison, which allows a compact locating bearing and contributes to this pump type's reputation for long, reliable runs at large flows.

Largely cancelling is not the same as cancelling. Residual thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances, axial mispositioning of the impeller, uneven wear-ring clearances, unequal flow to the two eyes from poor suction piping, part-load recirculation or cavitation at one eye, and transients. Its size and direction can change with flow rate and over the pump's life as clearances wear.

Thrust-bearing duty is therefore never zero, and the OEM assesses it over the full operating range. When the conditions that keep the impeller balanced deteriorate, the signs are rising non-drive-end bearing temperature, higher axial vibration and shorter bearing life.

Caution: Never assume that double suction eliminates axial thrust. Residual thrust always exists, which is why the pump has a locating bearing.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing temperature
keyConcepts.body:
Temperature is one of the simplest and most useful indicators of bearing condition. After start-up it rises and then settles at a level set by load, speed, lubricant, ambient conditions and how easily heat flows away to the casing and baseplate. The settled value, recorded at commissioning at a known operating point, becomes the baseline for that bearing.

Trend monitoring compares readings with that baseline, with the other bearing, with ambient temperature and with the operating point at the time. A gradual rise can indicate lubricant degradation, contamination or developing damage. A sudden rise can point to loss of lubricant, over-greasing, a floating bearing that has locked, increased thrust, misalignment or a rubbing housing seal. A short-lived rise after regreasing is normal while excess grease is purged.

Temperature may be measured by permanently installed resistance temperature detectors or thermocouples, where fitted, or with contact or infrared thermometers on the housing surface. Readings taken by different methods or at different points are not directly comparable; a housing surface is cooler than the bearing outer ring. For trending, use the same method at the same marked point every time.

Alarm and trip settings and acceptable temperatures must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site procedure.

Caution: Do not judge temperature by touching the housing; it can be hot enough to burn, and the coupling and shaft are close by. Use instruments and keep clear of rotating parts.

bearing-nde-duplex.summary: The locating (thrust) bearing in the baseline arrangement: carries residual axial thrust in both directions plus its share of radial load at the non-drive end, and holds the rotor in a fixed axial position.
bearing-nde-duplex.function: The locating (thrust) bearing in the baseline arrangement: carries residual axial thrust in both directions plus its share of radial load at the non-drive end, and holds the rotor in a fixed axial position.
bearing-nde-duplex.operatingPrinciple:
In an angular-contact ball bearing the raceways are offset so that the line of contact between ball and raceways is inclined to the radial plane at the contact angle. Each bearing can therefore carry combined radial and axial load, but axial load in one direction only. Mounting two bearings back-to-back (wide outer-ring faces together, sometimes called the O arrangement) lets the pair take thrust in both directions, one bearing per direction. In this arrangement the load lines diverge towards the shaft axis, giving a wide effective spread and good stiffness against tilting.

The bearings are supplied as matched or universally matchable sets made to give a defined internal clearance or preload once the rings are clamped. The inner rings are clamped together against a shaft shoulder by the locknut, and the outer rings are clamped between the housing shoulder and the blind end cover.
bearing-nde-duplex.construction: Two single-row angular-contact ball bearings mounted back-to-back. Contact angle, preload or clearance class, cage design and fits are chosen by the OEM and the bearing manufacturer. Some manufacturers mark matched sets, for example with a V-shaped mark across the outer rings, to show the correct orientation.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Because a double-suction impeller is never perfectly balanced axially, this bearing is essential. Mounting errors are serious: a pair fitted in tandem or face-to-face instead of back-to-back, bearings from different sets mixed, or rings not properly clamped change the preload, reduce the thrust capacity in one direction or allow the rotor to move. If residual thrust rises, for example because of uneven wear-ring wear, poor suction flow or off-design operation, this bearing runs hotter and its life shortens.

keyConcepts.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.

Caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

keyConcepts.title: Why residual axial thrust still exists
keyConcepts.body:
Real pumps depart from the ideal symmetrical arrangement in several ways. Each departure leaves a net axial force, the residual thrust, which can act towards either end and can change with operating conditions.

Asymmetric inflow: elbows, valves or strainers near the suction, or vortices in the intake, give the two eyes different flow and velocity profiles. Wear-ring clearances: new rings have tolerances, and in service the rings at the two eyes rarely wear at the same rate; a larger clearance on one side increases leakage through that side room and changes its swirl and pressure. Casting variations: shroud profiles, vane positions and side-room widths are never perfectly identical. Rotor axial position: if the impeller is not centred on the volute, the side rooms differ; centring is set during assembly by the OEM procedure. Off-design operation: at low flow, recirculation at the eyes and outlet need not be symmetrical, and the force can fluctuate. Unequal seal chamber pressures act on the shaft cross-section. Transients such as starting, stopping and one-sided cavitation add temporary thrust.

In this design the residual thrust is carried by the NDE locating bearing. Because its direction can reverse, the baseline uses paired angular-contact bearings mounted back to back, which carry axial load in both directions; the deep-groove ball bearing variant also carries moderate axial load in both directions.

Caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A rise in NDE bearing temperature or a change in axial vibration after wear-ring renewal, rotor reassembly or piping changes can indicate increased residual thrust and should be investigated.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft bending
keyConcepts.body:
Between its two bearings the shaft behaves like a beam. The main transverse loads are the weight of impeller and shaft, the radial hydraulic force from the volute, the rotating force from residual unbalance, and forces from the coupling, which increase with misalignment. Because the impeller sits roughly at mid-span in this design, a simple model is a simply supported beam with a central point load F over span L. The maximum bending moment is then M = F L / 4 at the load, and the bending stress at the surface of a solid round section of diameter d is sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3).

The key feature of a pump shaft is that it rotates while most of these loads, such as gravity and the volute radial force, stay fixed in direction. A point on the surface passes from tension to compression and back every revolution, so the bending stress is fully reversed. Over millions of cycles this is a fatigue problem: stresses must stay below the material's fatigue strength, with allowance for stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders, threads and press fits, and for surface condition and corrosion.

In a single volute the radial hydraulic load grows as operation moves away from BEP, so prolonged running at very low or very high flow raises bending stress and fatigue risk.

Caution: The beam formulas assume a uniform solid shaft, rigid simple supports and a single central load. Real shafts are stepped and run in flexible bearings; design checks are the OEM responsibility.

keyConcepts.title: Radial loads on the bearings
keyConcepts.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. keyConcepts.body:
Real pumps depart from the ideal symmetrical arrangement in several ways. Each departure leaves a net axial force, the residual thrust, which can act towards either end and can change with operating conditions.

keyConcepts.title: Axial loads on the rotor
keyConcepts.body:
Axial (thrust) loads act along the shaft axis. A double-suction impeller is nominally symmetrical, so the hydraulic thrusts from its two sides largely cancel, but never exactly.

Residual hydraulic thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances in the impeller and casing halves, an impeller not exactly centred in the volute, unequal wear-ring clearances (especially as the rings wear unevenly), unequal flow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping layout, recirculation or cavitation starting at one eye at part load, and transient conditions such as start-up, shutdown and pressure surges. Mechanical sources add to it: axial force through the coupling (for example a gear coupling that locks under torque, or a disc coupling installed at the wrong axial spacing), and thermally induced load if the floating bearing is unable to move.

This residual thrust can act in either direction and can change direction with operating conditions or as the pump wears. It therefore has to be carried by a bearing that takes thrust both ways and holds the rotor in a defined axial position: the locating bearing at the non-drive end. The drive-end bearing is deliberately left free axially so that it carries radial load only.

Rotor weight does not create axial load on a horizontal shaft, although it does on a vertical one; load paths always depend on machine orientation.

Caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A locating (thrust) bearing is always required.

keyConcepts.title: Locating and floating bearing arrangement
keyConcepts.body:
The two bearings in this pump do different jobs, and they are not interchangeable.

The non-drive-end bearing is the locating (fixed) bearing. Both of its rings are clamped: the inner rings against a shaft shoulder by the locknut, the outer rings between a housing shoulder and the blind end cover. It holds the rotor in a defined axial position and carries residual thrust in both directions as well as its share of radial load. In the baseline it is a back-to-back pair of angular-contact ball bearings; a single deep-groove ball bearing is the variant for lighter thrust duty.

The drive-end bearing is the floating (non-locating) bearing. Its inner ring is clamped to the shaft, but its outer ring can slide axially in the housing bore, so it carries radial load only.

Why only one locating bearing? The shaft and casing run at different temperatures and may be made of different materials, so they change length by different amounts. If both bearings were fixed axially, that difference would be forced into the bearings as an axial load, possibly a large one, causing heat, high contact stress and early failure. One locating bearing fixes the rotor; the floating bearing absorbs the change in length.

The locating bearing also fixes the impeller's axial position in the volute and wear rings, which matters for hydraulic symmetry and therefore for the level of residual thrust. Some manufacturers put the locating bearing at the drive end, or use other bearing types.

Caution: A floating bearing that has seized in its bore, or has been clamped by a wrong cover or gasket, silently turns the arrangement into two locating bearings. Check axial freedom after assembly as the OEM specifies.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction affects thrust-bearing duty
keyConcepts.body:
In a single-suction closed impeller, the pressure behind the back shroud acts over a larger area than the pressure on the front shroud, where the eye is at low suction pressure. The result is a substantial net axial thrust towards the suction side. Single-suction pumps therefore need balancing features (balance holes, back wear rings or pump-out vanes) and a thrust bearing sized for what remains.

A double-suction impeller is, in effect, two single-suction impellers back to back on one hub. Liquid enters through two opposed eyes and the pressure distributions on the two shrouds are mirror images, so their thrusts largely cancel. The thrust bearing in a double-suction pump therefore typically carries a residual load that is small in comparison, which allows a compact locating bearing and contributes to this pump type's reputation for long, reliable runs at large flows.

Largely cancelling is not the same as cancelling. Residual thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances, axial mispositioning of the impeller, uneven wear-ring clearances, unequal flow to the two eyes from poor suction piping, part-load recirculation or cavitation at one eye, and transients. Its size and direction can change with flow rate and over the pump's life as clearances wear.

Thrust-bearing duty is therefore never zero, and the OEM assesses it over the full operating range. When the conditions that keep the impeller balanced deteriorate, the signs are rising non-drive-end bearing temperature, higher axial vibration and shorter bearing life.

Caution: Never assume that double suction eliminates axial thrust. Residual thrust always exists, which is why the pump has a locating bearing.

bearing-locknut-nde.summary: Clamps the locating bearing's inner rings against the shaft shoulder, so that they rotate as one with the shaft and transmit thrust in both directions between shaft and bearing.
bearing-locknut-nde.function: Clamps the locating bearing's inner rings against the shaft shoulder, so that they rotate as one with the shaft and transmit thrust in both directions between shaft and bearing.
bearing-locknut-nde.operatingPrinciple: Thrust towards the shoulder passes from the inner rings into the shoulder; thrust in the opposite direction passes through the locknut and its thread. Unlike the drive-end nut, this nut is therefore part of the thrust load path.

keyConcepts.title: Common bearing failures
keyConcepts.body:
Most rolling-bearing failures in pumps start with a cause outside the bearing itself.

Lubrication problems: too little lubricant, the wrong grade, degraded oil, over-greasing that causes churning and heat, or incompatible greases mixed together. Signs include rising temperature, noise and discoloured or glazed surfaces.

Contamination: water from seal or packing leakage, or from washdown and condensation, and solid particles. Water causes corrosion and weakens the film; particles dent the raceways and start early spalling. Milky oil and dented, rusty or etched raceways are typical findings.

Misalignment and excessive load: shaft-to-motor misalignment, pipe strain, soft foot, or thrust above design from off-design operation or wear. These produce abnormal wear paths, overheating and early fatigue; at the locating bearing, excess thrust shows as high axial vibration and heat.

Mounting errors: hammering, force passed through the rolling elements, wrong fits, angular-contact pairs mounted in the wrong orientation or mixed between sets, a floating bearing that cannot move, or a loose locknut.

Standstill damage: false brinelling, which marks raceways at ball spacing when a stationary standby pump is exposed to vibration from nearby machines.

Electrical erosion: current passing through the bearing, more common in motor bearings with variable-speed drives, produces pitting and fluting.

ISO 15243 classifies the damage modes. Examining the failed bearing, its lubricant and its mounting surfaces is the key to fixing the root cause rather than just replacing the bearing.

Caution: Replacing a failed bearing without finding why it failed usually leads to a repeat failure.

lockwasher-nde.summary: Locks the bearing locknut so that it cannot slacken in service.
lockwasher-nde.function: Locks the bearing locknut so that it cannot slacken in service.
lockwasher-nde.operatingPrinciple: An internal tang on the washer engages a slot or keyway in the threaded part of the shaft, so the washer cannot turn on the shaft. After the locknut has been tightened, one of the washer's external tabs is bent into a slot in the nut, locking nut and shaft together.
lockwasher-nde.construction: A thin pressed-steel tab washer matched to the locknut size, fitted between the bearing inner ring (or a spacer) and the locknut.

bearing-gaskets-nde.summary: Seal the bolted joints between the bearing housing and its covers, so that lubricant stays in and water, dust and process liquid stay out.
bearing-gaskets-nde.function: Seal the bolted joints between the bearing housing and its covers, so that lubricant stays in and water, dust and process liquid stay out.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Grease quantity is critical. Too much grease is churned by the rolling elements, which raises temperature and can force grease past the housing seals; too little starves the bearing. Greases with incompatible thickeners or base oils can soften or harden when mixed and lose their lubricating ability, so the grease type must not be changed without checking compatibility.

keyConcepts.title: Oil versus grease lubrication
keyConcepts.body:
Both methods are widely used on split case pumps, and the choice is made by the OEM for the bearing size, speed, load, temperature and maintenance regime.

Oil bath lubrication (the baseline): the lower part of the bearing runs in an oil sump held at a set level by a constant-level oiler and checked through a sight glass. Oil removes heat well, suits higher speeds and loads, and makes condition easy to check: level, colour and water can be seen, samples can be taken, and contaminants are removed when the oil is drained. In return it needs correct level setting, effective housing seals to keep oil in and water out, and regular attention to oilers and oil changes. Leaks and incorrect levels are common problems.

Grease lubrication (the variant): grease is a base oil held in a thickener, which stays in the bearing and helps seal it against contaminants. The arrangement is simpler, with no level to control and less risk of leakage. However, grease removes little heat, and its success depends on getting the type, quantity and regreasing interval right. Over-greasing causes churning and high temperature, under-greasing starves the bearing, and mixing incompatible greases can destroy lubrication. The relief plug must be used as the OEM instructs so that old grease can escape.

Some larger pumps use oil rings, flinger discs, oil mist or circulating oil systems instead.

Caution: Never mix lubricants or change grease type without confirming compatibility with the OEM or lubricant supplier.

Non-drive end: lubricates the locating bearing, which also carries thrust, so correct grease quantity matters as much here as at the drive end.

mech-seal-de-springs.summary: Provide the mechanical closing force that keeps the seal faces in contact when there is little or no liquid pressure, and keep them closed as the faces wear and the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
mech-seal-de-springs.function: Provide the mechanical closing force that keeps the seal faces in contact when there is little or no liquid pressure, and keep them closed as the faces wear and the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
mech-seal-de-springs.operatingPrinciple: When the seal is set to its working length the springs are compressed by a defined amount, giving a known spring load. In operation, the pressure in the seal chamber adds hydraulic closing force, so the total face load is spring load plus hydraulic load; the hydraulic share depends on the seal's balance.
mech-seal-de-springs.construction: Either a single large coil spring or several small springs spaced around the retainer. In metal bellows seals the welded bellows acts as both spring and secondary seal. In the baseline the springs rotate with the shaft as part of the rotating unit.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: If the seal is set at the wrong length the springs are over- or under-compressed: too much load causes heat and rapid face wear, too little lets the faces open and leak. Springs in contact with the pumped liquid can clog with solids or corrode. Multiple small springs are generally more sensitive to clogging, while a single large spring tolerates dirt better but may be sensitive to the direction of rotation.

keyConcepts.title: Seal face contact and the fluid film
keyConcepts.body:
The primary seal of a mechanical seal is the interface between two flat, smooth faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary. The faces are lapped to extreme flatness, checked optically in light bands with an optical flat, because any waviness opens a leakage path or causes local contact.

Between the faces a very thin film of the sealed liquid lubricates and partly separates them. In many liquid applications the faces run in a mixed regime, partly supported by the film and partly in light contact. The film is what keeps friction, heat and wear acceptable; without it the faces run dry.

The faces are pushed together by the closing force, which is the spring force plus the liquid pressure acting on the closing area behind the flexible face. The film pressure between the faces pushes them apart. The net load divided by the face area is the face pressure, which governs film thickness, heat generation, leakage and wear. The balance ratio compares the hydraulic closing area with the face area. In an unbalanced seal, face pressure rises steeply with sealed pressure; a balanced seal uses a stepped sleeve or seal geometry to reduce the closing area so that face pressure rises more slowly, suiting higher pressures. Actual balance ratios and face pressures are design values of the seal manufacturer.

Anything that disturbs the faces, such as distortion from uneven gland tightening, thermal gradients, vibration, shaft runout or dry running, upsets the film and shortens seal life.

Caution: Dry running destroys the fluid film and can damage seal faces very quickly. Never run a mechanically sealed pump without liquid, even to check rotation.

mech-seal-de-secondary-seals.summary: Seals between the rotating seal parts and the shaft sleeve, so that liquid cannot bypass the faces along the sleeve, while still allowing the rotating face to move axially and tilt slightly.

mech-seal-de-secondary-seals.operatingPrinciple: In a pusher seal the secondary seal (an O-ring or wedge) slides a short distance along the sleeve as the face wears and the shaft moves. In an elastomer bellows seal the bellows flexes instead of sliding. Either way it must stay flexible for the face to follow.
mech-seal-de-secondary-seals.construction: An elastomer O-ring, a PTFE wedge or an elastomer bellows, fitted in the rotating unit on the sleeve.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance

keyConcepts.title: Seal face contact and the fluid film
keyConcepts.body:
The primary seal of a mechanical seal is the interface between two flat, smooth faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary. The faces are lapped to extreme flatness, checked optically in light bands with an optical flat, because any waviness opens a leakage path or causes local contact.

Between the faces a very thin film of the sealed liquid lubricates and partly separates them. In many liquid applications the faces run in a mixed regime, partly supported by the film and partly in light contact. The film is what keeps friction, heat and wear acceptable; without it the faces run dry.

The faces are pushed together by the closing force, which is the spring force plus the liquid pressure acting on the closing area behind the flexible face. The film pressure between the faces pushes them apart. The net load divided by the face area is the face pressure, which governs film thickness, heat generation, leakage and wear. The balance ratio compares the hydraulic closing area with the face area. In an unbalanced seal, face pressure rises steeply with sealed pressure; a balanced seal uses a stepped sleeve or seal geometry to reduce the closing area so that face pressure rises more slowly, suiting higher pressures. Actual balance ratios and face pressures are design values of the seal manufacturer.

Anything that disturbs the faces, such as distortion from uneven gland tightening, thermal gradients, vibration, shaft runout or dry running, upsets the film and shortens seal life.

Caution: Dry running destroys the fluid film and can damage seal faces very quickly. Never run a mechanically sealed pump without liquid, even to check rotation.

mech-seal-de-rotating-face.summary: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
mech-seal-de-rotating-face.function: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
mech-seal-de-rotating-face.operatingPrinciple: In the baseline seal the rotating face is the flexibly mounted ring. The springs push it against the stationary seat, and it floats on its secondary seal so that it can follow face wear, small axial shaft movement and slight misalignment. Its lapped surface runs on a very thin film of the sealed liquid, across which a tiny leakage passes radially.
mech-seal-de-rotating-face.construction: A ring of carbon-graphite, or of a hard face material such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide, lapped flat and polished on its sealing face. It is driven by lugs, pins or notches in the retainer and sealed to the sleeve by the secondary seal. A common pairing is a carbon face against a hard face; hard-against-hard pairs are often used where abrasive particles are present.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The face material pair decides wear rate, tolerance of brief dry running, resistance to abrasives and chemical compatibility. Face materials are hard but brittle: they chip if knocked, can crack from thermal shock and lose flatness if distorted, and any of these causes leakage.

keyConcepts.title: Mechanical seal versus gland packing
keyConcepts.body:
Both arrangements are legitimate and widely used on split case pumps; each has trade-offs.

Leakage: packing must leak continuously to stay cool and lubricated. A mechanical seal's leakage is very small and often not visible. Where the pumped liquid is hazardous, valuable or environmentally harmful, a mechanical seal, often a dual seal, is normally required.

Power and wear: packing rubs on the sleeve and absorbs more power, and over time it grooves the sleeve. A mechanical seal absorbs less power and the sleeve wears little, although pusher seals can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.

Maintenance: packing needs periodic gland adjustment and repacking, but in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. A mechanical seal needs little routine attention, but replacing it usually means removing the coupling spacer and the bearing housing, or lifting the rotor, unless a split or cartridge design simplifies the job.

Tolerance: packing tolerates shaft movement, brief dry periods and poor conditions better, and fails gradually by leaking more. Mechanical seals are sensitive to dry running, vibration, misalignment and poor flush, and can fail suddenly.

Cost and skills: packing is cheaper to buy; mechanical seals often cost less over their life once leakage, water use, power and sleeve wear are counted, but they need careful installation.

The choice depends on the liquid, environmental and safety requirements, site practice and life-cycle cost.

keyConcepts.title: Common causes of seal failure
keyConcepts.body:
Most mechanical seal failures are caused by the conditions around the seal rather than by the seal itself.

Dry running: starting without priming, an air-bound casing or seal chamber that was not vented, loss of suction, or running against a closed suction valve. Face damage can occur very quickly.

Flush problems: blocked orifices or strainers, closed valves, a failed external supply or the wrong piping plan, leading to overheating and vaporisation at the faces.

Solids and deposits: abrasive particles wearing the faces, or crystals and deposits that clog springs and hang up pusher secondary seals.

Mechanical causes: misalignment between pump and motor, pipe strain, excessive shaft runout or end play, worn bearings, and vibration from unbalance or cavitation.

Operation: running far from the best efficiency point, which increases shaft deflection and vibration; cavitation; and pressure or temperature outside the seal's design.

Installation errors: wrong setting length, dirty or damaged faces, wrong or damaged O-rings, incompatible fitting lubricants, uneven gland tightening, cartridge setting clips left in place, and a step or protruding gasket at the split-case chamber face.

Chemical and thermal attack: elastomers incompatible with the liquid or temperature, and thermal shock to brittle faces.

For packing, the equivalent problems are overtightening, loss of seal water, poor installation, worn sleeves and abrasive liquids. Examining the failed parts, especially the wear pattern on the faces, usually reveals which of these was the cause.

mech-seal-de-gland.summary: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
mech-seal-de-gland.function: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
mech-seal-de-gland.operatingPrinciple: The gland is the reference that keeps the seat square and centred, and uneven tightening distorts the seat. Cartridge seals have their own gland, supplied with setting clips or plates fitted for installation.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: A blocked orifice, a closed valve or a failed external supply removes the seal's cooling and lubrication, and is a common cause of seal overheating and failure.

keyConcepts.title: Cooling and flushing
keyConcepts.body:
Seal faces and packing generate heat by friction, and that heat must be removed continuously. Flush (for mechanical seals) and seal water (for packing) do this, and serve several other purposes: they keep the sealing surfaces wetted, keep the liquid around the seal from flashing to vapour, sweep solids away, and help prevent air or vapour from collecting in the top of a horizontal chamber.

In clean-water service a common arrangement takes liquid from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or volute, through small-bore tubing with an orifice into each seal chamber. In many water-service pumps the flush is taken by a small external line, and some designs use internal passages. Where the pumped liquid contains solids or is otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid is injected from an external source, and accessories such as strainers, cyclone separators or coolers may be added. Dual seals use a separate buffer or barrier fluid system.

The numbered seal piping plans defined in API 682 are widely used, even outside the oil and gas industry, as a shorthand for these arrangements; for example, one plan describes recirculation from the pump discharge to the seal chamber, and another describes injection of clean fluid from an external source. The plan for a given pump is stated on its seal datasheet.

For packing, seal water to the lantern ring must be at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure; it cools and lubricates the packing and, under suction lift, stops air ingress.

Caution: Do not isolate, re-route or resize flush lines without consulting the seal manufacturer. A blocked or closed flush is a common cause of seal failure.

packing-rings-de.summary: The sealing elements of the stuffing box: deformable rings compressed against the sleeve and bore to restrict leakage along the shaft.
packing-rings-de.function: The sealing elements of the stuffing box: deformable rings compressed against the sleeve and bore to restrict leakage along the shaft.
packing-rings-de.operatingPrinciple: Under gland load the rings deform and bear lightly on the rotating sleeve. Friction at this contact generates heat, which the controlled leakage removes. In service the rings consolidate and lose some of their impregnated lubricant, so the gland has to be re-tightened from time to time to hold the leakage rate.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Correct size, number of rings and installation are essential. Oversize rings hammered into the box, a continuous spiral instead of separate rings, or excessive gland tightening cause overheating, burned packing, a grooved sleeve and high power absorption. Too little compression gives excessive leakage.

keyConcepts.title: Mechanical seal versus gland packing
keyConcepts.body:
Both arrangements are legitimate and widely used on split case pumps; each has trade-offs.

Leakage: packing must leak continuously to stay cool and lubricated. A mechanical seal's leakage is very small and often not visible. Where the pumped liquid is hazardous, valuable or environmentally harmful, a mechanical seal, often a dual seal, is normally required.

Power and wear: packing rubs on the sleeve and absorbs more power, and over time it grooves the sleeve. A mechanical seal absorbs less power and the sleeve wears little, although pusher seals can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.

Maintenance: packing needs periodic gland adjustment and repacking, but in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. A mechanical seal needs little routine attention, but replacing it usually means removing the coupling spacer and the bearing housing, or lifting the rotor, unless a split or cartridge design simplifies the job.

Tolerance: packing tolerates shaft movement, brief dry periods and poor conditions better, and fails gradually by leaking more. Mechanical seals are sensitive to dry running, vibration, misalignment and poor flush, and can fail suddenly.

Cost and skills: packing is cheaper to buy; mechanical seals often cost less over their life once leakage, water use, power and sleeve wear are counted, but they need careful installation.

The choice depends on the liquid, environmental and safety requirements, site practice and life-cycle cost.

keyConcepts.title: Common causes of seal failure
keyConcepts.body:
Most mechanical seal failures are caused by the conditions around the seal rather than by the seal itself.

Dry running: starting without priming, an air-bound casing or seal chamber that was not vented, loss of suction, or running against a closed suction valve. Face damage can occur very quickly.

Flush problems: blocked orifices or strainers, closed valves, a failed external supply or the wrong piping plan, leading to overheating and vaporisation at the faces.

Solids and deposits: abrasive particles wearing the faces, or crystals and deposits that clog springs and hang up pusher secondary seals.

Mechanical causes: misalignment between pump and motor, pipe strain, excessive shaft runout or end play, worn bearings, and vibration from unbalance or cavitation.

Operation: running far from the best efficiency point, which increases shaft deflection and vibration; cavitation; and pressure or temperature outside the seal's design.

Installation errors: wrong setting length, dirty or damaged faces, wrong or damaged O-rings, incompatible fitting lubricants, uneven gland tightening, cartridge setting clips left in place, and a step or protruding gasket at the split-case chamber face.

Chemical and thermal attack: elastomers incompatible with the liquid or temperature, and thermal shock to brittle faces.

For packing, the equivalent problems are overtightening, loss of seal water, poor installation, worn sleeves and abrasive liquids. Examining the failed parts, especially the wear pattern on the faces, usually reveals which of these was the cause.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The lantern ring only works if it sits under the flush port. Because packing consolidates as the gland is tightened, it is positioned so that it ends up under the port in service. A misplaced lantern ring blocks the seal water, so the packing runs dry and air can enter.

keyConcepts.title: Why two sealing locations are required
keyConcepts.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.

Caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

keyConcepts.title: Cooling and flushing
keyConcepts.body:
Seal faces and packing generate heat by friction, and that heat must be removed continuously. Flush (for mechanical seals) and seal water (for packing) do this, and serve several other purposes: they keep the sealing surfaces wetted, keep the liquid around the seal from flashing to vapour, sweep solids away, and help prevent air or vapour from collecting in the top of a horizontal chamber.

In clean-water service a common arrangement takes liquid from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or volute, through small-bore tubing with an orifice into each seal chamber. In many water-service pumps the flush is taken by a small external line, and some designs use internal passages. Where the pumped liquid contains solids or is otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid is injected from an external source, and accessories such as strainers, cyclone separators or coolers may be added. Dual seals use a separate buffer or barrier fluid system.

The numbered seal piping plans defined in API 682 are widely used, even outside the oil and gas industry, as a shorthand for these arrangements; for example, one plan describes recirculation from the pump discharge to the seal chamber, and another describes injection of clean fluid from an external source. The plan for a given pump is stated on its seal datasheet.

For packing, seal water to the lantern ring must be at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure; it cools and lubricates the packing and, under suction lift, stops air ingress.

Caution: Do not isolate, re-route or resize flush lines without consulting the seal manufacturer. A blocked or closed flush is a common cause of seal failure.

keyConcepts.title: Leakage control
keyConcepts.body:
Packing and mechanical seals control leakage in fundamentally different ways.

Packing works by throttling, and it needs a controlled leakage: the liquid passing along the sleeve lubricates the packing and carries away frictional heat. The gland follower is adjusted to give the leakage rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends. Tightening to stop the leak completely makes the packing overheat, harden and burn, scores the sleeve, raises power absorption and eventually leads to more leakage, not less. New packing is started with generous leakage and taken up gradually as it beds in. Adjust the nuts evenly in small steps and allow time between adjustments.

A mechanical seal has very small leakage across its faces, much of which evaporates and is not visible. A steady visible drip generally indicates a problem, although some seals show slight leakage while bedding in; the seal manufacturer states what is acceptable. Rising leakage over time shows face wear, damage or a secondary seal problem.

In both cases, leakage must be collected and drained safely, for example to a gland drain or the baseplate drain rim, especially where the liquid is hot, hazardous or slippery, and it must be kept away from the bearing housings, where shaft deflectors and housing seals provide protection. Under suction lift, a sealing point can leak air in rather than liquid out; reduced performance or noise may be the only sign.

Caution: Gland adjustment on a running pump puts hands close to the rotating shaft and coupling. Do it only where the site procedure permits, with all guards fitted and loose clothing and tools kept clear.

mech-seal-nde-rotating-face.summary: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
mech-seal-nde-rotating-face.function: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
mech-seal-nde-rotating-face.operatingPrinciple: In the baseline seal the rotating face is the flexibly mounted ring. The springs push it against the stationary seat, and it floats on its secondary seal so that it can follow face wear, small axial shaft movement and slight misalignment. Its lapped surface runs on a very thin film of the sealed liquid, across which a tiny leakage passes radially.
mech-seal-nde-rotating-face.construction: A ring of carbon-graphite, or of a hard face material such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide, lapped flat and polished on its sealing face. It is driven by lugs, pins or notches in the retainer and sealed to the sleeve by the secondary seal. A common pairing is a carbon face against a hard face; hard-against-hard pairs are often used where abrasive particles are present.

mech-seal-nde-gland.summary: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
mech-seal-nde-gland.function: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
mech-seal-nde-gland.operatingPrinciple: The gland is the reference that keeps the seat square and centred, and uneven tightening distorts the seat. The register, not the bolts, should provide concentricity. With cartridge seals the setting devices must be removed or disengaged after the gland is bolted up and the sleeve is locked, and before the shaft is turned; leaving them in place is a classic cause of immediate failure.
mech-seal-nde-gland.construction: A machined plate with a register or spigot that centres it on the seal chamber, a recess for the seat and its O-ring, tapped ports, and bolt holes for the studs and nuts on the seal chamber face. Cartridge seals have their own gland, supplied with setting clips or plates fitted for installation.

seal-flush-nde.summary: Supplies a controlled flow of liquid to the seal chamber close to the seal faces, to carry away the heat generated at the faces, keep them wetted, stop the liquid around them from flashing to vapour, and help keep solids and trapped air or vapour away from the seal.

seal-flush-nde.construction: A tapped connection in the gland plate or seal chamber, with tubing, an orifice or other flow control, an isolating valve and, in some arrangements, a strainer, cyclone separator or cooler.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: A blocked orifice, a closed valve or a failed external supply removes the seal's cooling and lubrication, and is a common cause of seal overheating and failure.

keyConcepts.title: Cooling and flushing
keyConcepts.body:
Seal faces and packing generate heat by friction, and that heat must be removed continuously. Flush (for mechanical seals) and seal water (for packing) do this, and serve several other purposes: they keep the sealing surfaces wetted, keep the liquid around the seal from flashing to vapour, sweep solids away, and help prevent air or vapour from collecting in the top of a horizontal chamber.

In clean-water service a common arrangement takes liquid from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or volute, through small-bore tubing with an orifice into each seal chamber. In many water-service pumps the flush is taken by a small external line, and some designs use internal passages. Where the pumped liquid contains solids or is otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid is injected from an external source, and accessories such as strainers, cyclone separators or coolers may be added. Dual seals use a separate buffer or barrier fluid system.

The numbered seal piping plans defined in API 682 are widely used, even outside the oil and gas industry, as a shorthand for these arrangements; for example, one plan describes recirculation from the pump discharge to the seal chamber, and another describes injection of clean fluid from an external source. The plan for a given pump is stated on its seal datasheet.

For packing, seal water to the lantern ring must be at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure; it cools and lubricates the packing and, under suction lift, stops air ingress.

Caution: Do not isolate, re-route or resize flush lines without consulting the seal manufacturer. A blocked or closed flush is a common cause of seal failure.

Where both seals are flushed from one source, each line normally has its own orifice or flow control so that both chambers receive flow.

packing-rings-nde.summary: The sealing elements of the stuffing box: deformable rings compressed against the sleeve and bore to restrict leakage along the shaft.
packing-rings-nde.function: The sealing elements of the stuffing box: deformable rings compressed against the sleeve and bore to restrict leakage along the shaft.
packing-rings-nde.operatingPrinciple: Under gland load the rings deform and bear lightly on the rotating sleeve. Friction at this contact generates heat, which the controlled leakage removes. In service the rings consolidate and lose some of their impregnated lubricant, so the gland has to be re-tightened from time to time to hold the leakage rate.
packing-rings-nde.construction: Typically square-section braided rings made from yarns such as PTFE, graphite-filled PTFE, carbon or aramid fibres with lubricating impregnants, or die-formed rings of flexible graphite. Braided packing is cut into individual rings with butt or skive joints, and the joints of successive rings are staggered around the shaft.

keyConcepts.body: The lantern ring only works if it sits under the flush port. Because packing consolidates as the gland is tightened, it is positioned so that it ends up under the port in service. A misplaced lantern ring blocks the seal water, so the packing runs dry and air can enter.

keyConcepts.title: Why two sealing locations are required
keyConcepts.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.

Caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

gland-follower-nde.operatingPrinciple: The follower must enter the box squarely. gland-follower-nde.construction: A flanged ring whose spigot enters the stuffing box bore, with holes or slots for the gland studs. It is often split so that it can be removed from the shaft without dismantling the pump.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Loss of seal water lets the packing overheat and, if the stuffing box is below atmospheric pressure, allows air into the pump, which reduces performance and can cause loss of prime.

keyConcepts.title: Cooling and flushing
keyConcepts.body:
Seal faces and packing generate heat by friction, and that heat must be removed continuously. Flush (for mechanical seals) and seal water (for packing) do this, and serve several other purposes: they keep the sealing surfaces wetted, keep the liquid around the seal from flashing to vapour, sweep solids away, and help prevent air or vapour from collecting in the top of a horizontal chamber.

In clean-water service a common arrangement takes liquid from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or volute, through small-bore tubing with an orifice into each seal chamber. In many water-service pumps the flush is taken by a small external line, and some designs use internal passages. Where the pumped liquid contains solids or is otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid is injected from an external source, and accessories such as strainers, cyclone separators or coolers may be added. Dual seals use a separate buffer or barrier fluid system.

The numbered seal piping plans defined in API 682 are widely used, even outside the oil and gas industry, as a shorthand for these arrangements; for example, one plan describes recirculation from the pump discharge to the seal chamber, and another describes injection of clean fluid from an external source. The plan for a given pump is stated on its seal datasheet.

For packing, seal water to the lantern ring must be at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure; it cools and lubricates the packing and, under suction lift, stops air ingress.

Caution: Do not isolate, re-route or resize flush lines without consulting the seal manufacturer. A blocked or closed flush is a common cause of seal failure.
