keyConcepts.title: How the shaft transmits torque
keyConcepts.body:
Power flows from the motor shaft through the motor coupling hub, the flexible elements and spacer, and the pump coupling hub into the pump shaft at its drive-end extension. The shaft then carries the torque past the DE bearing and DE seal to the impeller seat, where the impeller key transfers it into the hub. The NDE section beyond the impeller carries only small torques from bearing and seal friction.

Torque, power and speed are related by P = T omega, with omega = 2 pi N / 60 for N in rev/min. In practical units, T (N m) = 9549 x P (kW) / N (rev/min). For example, a pump absorbing 200 kW at 1480 rev/min transmits about 9549 x 200 / 1480, roughly 1290 N m, through its DE shaft section. This is an illustrative calculation only.

At each keyed joint the torque is passed as a tangential force at the shaft surface, approximately F = 2T / d, carried by contact pressure on the key sides and by shear across the key section. Keyed joints are therefore checked for key shear, key-side bearing pressure and keyway stress. Starting transients, for example direct-on-line starting, can produce torques above the steady running value, so the OEM sizes the shaft and keys with margin for such conditions.

Caution: The worked figure is illustrative. Shaft and key sizing for a real pump is done by the OEM, including starting and transient torques.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing reactions: a simple beam model
keyConcepts.body:
For a first estimate, treat the rotor as a simply supported beam: the drive-end bearing is one support, the non-drive-end bearing the other, and L is the span between bearing centres. Let a radial load F act at the impeller, at distance a from the drive-end bearing and distance b from the non-drive-end bearing, so that a + b = L.

Taking moments about the non-drive-end bearing: R_DE × L = F × b, so R_DE = F × b / L. Taking moments about the drive-end bearing: R_NDE = F × a / L. As a check, R_DE + R_NDE = F. The bearing nearer the load carries the larger share; with the impeller at mid-span each carries half.

The rotor weight W acts vertically downwards, while the hydraulic radial force acts in a direction set by the operating point. In practice each load is resolved into vertical and horizontal components, the reactions are found for each component, and the components are combined vectorially to give the resultant reaction at each bearing.

An overhung load outside the span, such as a coupling weight W_c at distance c outboard of the drive-end bearing, increases R_DE by W_c × (L + c) / L and reduces R_NDE by W_c × c / L.

This model ignores shaft flexibility, bearing stiffness, dynamic loads and misalignment forces; OEMs use more detailed rotor analysis. It is, however, the starting point for most bearing-load calculations in machine design.

Caution: This is a teaching model for understanding load sharing, not a substitute for the OEM's bearing selection and rotor analysis.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission
keyConcepts.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

The torque path runs from the motor rotor through the motor shaft, the motor key and hub, the first flexible element, the spacer, the second flexible element, the pump hub and key, and into the pump shaft, which carries it to the impeller. Keys transmit torque through shear and bearing pressure on their sides; in some designs hubs are mounted by an interference fit that carries torque by friction, with or without a key.

The coupling must carry the steady operating torque and also transient torques. A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

Coupling size, type, bore fits and fastener tightening values come from the coupling manufacturer and the OEM. A coupling that has been under-selected, or assembled with the wrong bolts, can fail suddenly, which is one reason the guard must always be in place.

keyConcepts.title: What a flexible coupling does
keyConcepts.body:
A flexible coupling transmits torque while accommodating small amounts of angular, parallel and axial misalignment between two shafts. Some types also damp torsional vibration and shock. It cannot make poor alignment harmless: misalignment still produces reaction forces and moments on the bearings, wears or fatigues the flexible element, and causes vibration and heat. The coupling's misalignment capacity is for small changes in service, such as thermal growth and settling, not for installation errors.

A spacer coupling has two flexible planes separated by a spacer. This lets it take parallel offset as a small angle at each plane, and removing the spacer gives access to the drive-end seal and bearing housing, or allows the rotor to be lifted out, without moving the motor.

Common element types differ in important ways. Elastomeric couplings (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) are tolerant and damp vibration, but the elements age and wear, and some are not fail-safe if the element fails. Disc couplings use flexing stainless steel laminations; they need no lubrication and have low maintenance, but have limited misalignment capacity and definite axial stiffness, so their axial setting matters. Gear couplings carry high torque for their size, but need lubrication and can lock up and transmit axial force if the teeth wear or the lubricant fails. Grid couplings use a spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, offer some damping and need lubrication.

Allowable misalignment and service requirements are given in the coupling manufacturer's data.

keyConcepts.title: Angular misalignment
keyConcepts.body:
Angular misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines meet at an angle instead of lying on one straight line. It is usually described separately in the vertical and horizontal planes, and is commonly expressed as the difference in gap measured across the coupling face divided by the diameter at which it was measured, or as a slope.

As the shafts rotate, angular misalignment makes the flexible element bend back and forth once per revolution. In a spacer coupling the angle is taken at the two flexible planes. The effects include cyclic stress and wear in the element, extra reaction moments at the coupling-end bearings, heat in elastomeric elements, and vibration, typically with significant axial components at once and twice running speed.

Angularity in the vertical plane is corrected by changing the shims under the front and rear feet of the movable machine (normally the motor) by different amounts. Horizontal angularity is corrected by moving the front and rear of the movable machine sideways by different amounts, using the jacking screws. Because angular and parallel corrections interact, alignment calculations or alignment tools work out the moves needed at each foot.

Acceptable angular misalignment depends on speed and coupling type and must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Axial misalignment, end float and axial spacing
keyConcepts.body:
Axial misalignment means the shafts are not at the correct axial spacing. The coupling manufacturer specifies a distance between shaft ends, or a gap between hubs, that suits the spacer and flexible elements, often with an allowable range.

The pump rotor's axial position is fixed by its locating bearing, and the motor rotor's by the motor's own bearings. Each rotor still has some end float, and both shafts grow as they warm up, so the actual spacing changes between cold and hot conditions.

The effect of a wrong spacing depends on the coupling type. Disc couplings have definite axial stiffness, so incorrect spacing pre-stresses the discs, shortens their fatigue life and pushes an axial force into the pump's locating bearing and the motor bearings. Gear couplings allow axial sliding, but under torque the teeth can lock, transmitting axial force. Elastomeric couplings tolerate some axial variation, but compressing or stretching the element shortens its life.

Motors with sleeve bearings have a magnetic centre: the rotor tends to run at a particular axial position within its end float. For such motors the coupling must be set with the motor at its magnetic centre, and limited-end-float couplings are often used to keep the motor rotor within its float. The typical rolling-bearing TEFC motor shown in the model is located axially by its own bearings.

Set the spacing to the coupling manufacturer's and OEM's values, and check it when the spacer is refitted.

coupling-key-pump.function: Transmit torque between each shaft and its coupling hub through shear in the key and bearing pressure on the key sides.
coupling-key-pump.operatingPrinciple: Worn or loose keys allow movement that frets the keyway, and can lead to cracking or loss of drive. coupling-element.summary: The flexible members that transmit torque between the hubs and the spacer while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement between the shafts.
coupling-element.function: The flexible members that transmit torque between the hubs and the spacer while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement between the shafts.
coupling-element.operatingPrinciple: Each flexible plane allows a small angle between the parts on either side of it. With a spacer coupling there are two flexible planes, one at each end of the spacer, so a parallel offset between the shafts is taken up as a small angle at each plane, and angular misalignment is shared between them. Depending on type, flexibility comes from deforming an elastomer, flexing thin metal discs, sliding of crowned gear teeth, or flexing of a spring-steel grid.
coupling-element.construction: Elastomeric types (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) use rubber or polyurethane elements and give some damping. Disc couplings use laminated packs of thin stainless steel discs bolted alternately to hub and spacer flanges, need no lubrication, and have limited misalignment capacity and a definite axial stiffness. Gear couplings use crowned external teeth in internal sleeve teeth, carry high torque for their size, and need lubrication. Grid couplings use a tapered spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, need lubrication and give some damping.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: The coupling's misalignment capacity is there for small changes in service, not to excuse poor alignment; misalignment still loads the bearings, wears or fatigues the element and causes vibration. Elastomers age with heat, ozone, oils and chemicals; disc packs crack from excessive misalignment or wrong axial spacing; gear and grid types wear rapidly and can lock up without lubrication, transmitting axial force to the bearings. Some elastomeric designs are fail-safe and keep driving if the element fails; others are not.

keyConcepts.title: Radial loads on the bearings
keyConcepts.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. Dynamic loads are added by residual unbalance, hydraulic pulsations and rotor-dynamic effects.

The hydraulic radial force exists because the pressure around the impeller periphery is not perfectly uniform. In a single-volute casing it is typically smallest near the best efficiency point (BEP) and grows as the flow moves away from BEP, towards both shut-off and run-out. A double-volute casing, with its splitter rib, substantially reduces this force by setting two opposed volute passages against each other, but does not remove it. The direction of the force also changes with flow rate, so the bearings see a load that varies in both size and direction.

Both bearings share the radial load; how much each carries depends on where the impeller sits along the span and on any overhung load at the coupling end (see 'Bearing reactions'). The drive-end floating bearing carries radial load only; the non-drive-end locating bearing carries its radial share plus the residual axial thrust.

Sustained operation far from BEP increases radial load, shaft deflection, the risk of wear-ring and seal contact, and bearing temperature.

Caution: A double volute or robust bearings do not make every operating point acceptable. Operate within the allowable operating region stated by the OEM.

keyConcepts.title: Axial loads on the rotor
keyConcepts.body:
Axial (thrust) loads act along the shaft axis. A double-suction impeller is nominally symmetrical, so the hydraulic thrusts from its two sides largely cancel, but never exactly.

Residual hydraulic thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances in the impeller and casing halves, an impeller not exactly centred in the volute, unequal wear-ring clearances (especially as the rings wear unevenly), unequal flow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping layout, recirculation or cavitation starting at one eye at part load, and transient conditions such as start-up, shutdown and pressure surges. Mechanical sources add to it: axial force through the coupling (for example a gear coupling that locks under torque, or a disc coupling installed at the wrong axial spacing), and thermally induced load if the floating bearing is unable to move.

This residual thrust can act in either direction and can change direction with operating conditions or as the pump wears. It therefore has to be carried by a bearing that takes thrust both ways and holds the rotor in a defined axial position: the locating bearing at the non-drive end. The drive-end bearing is deliberately left free axially so that it carries radial load only.

Rotor weight does not create axial load on a horizontal shaft, although it does on a vertical one; load paths always depend on machine orientation.

Caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A locating (thrust) bearing is always required.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing vibration
keyConcepts.body:
Vibration is measured at the bearing housings because that is where the rotor's forces pass into the stationary structure. Readings are normally taken in three directions (horizontal, vertical and axial) at both bearings, with permanently mounted sensors or portable instruments at marked points so that results can be trended.

Overall vibration, often expressed as velocity, indicates the general condition of the machine and is compared with the OEM's limits, the applicable vibration standard or site criteria. Spectrum analysis then helps find the cause. A dominant component at running speed (1x) commonly suggests unbalance. 1x and 2x components with high axial readings often suggest misalignment. Vane-pass frequency (number of impeller vanes multiplied by running speed) relates to the interaction between impeller and volute tongue. Broad-band, random vibration may indicate cavitation or recirculation. Non-synchronous frequencies linked to bearing geometry indicate rolling-bearing defects.

Early bearing defects produce small, high-frequency impacts that are often hidden in overall readings, so techniques such as acceleration enveloping (demodulation), shock pulse or other high-frequency methods are used. The defect frequencies for outer race, inner race, rolling elements and cage are calculated from the bearing geometry and speed.

At the non-drive-end locating bearing, axial vibration deserves particular attention because it reflects thrust conditions. As with temperature, trends matter more than single readings.

Caution: Use acceptance limits from the OEM, the applicable standard or the site procedure; do not import limits from unrelated machines.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission
keyConcepts.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

The torque path runs from the motor rotor through the motor shaft, the motor key and hub, the first flexible element, the spacer, the second flexible element, the pump hub and key, and into the pump shaft, which carries it to the impeller. Keys transmit torque through shear and bearing pressure on their sides; in some designs hubs are mounted by an interference fit that carries torque by friction, with or without a key.

The coupling must carry the steady operating torque and also transient torques. A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

Coupling size, type, bore fits and fastener tightening values come from the coupling manufacturer and the OEM. A coupling that has been under-selected, or assembled with the wrong bolts, can fail suddenly, which is one reason the guard must always be in place.

coupling-spacer.summary: Spans the gap between the pump and motor hubs.
coupling-spacer.function: Spans the gap between the pump and motor hubs. Removing it leaves a clear space between the shaft ends, so that the drive-end bearing housing and seal can be worked on, or the rotor lifted out, without moving the motor and losing its alignment.
coupling-spacer.operatingPrinciple: Spacer length sets the geometry of the two flexible planes; for a given parallel offset, a longer spacer means a smaller angle at each plane. The spacer and its bolts form part of the balanced rotating assembly, so their orientation and fasteners matter.
coupling-spacer.construction: A tube or flanged spool bolted to the flexible elements at each end. Its length matches the specified distance between shaft ends.

keyConcepts.title: Shaft alignment
keyConcepts.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.

Caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

keyConcepts.title: Bearing reactions: a simple beam model
keyConcepts.body:
For a first estimate, treat the rotor as a simply supported beam: the drive-end bearing is one support, the non-drive-end bearing the other, and L is the span between bearing centres. Let a radial load F act at the impeller, at distance a from the drive-end bearing and distance b from the non-drive-end bearing, so that a + b = L.

Taking moments about the non-drive-end bearing: R_DE × L = F × b, so R_DE = F × b / L. Taking moments about the drive-end bearing: R_NDE = F × a / L. As a check, R_DE + R_NDE = F. The bearing nearer the load carries the larger share; with the impeller at mid-span each carries half.

The rotor weight W acts vertically downwards, while the hydraulic radial force acts in a direction set by the operating point. In practice each load is resolved into vertical and horizontal components, the reactions are found for each component, and the components are combined vectorially to give the resultant reaction at each bearing.

An overhung load outside the span, such as a coupling weight W_c at distance c outboard of the drive-end bearing, increases R_DE by W_c × (L + c) / L and reduces R_NDE by W_c × c / L.

This model ignores shaft flexibility, bearing stiffness, dynamic loads and misalignment forces; OEMs use more detailed rotor analysis. It is, however, the starting point for most bearing-load calculations in machine design.

Caution: This is a teaching model for understanding load sharing, not a substitute for the OEM's bearing selection and rotor analysis.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission
keyConcepts.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

keyConcepts.title: What a flexible coupling does
keyConcepts.body:
A flexible coupling transmits torque while accommodating small amounts of angular, parallel and axial misalignment between two shafts. Some types also damp torsional vibration and shock. It cannot make poor alignment harmless: misalignment still produces reaction forces and moments on the bearings, wears or fatigues the flexible element, and causes vibration and heat. The coupling's misalignment capacity is for small changes in service, such as thermal growth and settling, not for installation errors.

A spacer coupling has two flexible planes separated by a spacer. This lets it take parallel offset as a small angle at each plane, and removing the spacer gives access to the drive-end seal and bearing housing, or allows the rotor to be lifted out, without moving the motor.

Common element types differ in important ways. Elastomeric couplings (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) are tolerant and damp vibration, but the elements age and wear, and some are not fail-safe if the element fails. Disc couplings use flexing stainless steel laminations; they need no lubrication and have low maintenance, but have limited misalignment capacity and definite axial stiffness, so their axial setting matters. Gear couplings carry high torque for their size, but need lubrication and can lock up and transmit axial force if the teeth wear or the lubricant fails. Grid couplings use a spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, offer some damping and need lubrication.

Allowable misalignment and service requirements are given in the coupling manufacturer's data.

coupling-guard.summary: A fixed guard that encloses the coupling and the exposed shaft ends between the pump and motor, preventing contact with rotating parts and helping to contain debris if the coupling fails.
coupling-guard.function: A fixed guard that encloses the coupling and the exposed shaft ends between the pump and motor, preventing contact with rotating parts and helping to contain debris if the coupling fails.
coupling-guard.operatingPrinciple: Rotating couplings and shafts can catch clothing, hair, gloves or tools in a fraction of a second, causing severe injury or death; at running speed a coupling can look stationary or blurred. Machinery safety regulations require a guard to be in place whenever the machine can run. Where the atmosphere is potentially explosive, guard material and design may also have to meet hazardous-area requirements.
coupling-guard.construction: Usually two or more sheet-metal or mesh sections fastened to the baseplate or bearing housing so that they can only be removed with a tool. It must cover the full rotating length and keep a clearance to rotating parts. Any openings must be small enough, and far enough from the rotating parts, to prevent a hand or finger reaching them.

keyConcepts.title: Coupling guard safety
keyConcepts.body:
Rotating couplings and shaft ends are among the most dangerous parts of a pump set. They can catch clothing, hair, gloves, rags or tools in a fraction of a second, causing entanglement, amputation or death. At operating speed a coupling can look blurred or almost stationary, which misleads people about the danger.

The coupling guard is a fixed guard: it is fastened so that it can only be removed with a tool, it covers the coupling and all exposed shaft between the bearing housing and the motor, and any openings are sized and placed so that fingers and hands cannot reach rotating parts. Machinery safety regulations and standards require such guarding; safety-distance standards such as ISO 13857 relate opening sizes to reach distances. In potentially explosive atmospheres, guard materials and clearances may also need to meet hazardous-area requirements so that contact cannot cause sparks.

Rules that apply on every site:

Never run the pump with the guard removed, open or damaged.

Remove the guard only after the driver has been electrically isolated and locked out under the permit system, and zero energy has been verified. Consider also that liquid flowing back through the pump can turn the rotor.

Refit and secure the guard before the isolation is removed and before any test run.

For an uncoupled motor rotation check, remove or secure the motor key and keep clear of the shaft end.

Check the guard on rounds for security, damage and rubbing marks.

Caution: The 3D viewer can hide or make the guard transparent for learning purposes. A real pump must never be operated without its guard fitted and secure.

motor-frame.summary: Houses and supports the stator, carries the end shields that hold the motor bearings, provides the feet and terminal box mounting, and dissipates the motor's losses as heat through its fins.
motor-frame.function: Houses and supports the stator, carries the end shields that hold the motor bearings, provides the feet and terminal box mounting, and dissipates the motor's losses as heat through its fins.
motor-frame.operatingPrinciple: In a totally enclosed fan-cooled (TEFC) motor the inside is sealed from the outside air. Heat from the windings and core passes into the frame, and the external fan blows air along the fins to carry it away.
motor-frame.construction: A cast iron, aluminium or fabricated steel frame with external axial cooling fins, machined spigots for the end shields, cast or bolted feet, lifting eyes and an earth terminal.

keyConcepts.title: Motor end shields
keyConcepts.body: Close the ends of the motor frame, house the motor bearings, and centre the rotor in the stator bore so that the air gap is uniform. Cast end shields spigoted into the frame, with machined bearing seats, bearing caps and, on larger motors, grease nipples and grease relief outlets.

motor-stator.summary: The stationary electromagnetic part of the motor.
motor-stator.function: The stationary electromagnetic part of the motor. When its three-phase winding is connected to an alternating supply, it produces a magnetic field that rotates at synchronous speed.
motor-stator.operatingPrinciple: The three phase currents, displaced in time and in space around the stator, combine to give a rotating field. Its speed, the synchronous speed, is n_s = 120 f / p rpm, where f is the supply frequency in Hz and p is the number of poles. The field induces currents in the rotor cage, and their interaction with the field produces torque.
motor-stator.construction: A core of thin, insulated electrical steel laminations (to limit eddy-current loss) with slots holding insulated copper windings, varnish-impregnated as a unit. Where fitted, winding temperature detectors and anti-condensation heaters are built in.

motor-rotor.summary: The rotating electromagnetic part of the induction motor; currents induced in its cage conductors interact with the stator field to produce torque.
motor-rotor.function: The rotating electromagnetic part of the induction motor; currents induced in its cage conductors interact with the stator field to produce torque.
motor-rotor.operatingPrinciple: The rotor turns slightly slower than the stator field. This difference, the slip, is what allows the field to induce current in the cage bars; the slip increases with load.
motor-rotor.construction: A laminated electrical steel core shrunk or keyed onto the motor shaft, with conductor bars in its slots joined by end rings to form a squirrel cage; the cage is commonly die-cast aluminium or fabricated copper. The rotor is dynamically balanced.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Runout and keyway condition at the shaft extension affect coupling fit and alignment readings. The motor rotor's axial position and end float influence the coupling's axial setting.

keyConcepts.title: Torque transmission
keyConcepts.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

The torque path runs from the motor rotor through the motor shaft, the motor key and hub, the first flexible element, the spacer, the second flexible element, the pump hub and key, and into the pump shaft, which carries it to the impeller. Keys transmit torque through shear and bearing pressure on their sides; in some designs hubs are mounted by an interference fit that carries torque by friction, with or without a key.

The coupling must carry the steady operating torque and also transient torques. A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

Coupling size, type, bore fits and fastener tightening values come from the coupling manufacturer and the OEM. A coupling that has been under-selected, or assembled with the wrong bolts, can fail suddenly, which is one reason the guard must always be in place.

keyConcepts.title: Axial misalignment, end float and axial spacing
keyConcepts.body:
Axial misalignment means the shafts are not at the correct axial spacing. The coupling manufacturer specifies a distance between shaft ends, or a gap between hubs, that suits the spacer and flexible elements, often with an allowable range.

The pump rotor's axial position is fixed by its locating bearing, and the motor rotor's by the motor's own bearings. Each rotor still has some end float, and both shafts grow as they warm up, so the actual spacing changes between cold and hot conditions.

The effect of a wrong spacing depends on the coupling type. Disc couplings have definite axial stiffness, so incorrect spacing pre-stresses the discs, shortens their fatigue life and pushes an axial force into the pump's locating bearing and the motor bearings. Gear couplings allow axial sliding, but under torque the teeth can lock, transmitting axial force. Elastomeric couplings tolerate some axial variation, but compressing or stretching the element shortens its life.

Motors with sleeve bearings have a magnetic centre: the rotor tends to run at a particular axial position within its end float. For such motors the coupling must be set with the motor at its magnetic centre, and limited-end-float couplings are often used to keep the motor rotor within its float. The typical rolling-bearing TEFC motor shown in the model is located axially by its own bearings.

Set the spacing to the coupling manufacturer's and OEM's values, and check it when the spacer is refitted.

keyConcepts.body: If one foot does not sit flat on its pad and shims (soft foot), tightening the hold-down bolt distorts the frame, which changes alignment, can alter the air gap and increases vibration. Bolts that bind in their holes ('bolt bound') limit the horizontal adjustment available.

keyConcepts.title: Angular misalignment
keyConcepts.body:
Angular misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines meet at an angle instead of lying on one straight line. It is usually described separately in the vertical and horizontal planes, and is commonly expressed as the difference in gap measured across the coupling face divided by the diameter at which it was measured, or as a slope.

As the shafts rotate, angular misalignment makes the flexible element bend back and forth once per revolution. In a spacer coupling the angle is taken at the two flexible planes. The effects include cyclic stress and wear in the element, extra reaction moments at the coupling-end bearings, heat in elastomeric elements, and vibration, typically with significant axial components at once and twice running speed.

Angularity in the vertical plane is corrected by changing the shims under the front and rear feet of the movable machine (normally the motor) by different amounts. Horizontal angularity is corrected by moving the front and rear of the movable machine sideways by different amounts, using the jacking screws. Because angular and parallel corrections interact, alignment calculations or alignment tools work out the moves needed at each foot.

Acceptable angular misalignment depends on speed and coupling type and must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Parallel (offset) misalignment
keyConcepts.body:
Parallel, or offset, misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines are parallel but displaced from each other. Like angularity, it is described in the vertical and horizontal planes and is measured at a stated position, usually at the coupling or at the flexible planes.

In a spacer coupling, offset is taken up as an angle at each flexible plane. For small angles that angle is approximately the offset divided by the distance between the flexible planes, so for the same offset a longer spacer gives a smaller angle at each element. Real installations normally have a combination of offset and angularity in both planes.

Offset causes radial forces on the coupling-end bearings and cyclic loading of the element, and typically shows as radial vibration at once and twice running speed. It also adds to seal and bearing problems through shaft deflection.

Vertical offset is corrected by adding or removing equal shim thickness under all feet of the movable machine. Horizontal offset is corrected by moving the whole movable machine sideways with the jacking screws.

Pump and motor shafts often grow by different amounts as they reach operating temperature, so the cold alignment target may deliberately include an offset that disappears when the machines are hot. Any such allowance must come from the OEM, and acceptable offset from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment procedures
keyConcepts.body:
Shaft alignment brings the motor shaft into line with the pump shaft within the tolerance specified by the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard. The pump is usually the stationary machine, since it is connected to the piping, and the motor is moved.

Preparation comes first: isolate and lock out the driver, clean feet and pads, check that the baseplate is grouted and the pipework connected without strain, and check hub runout. Then check soft foot: with indicators or an alignment system on the shafts, slacken each hold-down bolt in turn and correct any foot that moves, whether by parallel gap, angular gap or a springy shim pack. Measuring alignment with soft foot present gives unreliable results.

The main measuring methods are:

Rim and face: one dial indicator reads the hub rim (offset), another the hub face (angularity); face readings are affected by axial float.

Reverse indicator: rim readings are taken on both hubs from brackets on the opposite shaft. It is less affected by axial float and suits spacer couplings and longer spans. Indicator bracket sag must be measured and allowed for.

Laser alignment: laser emitters and detectors on both shafts calculate offset, angularity and the corrections at each foot directly.

Correct vertical misalignment with shims and horizontal misalignment with the jacking screws, then re-measure. Apply any thermal growth allowance that the OEM specifies. Record the final readings, then re-check after the piping is finally connected and, where specified, after a hot run.

Caution: Alignment work is done with the driver isolated and locked out. Numerical alignment tolerances must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment and the baseplate
keyConcepts.body:
Good shaft alignment depends on a good baseplate installation; the baseplate is the reference to which both machines are bolted.

Before grouting, the baseplate is levelled and its machined pads checked for flatness and co-planarity, against values from the OEM, using levelling screws or packers. If the pads are twisted or uneven, the machines will distort when they are bolted down, producing soft foot that no amount of alignment can correct. After grouting and anchor bolt tightening the pads are checked again, because grouting and bolting can shift the baseplate.

The pump is normally fixed first as the stationary machine, because the piping will be attached to it; its feet should sit on the pads with little or no shimming. The motor is the movable machine. Its pads are often slightly low so that it sits on a shim pack, allowing adjustment both up and down, and the jacking screws on the baseplate allow controlled sideways moves.

A typical sequence is: rough alignment before piping is connected; connection of piping without strain; checks for soft foot and pipe strain; precise alignment; and recording of the results. Some sites dowel the machines after final alignment. Alignment is re-checked after commissioning runs and whenever the baseplate, piping or foundation has been disturbed.

baseplate.summary: The common support for pump and motor.
baseplate.function: The common support for pump and motor. It holds them in alignment, carries their weight and operating loads into the foundation through the grout and anchor bolts, and in many designs collects leakage in a drain rim.
baseplate.operatingPrinciple: The baseplate on its own is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to a sound foundation, becoming one structure with it. Flatness and co-planarity of the pads, and the stiffness of the grouted assembly, determine how well alignment holds and how much vibration is transmitted.
baseplate.construction: Typically a fabricated structure of steel sections with a deck or top plates, machined mounting pads for pump and motor, grout and vent holes, levelling-screw bosses, lifting lugs and a drain connection. Some baseplates are delivered pre-filled with grout in the factory.

keyConcepts.title: Leakage control
keyConcepts.body:
Packing and mechanical seals control leakage in fundamentally different ways.

Packing works by throttling, and it needs a controlled leakage: the liquid passing along the sleeve lubricates the packing and carries away frictional heat. The gland follower is adjusted to give the leakage rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends. Tightening to stop the leak completely makes the packing overheat, harden and burn, scores the sleeve, raises power absorption and eventually leads to more leakage, not less. New packing is started with generous leakage and taken up gradually as it beds in. Adjust the nuts evenly in small steps and allow time between adjustments.

A mechanical seal has very small leakage across its faces, much of which evaporates and is not visible. A steady visible drip generally indicates a problem, although some seals show slight leakage while bedding in; the seal manufacturer states what is acceptable. Rising leakage over time shows face wear, damage or a secondary seal problem.

In both cases, leakage must be collected and drained safely, for example to a gland drain or the baseplate drain rim, especially where the liquid is hot, hazardous or slippery, and it must be kept away from the bearing housings, where shaft deflectors and housing seals provide protection. Under suction lift, a sealing point can leak air in rather than liquid out; reduced performance or noise may be the only sign.

Caution: Gland adjustment on a running pump puts hands close to the rotating shaft and coupling. Do it only where the site procedure permits, with all guards fitted and loose clothing and tools kept clear.

keyConcepts.title: Importance of foundation stiffness
keyConcepts.body:
The foundation's job is to hold the pump and motor so steadily that alignment does not change and vibration is not amplified. It must carry the static weight of the machines, baseplate and liquid; react the torque between pump and motor; resist the dynamic forces from residual unbalance and hydraulic pulsation; and take any loads that the piping applies.

Stiffness and mass work together. A stiff, massive foundation deflects little under load, so the shafts stay aligned, and it raises the natural frequencies of the installed system. Ideally those natural frequencies are well separated from running speed and its main multiples, because operating near a resonance can turn a small force into large vibration. A flexible or lightweight foundation, or one standing on soft or settling ground, lets the baseplate move and the alignment drift.

The baseplate alone is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to the foundation so that both act as one body. Many installations isolate the foundation block from the surrounding floor slab with a joint, so that vibration is not passed to the building and other machines do not shake the pump.

Rules of thumb relating foundation mass to machine mass are often quoted, but foundation design should follow the OEM's loading data, the applicable guidance and the work of a civil or structural engineer.

keyConcepts.title: Grouting
keyConcepts.body:
Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation. When it is placed correctly it makes full contact with both surfaces, spreads the load, bonds the baseplate to the foundation so they behave as one stiff structure, adds damping and protects the underside of the baseplate.

The usual sequence is: prepare the foundation surface by removing the weak top layer to sound concrete and cleaning it; set the baseplate on its levelling screws or packers and level it as the OEM specifies; build formwork; prepare anchor bolt sleeves and protect the levelling screw threads; then place the grout through the grout holes, working from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, until the space is completely filled. The grout is then cured as its manufacturer specifies.

Epoxy grouts generally offer higher strength, better bond and better resistance to oil and chemicals, and cure quickly, but they are sensitive to temperature during placement and cure and are more expensive. Non-shrink cementitious grouts are cheaper and simpler to use but need careful curing, and they are attacked by oil over time.

After curing, the baseplate is tapped to find hollow-sounding voids, which are filled by injection as the grout manufacturer recommends. Only then are the anchor bolts tightened and, in many procedures, the levelling screws backed off so the grout carries the load. Alignment is then checked again.

Factory pre-grouted baseplates reduce the risk of voids under the deck but still need field grouting.

Caution: Grout materials, thicknesses, temperatures and curing times must come from the grout manufacturer, the OEM and the project specification.

keyConcepts.title: Pipe strain
keyConcepts.body:
Pipe strain is the force and moment that the connected piping applies to the pump nozzles. It arises when flanges are pulled together that did not line up, when pipes and valves are not properly supported, when thermal expansion is not accommodated, and when expansion joints are left unrestrained.

In a split case pump, nozzle loads act on the lower casing half. Excessive loads can distort the casing, upsetting internal clearances and the split joint; shift the pump on its pads; and move the shaft out of alignment with the motor. The results are bearing overloading, seal failures, coupling wear, vibration and casing joint leaks. An unrestrained expansion joint is especially damaging, because the pressure inside it pushes on the pump with a force equal to the pressure times the joint's effective area.

Good practice is to support the pipes independently near the pump, so that the pump does not carry their weight; to make flanges meet squarely and concentrically, with the right gap, before any bolt is tightened; to restrain expansion joints with tie rods or anchors; and to make the final connection at the pump after the pipework is fixed. A practical check is to mount dial indicators on the coupling, or use the alignment system, and watch for movement while the flange bolts are tightened or loosened; significant movement shows strain that must be corrected in the piping, not by forcing the pump.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM.

Caution: Never use the pump as an anchor for the piping, and never pull misaligned flanges together with the bolts.

keyConcepts.body:

keyConcepts.body:

Any such allowance must come from the OEM, and acceptable offset from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment procedures
keyConcepts.body:
Shaft alignment brings the motor shaft into line with the pump shaft within the tolerance specified by the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard. The pump is usually the stationary machine, since it is connected to the piping, and the motor is moved.

Preparation comes first: isolate and lock out the driver, clean feet and pads, check that the baseplate is grouted and the pipework connected without strain, and check hub runout. Then check soft foot: with indicators or an alignment system on the shafts, slacken each hold-down bolt in turn and correct any foot that moves, whether by parallel gap, angular gap or a springy shim pack. Measuring alignment with soft foot present gives unreliable results.

The main measuring methods are:

Rim and face: one dial indicator reads the hub rim (offset), another the hub face (angularity); face readings are affected by axial float.

Reverse indicator: rim readings are taken on both hubs from brackets on the opposite shaft. It is less affected by axial float and suits spacer couplings and longer spans. Indicator bracket sag must be measured and allowed for.

Laser alignment: laser emitters and detectors on both shafts calculate offset, angularity and the corrections at each foot directly.

Caution: Alignment work is done with the driver isolated and locked out. Numerical alignment tolerances must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment and the baseplate
keyConcepts.body:

A typical sequence is: rough alignment before piping is connected; connection of piping without strain; checks for soft foot and pipe strain; precise alignment; and recording of the results. Some sites dowel the machines after final alignment. Alignment is re-checked after commissioning runs and whenever the baseplate, piping or foundation has been disturbed.

keyConcepts.title: Grouting
keyConcepts.body:
Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation. When it is placed correctly it makes full contact with both surfaces, spreads the load, bonds the baseplate to the foundation so they behave as one stiff structure, adds damping and protects the underside of the baseplate.

The usual sequence is: prepare the foundation surface by removing the weak top layer to sound concrete and cleaning it; set the baseplate on its levelling screws or packers and level it as the OEM specifies; build formwork; prepare anchor bolt sleeves and protect the levelling screw threads; then place the grout through the grout holes, working from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, until the space is completely filled. Factory pre-grouted baseplates reduce the risk of voids under the deck but still need field grouting.

grout.operatingPrinciple: Properly placed grout makes full, void-free contact with both the baseplate and the foundation, so static and dynamic loads pass into the concrete over a large area instead of through a few points. keyConcepts.title: Importance of foundation stiffness
keyConcepts.body:
The foundation's job is to hold the pump and motor so steadily that alignment does not change and vibration is not amplified. It must carry the static weight of the machines, baseplate and liquid; react the torque between pump and motor; resist the dynamic forces from residual unbalance and hydraulic pulsation; and take any loads that the piping applies.

Stiffness and mass work together. A stiff, massive foundation deflects little under load, so the shafts stay aligned, and it raises the natural frequencies of the installed system. Ideally those natural frequencies are well separated from running speed and its main multiples, because operating near a resonance can turn a small force into large vibration. A flexible or lightweight foundation, or one standing on soft or settling ground, lets the baseplate move and the alignment drift.

The baseplate alone is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to the foundation so that both act as one body. Many installations isolate the foundation block from the surrounding floor slab with a joint, so that vibration is not passed to the building and other machines do not shake the pump.

Rules of thumb relating foundation mass to machine mass are often quoted, but foundation design should follow the OEM's loading data, the applicable guidance and the work of a civil or structural engineer.

keyConcepts.title: Grouting
keyConcepts.body:
Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation. When it is placed correctly it makes full contact with both surfaces, spreads the load, bonds the baseplate to the foundation so they behave as one stiff structure, adds damping and protects the underside of the baseplate.

The usual sequence is: prepare the foundation surface by removing the weak top layer to sound concrete and cleaning it; set the baseplate on its levelling screws or packers and level it as the OEM specifies; build formwork; prepare anchor bolt sleeves and protect the levelling screw threads; then place the grout through the grout holes, working from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, until the space is completely filled. The grout is then cured as its manufacturer specifies.

Epoxy grouts generally offer higher strength, better bond and better resistance to oil and chemicals, and cure quickly, but they are sensitive to temperature during placement and cure and are more expensive. Non-shrink cementitious grouts are cheaper and simpler to use but need careful curing, and they are attacked by oil over time.

After curing, the baseplate is tapped to find hollow-sounding voids, which are filled by injection as the grout manufacturer recommends. Only then are the anchor bolts tightened and, in many procedures, the levelling screws backed off so the grout carries the load. Alignment is then checked again.

Factory pre-grouted baseplates reduce the risk of voids under the deck but still need field grouting.

Caution: Grout materials, thicknesses, temperatures and curing times must come from the grout manufacturer, the OEM and the project specification.

keyConcepts.title: Foundation vibration
keyConcepts.body:
Vibration measured on a pump is not always caused by the pump. Weaknesses in the baseplate, grout, anchor bolts or foundation can allow normal forces to produce excessive vibration, or can amplify it through resonance.

Typical causes include voids under the baseplate, cracked or delaminated grout, loose anchor or hold-down bolts, soft foot, a foundation that is too light or flexible, a natural frequency close to running speed or one of its multiples, foundation settlement, and vibration from nearby machines transmitted through a shared floor.

Symptoms include vibration that stays high after balancing and alignment are corrected, vibration that changes greatly with small changes in speed (a sign of resonance), and readings that are higher in one direction, often horizontal, than would be expected.

Investigation compares vibration measured on the machine feet, the baseplate, the grout and the foundation at the same time. A sudden step in amplitude or phase across a joint shows looseness at that joint. An impact (bump) test with the machine stopped identifies natural frequencies. Tap-testing the baseplate locates voids. Checking bolt tightness and soft foot is quick and often revealing.

Corrective action targets the cause: re-grouting or injecting voids, tightening or replacing anchors, correcting soft foot, or stiffening or detuning the structure under engineering guidance. In building services, spring-isolated inertia bases with flexible pipe connectors are sometimes used to limit transmission, but they must be designed for the purpose.

keyConcepts.title: Baseplate deflection
keyConcepts.body:
A baseplate must stay flat and stable so that the pump and motor shafts stay aligned. Any deflection or twist between the pump and motor pads appears directly as misalignment.

Deflection can occur at several stages. During lifting and transport, an ungrouted fabricated baseplate is relatively flexible; lifting it at the wrong points, or with equipment mounted when the OEM does not allow it, can bend or twist it. During installation, levelling on too few supports, uneven levelling screws or tightening anchor bolts over voids can distort it. In service, loads from unsupported or strained piping, the reaction torque between pump and motor, and thermal effects (for example a hot pump on one side) can deflect it.

Designers provide stiffness with deep sections, cross members and torsional bracing between the pump and motor pads; pumping standards for some industries specify stiffness requirements or tests. The most important stiffening step on site is correct, void-free grouting, which turns the baseplate and foundation into one body.

On site, check pad flatness and co-planarity after levelling and again after grouting; check that alignment does not change when anchor bolts are tightened, when piping is connected or after the pump has reached operating temperature; and investigate any alignment that repeatedly drifts, since it often points to deflection, a weak foundation or pipe strain.

Caution: Lift the baseplate only at its designated points and in the condition (empty or with equipment mounted) that the OEM permits.

suction-reducer.summary: Joins the larger suction pipe to the smaller pump suction nozzle without creating a high point where air or vapour could collect.
suction-reducer.function: Joins the larger suction pipe to the smaller pump suction nozzle without creating a high point where air or vapour could collect.
suction-reducer.operatingPrinciple: With the flat side on top, the crown of the pipe stays continuous into the nozzle, so there is no pocket for air. A concentric reducer, or an eccentric reducer installed flat side down, leaves a pocket at the top where air can accumulate, reducing the flow area, disturbing the flow into the impeller and sometimes releasing into the pump as a slug of air.
suction-reducer.construction: A flanged or welded eccentric reducer installed directly at, or close to, the suction flange.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: Air pockets in suction lines cause noisy, unsteady operation, reduced performance and possible loss of prime. Under suction lift, flange leaks on the suction side draw air in rather than letting liquid out.

keyConcepts.title: Pipe strain
keyConcepts.body:
Pipe strain is the force and moment that the connected piping applies to the pump nozzles. It arises when flanges are pulled together that did not line up, when pipes and valves are not properly supported, when thermal expansion is not accommodated, and when expansion joints are left unrestrained.

In a split case pump, nozzle loads act on the lower casing half. Excessive loads can distort the casing, upsetting internal clearances and the split joint; shift the pump on its pads; and move the shaft out of alignment with the motor. The results are bearing overloading, seal failures, coupling wear, vibration and casing joint leaks. An unrestrained expansion joint is especially damaging, because the pressure inside it pushes on the pump with a force equal to the pressure times the joint's effective area.

Good practice is to support the pipes independently near the pump, so that the pump does not carry their weight; to make flanges meet squarely and concentrically, with the right gap, before any bolt is tightened; to restrain expansion joints with tie rods or anchors; and to make the final connection at the pump after the pipework is fixed. A practical check is to mount dial indicators on the coupling, or use the alignment system, and watch for movement while the flange bolts are tightened or loosened; significant movement shows strain that must be corrected in the piping, not by forcing the pump.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM.

Caution: Never use the pump as an anchor for the piping, and never pull misaligned flanges together with the bolts.

Illustrative spool for the installation lessons; hidden by default.

suction-pipe.summary: Delivers liquid to the pump with a steady, uniform flow and enough pressure (net positive suction head available) to avoid cavitation.
suction-pipe.function: Delivers liquid to the pump with a steady, uniform flow and enough pressure (net positive suction head available) to avoid cavitation.
suction-pipe.operatingPrinciple: For a double-suction pump, the flow arriving at the suction nozzle should be as uniform as possible so that both impeller eyes receive equal flow. An elbow close to the suction nozzle lying in a plane parallel to the shaft (a horizontal plane for this pump) can bias flow towards one eye, causing unequal loading, additional axial thrust, noise and cavitation at one eye. Guidance from the OEM and the Hydraulic Institute typically calls for a straight run before the nozzle and, where an elbow is unavoidable close to the pump, orienting it in the plane perpendicular to the shaft.
suction-pipe.construction: A pipe run sized for low velocity, laid without high points where air could collect, with an isolating valve that is kept fully open in service and, during commissioning, often a temporary strainer.

keyConcepts.title: Engineering importance
keyConcepts.body: For a double-suction pump, the flow arriving at the suction nozzle should be as uniform as possible so that both impeller eyes receive equal flow. An elbow close to the suction nozzle lying in a plane parallel to the shaft (a horizontal plane for this pump) can bias flow towards one eye, causing unequal loading, additional axial thrust, noise and cavitation at one eye. Guidance from the OEM and the Hydraulic Institute typically calls for a straight run before the nozzle and, where an elbow is unavoidable close to the pump, orienting it in the plane perpendicular to the shaft.

keyConcepts.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
keyConcepts.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.

Caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

keyConcepts.title: How double suction affects thrust-bearing duty
keyConcepts.body:
In a single-suction closed impeller, the pressure behind the back shroud acts over a larger area than the pressure on the front shroud, where the eye is at low suction pressure. The result is a substantial net axial thrust towards the suction side. Single-suction pumps therefore need balancing features (balance holes, back wear rings or pump-out vanes) and a thrust bearing sized for what remains.

A double-suction impeller is, in effect, two single-suction impellers back to back on one hub. Liquid enters through two opposed eyes and the pressure distributions on the two shrouds are mirror images, so their thrusts largely cancel. The thrust bearing in a double-suction pump therefore typically carries a residual load that is small in comparison, which allows a compact locating bearing and contributes to this pump type's reputation for long, reliable runs at large flows.

Largely cancelling is not the same as cancelling. Residual thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances, axial mispositioning of the impeller, uneven wear-ring clearances, unequal flow to the two eyes from poor suction piping, part-load recirculation or cavitation at one eye, and transients. Its size and direction can change with flow rate and over the pump's life as clearances wear.

Thrust-bearing duty is therefore never zero, and the OEM assesses it over the full operating range. When the conditions that keep the impeller balanced deteriorate, the signs are rising non-drive-end bearing temperature, higher axial vibration and shorter bearing life.

Caution: Never assume that double suction eliminates axial thrust. Residual thrust always exists, which is why the pump has a locating bearing.

keyConcepts.title: Pipe strain
keyConcepts.body:
Pipe strain is the force and moment that the connected piping applies to the pump nozzles. It arises when flanges are pulled together that did not line up, when pipes and valves are not properly supported, when thermal expansion is not accommodated, and when expansion joints are left unrestrained.

In a split case pump, nozzle loads act on the lower casing half. Excessive loads can distort the casing, upsetting internal clearances and the split joint; shift the pump on its pads; and move the shaft out of alignment with the motor. The results are bearing overloading, seal failures, coupling wear, vibration and casing joint leaks. An unrestrained expansion joint is especially damaging, because the pressure inside it pushes on the pump with a force equal to the pressure times the joint's effective area.

Good practice is to support the pipes independently near the pump, so that the pump does not carry their weight; to make flanges meet squarely and concentrically, with the right gap, before any bolt is tightened; to restrain expansion joints with tie rods or anchors; and to make the final connection at the pump after the pipework is fixed. A practical check is to mount dial indicators on the coupling, or use the alignment system, and watch for movement while the flange bolts are tightened or loosened; significant movement shows strain that must be corrected in the piping, not by forcing the pump.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM.

Caution: Never use the pump as an anchor for the piping, and never pull misaligned flanges together with the bolts.

keyConcepts.title: Alignment procedures
keyConcepts.body:
Shaft alignment brings the motor shaft into line with the pump shaft within the tolerance specified by the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard. The pump is usually the stationary machine, since it is connected to the piping, and the motor is moved.

Preparation comes first: isolate and lock out the driver, clean feet and pads, check that the baseplate is grouted and the pipework connected without strain, and check hub runout. Then check soft foot: with indicators or an alignment system on the shafts, slacken each hold-down bolt in turn and correct any foot that moves, whether by parallel gap, angular gap or a springy shim pack. Measuring alignment with soft foot present gives unreliable results.

The main measuring methods are:

Rim and face: one dial indicator reads the hub rim (offset), another the hub face (angularity); face readings are affected by axial float.

Reverse indicator: rim readings are taken on both hubs from brackets on the opposite shaft. It is less affected by axial float and suits spacer couplings and longer spans. Indicator bracket sag must be measured and allowed for.

Laser alignment: laser emitters and detectors on both shafts calculate offset, angularity and the corrections at each foot directly.

Correct vertical misalignment with shims and horizontal misalignment with the jacking screws, then re-measure. Apply any thermal growth allowance that the OEM specifies. Record the final readings, then re-check after the piping is finally connected and, where specified, after a hot run.

Caution: Alignment work is done with the driver isolated and locked out. Numerical alignment tolerances must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard, not from this module.

keyConcepts.title: Baseplate deflection
keyConcepts.body:
A baseplate must stay flat and stable so that the pump and motor shafts stay aligned. Any deflection or twist between the pump and motor pads appears directly as misalignment.

Deflection can occur at several stages. During lifting and transport, an ungrouted fabricated baseplate is relatively flexible; lifting it at the wrong points, or with equipment mounted when the OEM does not allow it, can bend or twist it. During installation, levelling on too few supports, uneven levelling screws or tightening anchor bolts over voids can distort it. In service, loads from unsupported or strained piping, the reaction torque between pump and motor, and thermal effects (for example a hot pump on one side) can deflect it.

Designers provide stiffness with deep sections, cross members and torsional bracing between the pump and motor pads; pumping standards for some industries specify stiffness requirements or tests. The most important stiffening step on site is correct, void-free grouting, which turns the baseplate and foundation into one body.

On site, check pad flatness and co-planarity after levelling and again after grouting; check that alignment does not change when anchor bolts are tightened, when piping is connected or after the pump has reached operating temperature; and investigate any alignment that repeatedly drifts, since it often points to deflection, a weak foundation or pipe strain.

Caution: Lift the baseplate only at its designated points and in the condition (empty or with equipment mounted) that the OEM permits.

ksb-lexicon-axially-split-design.note: Definition of an axially (horizontally) split casing divided along the shaft centreline, compared with radially split designs. Used for the overview and casing topics.

ksb-lexicon-double-entry-impeller.title: Double-entry impeller (KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon)
ksb-lexicon-double-entry-impeller.note: Double-entry (double-suction) impeller with an inlet on both sides, and its purpose in reducing axial thrust and NPSHR. Used for the impeller and working-principle topics.

ksb-lexicon-axial-thrust.title: Axial thrust (KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon)
ksb-lexicon-axial-thrust.note: Sources of axial thrust on a pump rotor, balancing by a double-entry impeller, and residual thrust at low-flow and overload conditions that a thrust (locating) bearing must carry. Used for the axial thrust lesson and the residual-thrust caution.

grundfos-ls-split-case-iom.title: LS Horizontal split case pump — Installation and operating instructions
grundfos-ls-split-case-iom.note: Typical OEM practice for a horizontal split case pump. Covers receiving and storage, foundation, base frame and grouting, piping and inlet pipe guidelines (eccentric reducers, elbows, pipe strain), soft foot, prestart checks, priming, start-up and final alignment. Also covers stuffing box/packing and mechanical shaft seal notes, operating checks, maintenance, and fault finding (no flow, low pressure, high power, vibration, cavitation noise, bearing overheating). Used for the installation, commissioning, checklist and troubleshooting topics. Values in the manual are model-specific and are not reproduced.

wilo-mather-platt-hsc-iom.title: Wilo Mather and Platt Horizontal Split Case Pumps — Installation and operating instructions (HSC_20131001_03)
wilo-mather-platt-hsc-iom.publisher: Wilo Mather and Platt Pumps Pvt. Ltd. (Wilo group)
wilo-mather-platt-hsc-iom.note: A second OEM view of split case practice. Covers lifting (including lifting points for the top casing only), storage, grouting, alignment, the sealing system (gland packing and mechanical seal), a pre-commissioning checklist, filling and venting, start-up, dismantling and reassembly, wear rings, and troubleshooting. Used for the procedure, sealing and commissioning topics. Values in the manual are model-specific and are not reproduced.

nsk-bearing-arrangement-guide.title: Technical Insight: Choosing the Right Bearing and Arrangement — a step-by-step guide
nsk-bearing-arrangement-guide.note: Locating/non-locating bearing arrangements: the locating bearing fixes the shaft axially and carries axial load, while the non-locating bearing carries radial load and lets the shaft grow axially with temperature. Also covers paired angular-contact (back-to-back and face-to-face) arrangements and the effect of shaft temperature on clearance. Used for the drive-end and non-drive-end bearing and thrust bearing topics.

eagleburgmann-lexicon-mechanical-seal.title: BURGMANN ABC lexicon — Mechanical seal
eagleburgmann-lexicon-mechanical-seal.note: How a mechanical seal works: rotating and stationary seal faces, secondary seals on the shaft and housing sides, spring loading, and the thin lubricating film between the faces. Used for the mechanical seal component and sealing topics.

chesterton-api-piping-plan-guide.title: API Piping Plan Guide for Mechanical Seals
chesterton-api-piping-plan-guide.note: Controlling the seal environment: flush, recirculation, quench and barrier/buffer piping plans, and why seal life depends on conditions at the seal faces. Used for the seal flush / auxiliary piping and mechanical-seal-failure topics.

ansi-hi-14-6.title: ANSI/HI 14.6-2022 - Rotodynamic Pumps for Hydraulic Performance Acceptance Tests
ansi-hi-14-6.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 14.6-2016, and HI's version history also lists earlier editions (2011, 2000).
ansi-hi-14-6.note: Verified on 2026-11-06 on the Hydraulic Institute product page (pumps.org). The page marks this as the current version, says it supersedes the 2016 edition, and HI's standards listing shows 2022 for this title. The HI page gives no ANSI approval date, and the ANSI Webstore returned HTTP 403, so that date is not verified. ansi-hi-9-6-6.title: ANSI/HI 9.6.6-2022 - Rotodynamic Pumps for Pump Piping
ansi-hi-9-6-6.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 9.6.6-2016; the earlier edition was 2009.

awwa-e103.title: ANSI/AWWA E103-21 - Horizontal Centrifugal and Vertical Line Shaft Pumps
awwa-e103.publisher: AWWA (American Water Works Association) — American National Standard
awwa-e103.note: Edition NOT verified from the issuing body: NOT VERIFIED against a readable AWWA page. api-610.title: API Std 610, 13th Edition (2026) / ISO 13709:2009 - Centrifugal Pumps for Petroleum, Petrochemical, and Natural Gas Industries (API Std 610); Centrifugal pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries (ISO 13709)

curves.title: Illustrative curves — educational split case model
curves.disclaimer: ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. Generated from generic dimensionless curve shapes for teaching; this is not manufacturer test data, not a rating and not suitable for pump selection or design. Use the OEM performance curve for the actual pump and impeller diameter.
curves.source: Generated in code: H = H_bep (1.25 - 0.1 q - 0.15 q^2), eta = eta_bep (2q - q^2), P = rho g Q H / eta, NPSHr = NPSHr_bep (0.55 + 0.45 q^2), with q = Q / Q_bep.
assumptions: All values are illustrative and were chosen for teaching, not taken from any pump.
Preferred (70-120 % of BEP flow) and allowable (50-125 %) regions are example values only; actual regions are defined by the manufacturer for each pump.
Shaft power near shut-off is an assumed fraction of BEP power (hydraulic power tends to zero there while losses do not).
Water at about 20 deg C; affinity-law scaling for other speeds is approximate.
